title: Harden the privacy and security requirements
body:
Third sweep PR (#18 merged; bases on `main`). `npm run render` succeeds; **411 requirements**, no duplicates, no dangling definitions.

This pass reviewed the document against privacy and security practice rather than against any implementation — asking what the specification *should* require, then checking whether it did.

## It found a defect in the specification itself

**VTI-SES-006** required a node to refuse a challenge to a subject with no entry. **VTI-CLT-016** required a client to report that condition distinguishably from other failures. Together they specified **an enumeration oracle**: a caller who can guess identifiers learns which ones a node holds authority for — the first step in targeting the humans behind them.

Fixed by separating who learns what. The refusal is now uniform to an unauthenticated caller (**VTI-SES-007**), and the client's signal is its own knowledge that it enrolled and has not obtained standing — which the legitimate client has and an attacker probing identifiers does not.

## Privacy

- **Identifiers per relationship; a client identifier never reused across contexts** (VTI-KEY-005–007). An identifier that spans contexts defeats the context boundary without touching a single credential — the observer only has to notice the same name twice. This is the identifier-layer form of the composition privacy requirement.
- **Routing identifiers per relationship** (VTI-TRN-026), because routing is the part a mediator necessarily sees, and shared routing hands it a cross-context activity graph for free. Operation-revealing metadata stays inside the envelope (VTI-TRN-025).
- **Wake notifications carry nothing** (VTI-TRN-028) — a push service is an intermediary nobody in the trust system chose.
- **Herd privacy that is actually a herd** (VTI-CRD-014): an issuer may not allocate status sets per subject, per cohort, or in issuance order. Otherwise the mechanism has the shape of herd privacy and the behaviour of a unique identifier — and the verifier doing the responsible thing generates the signal.
- **Erasure-compatible audit** (VTI-AUD-005): records refer to personal data or commit to it, rather than embedding it, so an erasure leaves the chain verifiable. Tamper-evidence and erasure are in genuine tension and it is resolved at write time or not at all — otherwise an operator is choosing which obligation to breach. Reads of the trail are authorized and audited (VTI-AUD-006); retention has a maximum (VTI-OPR-031).
- **Verifier non-disclosure** (VTI-CRD-043).

## Security

- **Replay** (VTI-OPS-025–027): every document carries a unique identifier and a node remembers what it accepted — **with the record shared across bindings**. A document captured from one binding is well-formed, signed and addressed on another; without a shared record, replay protection is as good as the least-used transport.
- **Downgrade** (VTI-OPS-046/047): discovery responses are authenticated, and every operation has a version floor a peer cannot argue a node below. Without the floor, retiring a version is advisory — every peer claiming not to have upgraded is served anyway, which is exactly the claim an attacker makes.
- **Refusals as answers** (VTI-OPS-035): a refusal distinguishing *not found* from *not permitted* turns an authorization boundary into a directory.
- **The signing oracle** (VTI-VTA-004–007): a VTA parses and constrains what it signs, checks issuer/audience/subject against the requesting entry's authority, records what it signed for whom, and **never signs opaque octets**. An oracle that signs anything is a general-purpose forgery service for its principal — and blind signing removes every bound at once, invisibly, because the signature is indistinguishable from an intended one. This is what makes delegating to an agent survivable.
- **What-you-see-is-what-you-sign** (VTI-APV-013): what the approver is shown is derived from the octets that are digested. Where display and digest come from different structures, the human approved a document that need not exist — and the whole ceremony still functions, which is what makes it hard to notice.
- **Two-party creation of unrestricted authority** (VTI-APV-014) — the one grant from which every other grant can be made, including removing the controls that governed it.
- **Retirable algorithms** (VTI-KEY-013), because an algorithm is retired at the moment it is broken, not at the next release.
- **Resource bounds** (VTI-TRN-029), and **containment that preserves evidence** (VTI-OPR-023) — the moment authority is withdrawn is the moment the record becomes evidence.

## Considerations

Security and Privacy Considerations updated to carry the new reasoning, still citing requirements rather than introducing any.

title: Harden the privacy and security requirements (#19)
body:
Harden the privacy and security requirements (#19)

A review of the document against privacy and security practice, rather
than against the behaviour of any implementation. Twenty-eight
requirements added across nine chapters, and one existing requirement
corrected.

The correction first. VTI-SES-006 required a node to refuse a challenge
to a subject with no entry, and VTI-CLT-016 required a client to report
that condition distinguishably — which together specified an
enumeration oracle: a caller who can guess identifiers learns which
ones a node holds authority for. The refusal is now uniform to an
unauthenticated caller (VTI-SES-007), and the client's signal is its
own knowledge that it enrolled and has not obtained standing, which an
attacker probing identifiers does not have.

Privacy: identifiers per relationship, and never a client identifier
reused across contexts, since an identifier that spans contexts defeats
the context boundary without touching a credential; routing identifiers
per relationship, so an intermediary cannot reconstruct activity across
contexts from routing alone; operation-revealing metadata kept inside
the envelope; wake notifications that carry nothing to the push
service; status sets large enough to be a herd and not allocated in a
way that reconstructs the identification; verifier non-disclosure; an
audit trail that refers to personal data rather than embedding it, so
erasure leaves the chain verifiable, with reads authorized and audited
and retention capped.

Security: document identifiers and a replay record shared across every
binding, since a document captured from one binding is well-formed on
another; authenticated discovery and a per-operation version floor a
peer cannot argue a node below; refusals that do not disclose the
existence of what the caller may not see; a signing oracle that parses
and constrains what it signs and never signs opaque octets; the
approver seeing the octets that are digested; a second party required
to create unrestricted authority; retirable algorithms; resource
bounds; and containment that suspends authority without destroying the
record of what was done.

title: feat(vta): a key can be marked as never leaving the VTA
body:
The VTA releases private keys to entitled callers — that is what
`vta/contexts/secrets` is for. For some keys that is exactly wrong: the key
signs something whose authority should never be reproducible outside the VTA,
and no future caller, however well authorised, should walk away with it.

Spec: trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#443, in trust-tasks-rs 0.20.2.

## `exportable` on `KeyRecord`

`Some(false)` means every export is refused and the key can only be *used*.

**`None` means exportable**, and it is `Option<bool>` rather than a
`#[serde(default)] bool` for a specific reason: a materialised default would
rewrite absent as an explicit `true` on the next save, turning "never asked"
into "asked and allowed" for every key that predates the member. New keys are
minted `None` for the same reason — recording `Some(true)` would be a claim
nobody made.

It says nothing about recoverability. `vta-backup` reads the `SeedStore`
directly rather than going through `get_key_secret`, so a restricted key still
restores from a whole-VTA backup. If it did not, operators would avoid the flag
for fear of stranding a key, which is the opposite of the intended effect.

## Enforced at the export surface, not the use surface

The check is in `get_key_secret` — the one place a private key leaves. Its
callers are `seeds/export-mnemonic`, `build_did_secrets_bundle` (and so
`vta/contexts/secrets`), and the operator's CLI export prompt.

`get_key_secret_internal` is deliberately **not** gated. That is the *use*
surface: it loads a key so the VTA can sign or decrypt with it, and nothing it
returns reaches a caller. A key that may not leave may still be used, and gating
it there would break the VTA's own signing while protecting nothing.

I checked this rather than assumed it — the four `did_webvh.rs` call sites of
`get_key_secret` look like internal signing and are not: two sit behind an
explicit "Export DID secrets bundle?" prompt, two are tests.

## The asymmetry is the feature

- Imposing (`exportable: false`) needs admin of the key's context.
- Lifting (`false` -> `true`) needs that **and** one of: super-admin, or a live
  step-up on the session.

A restriction that whoever imposed it can lift again protects against accident
but not against a compromised caller holding that party's credentials — which is
the case the restriction exists for. The spec requires "strictly stronger" and
deliberately does not name a mechanism (SPEC §7.3 item 13 forbids a spec from
mandating a step-up), so choosing these two is this VTA's policy; either
satisfies it.

Offering both matters operationally: a deployment with no super-admin session to
hand can still recover a key by stepping up, and one with no step-up policy can
still do it as super-admin. Requiring only one would strand somebody. The
refusal names both routes, because a caller told only "forbidden" cannot tell
which is open to it.

Only a real `false` -> `true` transition meets the stronger gate. Re-asserting
`true` on an open key takes nothing away, and gating it would demand super-admin
for a no-op — making a retried request harder to complete than the original.

Eight tests, including the one that matters: the context admin that restricted a
key cannot release it again.

## Ledgers

All four that had an opinion last time: published spec (0.20.2), retry safety
(`RetrySafe` — the state is absolute, so a retry converges rather than toggling),
the MCP risk census (`Sensitive`, beside the other custody operations — the verb
rule would read `set-exportability` as an ordinary mutation), and a conformance
witness built by serialising the real response type, which is what catches the
`key` wrapper the spec requires.

title: Make the task catalogue the API, and factor the shared components
body:
Second sweep PR (#17 merged; this bases on `main`). `npm run render` succeeds; 383 requirements, no duplicates, no dangling definitions.

## The framing change

The chapter said *prefer a canonical Trust Task where one exists*. That leaves open the reading that a node may also carry a REST or DIDComm interface of its own — which is how a stack ends up with two authorization paths, two error vocabularies and two versioning stories for one operation.

It now says: **the catalogue is the API, and each transport is a binding of it** (VTI-OPS-001, VTI-OPS-002). There is no REST API *beside* the tasks.

This is not tidiness. Every requirement in this specification about authorization, approval, idempotency and refusal is written once, against the task. Making the task the only surface is what causes those requirements to hold on **every** path into a node rather than on the paths somebody remembered to cover.

The cost is deliberate and worth stating to implementers: adding an operation means adding it to the catalogue, and that means writing down its payload, its refusals, its retry class and the authority it needs. An operation not worth that is not worth exposing.

## Shared components (the reusability ask)

Defined once, referenced everywhere: **envelope, refusal, page request/response, scope filter, idempotency key, the object shapes, and one instant format**.

- VTI-OPS-070/071 — a task may not restate a component; a node may not accept a task-local variant.
- **VTI-OPS-072 — a concept appearing in a second task is promoted to a component *before* that task is published.** The second occurrence is the moment the concept is shown to be general, and the last moment at which promoting it is cheap.
- VTI-OPS-073 — changing a component is changing every task that references it, and is versioned as such.

The failure this prevents is drift between two definitions of one idea: they begin identical, then one gains a binding rule, another a timezone, a third a member the others treat as unknown — and a security rule stated about "the cursor" turns out to hold for four cursors out of six.

## The required catalogue

Closes the placeholder that stood here. Tables by profile — `discovery`, `auth`, `acl`, `contexts`, `keys`, `credentials`, `approvals`, `audit` for Core; `delivery`; and `membership`, `registry`, `recognition` for Community — with the scope-filter and pagination components marked where they apply.

**VTI-OPS-083: every operation states the authority it requires as part of its definition**, not as implementation behaviour. That is what makes a node's authorization surface readable from the catalogue it claims to serve — and what lets VTI-OPR-050's operator questions be answered without reading source.

## Transport bindings

A binding maps the envelope, refusal and payload onto a transport and **defines no operations, adds no members, weakens no document requirement** (VTI-OPS-090–094). Once a binding may add a parameter, that parameter carries either nothing or authority that peers on other bindings cannot express — which makes a node's behaviour depend on how its caller arrived.

## Registries

The extension points had no registration policy, which is how extensibility becomes collisions and private forks. Canonical names require a published specification; private names are namespaced under a domain the definer controls; **no registered name is ever reused with a different meaning** — a retired name keeps it, so a consumer built years after a producer can still rely on what it meant.

## And one closing requirement

**VTI-OPS-110** — a node exposes no behaviour that is not attributable to a defined operation. A header a proxy adds, a parameter one binding accepts, an environment variable that changes an authorization outcome: undocumented inputs are the surface no review covers, because they belong to no definition. This puts them inside the model or removes them.

## Next

**Privacy and security hardening**: pairwise identifiers, metadata minimisation, erasure-compatible audit, blind-signing, what-you-see-is-what-you-sign, cross-transport replay, downgrade protection.

title: State the intended encodings, and add a divergence register
body:
First of three sweep PRs, reviewing the document as a specification that leads the implementation rather than describes it. `npm run render` succeeds; 360 requirements, no duplicate identifiers, no dangling definitions.

## What the sweep found

Three places where the specification had **encoded the implementation's shape and then warned about it**. That is the tell of a document written after the fact: the requirement describes a hazardous encoding accurately, and then adds a second requirement telling implementers not to misread the first.

| Was | Now |
|---|---|
| Act scope *derived* from (role, possibly-empty context list), where empty means everywhere for an administrative role and nowhere for every other — plus VTI-ACL-021 warning callers not to read the list alone | Act scope is an explicit three-valued member (`all` / `none` / non-empty list), independent of role. An empty list is **malformed**, not meaningful (VTI-ACL-020, VTI-ACL-021, VTI-ACL-023) |
| Key narrowing distinguished by absent-vs-empty, with a rule about serializers | An explicit three-valued member, and a general rule beneath it: **no element of authority is derived from the absence of a member, the emptiness of a collection, or a serializer's default** (VTI-ACL-006 – VTI-ACL-008) |
| A context-filtered listing with no direction defaults to `acting-in` | Refused (VTI-ACL-061). There is no safe default: either answers a question the caller did not ask, in a form indistinguishable from the one they did, and the caller most likely to be harmed is performing a revocation |

The verbosity is the point. `"act": "none"` cannot be mistaken for `"act": "all"`, and neither can be produced by a library's default configuration.

## Rationale paragraphs

Several requirements were justified by recounting an implementation defect — *"this requirement records a defect rather than a preference"*, *"a request-only check that had been reporting clean was found to have been…"*. Those now argue from the principle, which is what makes them checkable by someone with no knowledge of our history: transport authentication and document proof answer different questions; a producer-side test measures its own fixtures; a version number that promises nothing cannot be negotiated against.

## Appendix F — divergence register

The evidence moves here rather than being lost. Each entry states what the specification requires, what an implementation is reported to do, and the resolution — seeded across three areas (authority encoding; operations and versioning; transports, sessions and resolution).

Two normative rules keep it honest: **VTI-CNF-014**, a divergence never qualifies a requirement — an implementation listed here does not conform to the requirement listed beside it; and **VTI-CNF-015**, recording a divergence is not an exemption from it. Entries do not name vendors: the register describes behaviour so it is useful to every implementer facing the same question. F.4 says where a change proposal goes instead, because a register that grants exemptions becomes the specification.

## Smaller corrections

- The introduction now states the direction of travel explicitly — this document is written first, and where a system differs it is the system that diverges.
- Depth and segment-length limits are justified as **interoperability constants** (an identifier valid at one node is valid at every node) rather than as inherited implementation values.
- Re-parenting's prohibition is argued from identifier stability rather than "this version does not support it".
- Identifier stability (VTI-CNF-004) now binds **from the first approved version**, so the WG can still revise substance during a Working Draft — which this PR does.
- Appendix A.7's act-scope vectors are rewritten to the explicit form, and the two rows a suite is most likely to omit (empty list, absent member — both refused) are called out.

## Next in the sweep

**#18** Trust Tasks as the API surface, with the shared components factored once. **#19** privacy and security hardening.

title: State the intended encodings, and add a divergence register (#17)
body:
State the intended encodings, and add a divergence register (#17)

The specification carried three shapes in which authority was recovered
from the form of an encoding rather than stated: act scope derived from
a role paired with a possibly-empty context list, key narrowing
distinguished by absent-versus-empty, and a listing direction supplied
by default. Each was described accurately, and each was accompanied by
a requirement warning implementers not to misread it. A warning is what
a specification writes when it is describing an implementation.

These now state the intended shape instead. Act scope is an explicit
three-valued member independent of role, and an empty list is malformed
rather than meaningful. Key narrowing is the same three-valued member,
with a general rule beneath both: no element of authority is derived
from the absence of a member, the emptiness of a collection, or a
serializer's default. A context-filtered listing without a direction is
refused, because neither default is safe and the caller most likely to
be harmed by the wrong one is performing a revocation.

Rationale paragraphs that justified a requirement by recounting an
implementation's defect now argue from the principle instead. The
evidence moves to Appendix F, the divergence register: what this
specification requires, what an implementation is reported to do, and
the resolution. An entry there is a statement about an implementation
and never a qualification of a requirement, and VTI-CNF-014 and
VTI-CNF-015 say so normatively.

The introduction states the direction of travel, the depth and
identifier limits are justified as interoperability constants rather
than implementation choices, and identifier stability is scoped to bind
from the first approved version so the working group can still revise
substance during a Working Draft.

title: Draft appendices A–C and the references
body:
Stacked on #14. `npm run render` succeeds, no dangling definitions.

## Appendix A — client onboarding

Two **mermaid sequence diagrams** (spec-up-t renders them natively): enrolment, and the key roll with **the commit point marked as a line in the diagram** — everything above it is free to fail, and nothing optional may go below it.

A worked example scoping an agent to `acme/eng/team-a/summariser` rather than `acme/eng/team-a`, because authority over a context reaches every descendant and a team-level grant would reach every purpose the team ever adds beneath it.

A failure-case table either side of the commit, including the genuinely unrecoverable one — crash after commit, before persist — which is what VTI-CLT-033 exists to make as small as possible.

Then **test vectors**, for the parts decidable without a running node, each naming the requirement it exercises:

- **Context paths**, valid and invalid, including `acme/..` as a legal ordinary segment (VTI-CTX-014) and the eight-segment maximum.
- **Ancestry** — with the rows a string-prefix implementation gets wrong called out explicitly: `acme` is not an ancestor of `acme-evil`, and `acme/eng` is not an ancestor of `acme/engineering`. An implementation returning true for any row marked false has exactly the defect VTI-CTX-016 prevents.
- **Act scope decode** — whose third row (non-administrative role, empty context set → authorized *nowhere*, not everywhere) is the one that has been implemented backwards. A suite omitting it is not testing VTI-ACL-021.

## Appendix B — access control entry

A representative entry as JSON, a member-by-member table linking each to its requirement, and the two invariants that have been implemented incorrectly *from a correct-looking schema*: an empty scope list means opposite things depending on the role, and a serializer that drops empty collections converts `"allowedKeys": []` (no keys) into absent (every key the scopes reach).

## Appendix C — role and capability annex

The role set and the capability registry, **explicitly marked as a proposal for WG ratification** — the requirements referencing it (VTI-ACL-010/011, VTI-ACL-030–034) are written so the annex can be settled without touching them.

The table records *why* each separation exists, not just that it does: `sign-trust-task` so an agent can sign an envelope without holding the generic oracle; `credential-write` so a consumer can receive credentials without being able to destroy them; `memory-read`/`memory-write` split so a read-only consumer cannot rewrite what it reads. `holder` is the one additive capability, because it reaches above the context tree and deriving it from an administrative role would hand it to every context administrator on upgrade.

## References

The specifications this document binds, normative and informative, with an editorial note that locations and titles are to be confirmed before this leaves Working Draft. Entries are marked *(pending)* where the WG has yet to fix a stable reference — the DTG credentials and Trust Tasks specifications, TSP, the status mechanism, and a citable reference for each composition evidence family.

## After this

The remaining gaps in `STRUCTURE.md` are the ones only the WG can close: editors and the IPR working-group name, ratification of Appendix C, the minimum operation set (needs the catalogue references), and the test suite's governance.

title: feat(vta-sdk): fetch a context's secrets in one call, at Application
body:
`fetch_did_secrets_bundle` now dispatches `vta/contexts/secrets/1.0` instead of
walking the context itself — `get_context`, then `list_keys`, then one
`get_key_secret` per key.

## This fixes a latent bug, not just an N+1

`get_key_secret` dispatches `seeds/export-mnemonic/1.0`, whose handler opens
with `auth.require_admin()` — and `require_admin` demands `Role::Admin`
exactly, not admin *of a context*.

`room-host`'s own onboarding instructions tell the operator:

    vta import-did --did <ephemeral> --role application --context <CONTEXT>

So a host set up exactly as documented would enrol, receive its grant, connect,
and then fail at the secrets fetch with `admin role required`. It has never
worked as written; the only way to run it was to grant global Admin — authority
over every other context in the VTA — to a process that wanted the keys of one.

The new task is `require_write()` (Application or higher) plus `require_context`
on the context asked for, so the documented grant is now the grant that works.
`room-host` needs no change: it calls `fetch_did_secrets_bundle`, which is the
seam.

## The other two things the walk got wrong

- The kid-selection rule (`select_secret_kid`) had to be applied by every
  caller, so a second implementation could quietly disagree about which secrets
  belong to the DID. It now lives on one side of the wire.
- A bundle assembled from N independent answers has no single point at which the
  VTA decided to release it — nothing to audit as one act, and nothing for a
  future "this key may not leave" rule to hook.

## Falling back, and why it is temporary

A VTA older than the task answers `unsupportedType`, and this falls back to the
old walk so a service can be upgraded before the VTA it talks to is. Only that
rejection triggers it: a `Forbidden` must surface as itself rather than send the
caller down a path it is even less entitled to, and there is a test for that.

The fallback is the last caller of `seeds/export-mnemonic`. One of the tests
asserts it still reaches that URI — so when that assertion has nothing to find,
the fallback and the task can both go.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.20.2
body:
### Specifications

- **keys**: A key can be marked as never leaving its custodian ([#443](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/443))

A custodian holds private keys and will release some of them to an entitled
  caller — that is what `vta/contexts/secrets` exists for. For some keys that is
  exactly wrong: the key signs something whose authority should never be
  reproducible outside the custodian, and no future caller, however well
  authorised, should be able to walk away with it.

  Two parts.

  **`exportable` on the shared `KeyRecord`.** `false` means the custodian refuses
  every export of the key and serves only *uses* of it — signing, key agreement —
  so the material never leaves.

  Absence means the key may be exported. That is the permissive reading and it is
  deliberate: it is what every record written before this member existed already
  meant, so a custodian adding the member cannot silently retract access its
  callers already have. Stated in prose, and **no JSON Schema `default` is
  declared** — a declared default is materialised by the bindings, the field
  becomes non-optional, and an absent member would reappear as an explicit `true`
  on re-serialisation, breaking round-trip idempotence for every existing record.
  The generated field is `Option<bool>`, which is the check that this was done
  right. There is a `$comment` in the schema saying so, because the mistake is
  easy to make twice.

  The member also does not speak to recoverability: a custodian's whole-store
  backup is a different mechanism from an export to a caller. If it did, operators
  would avoid the flag for fear of stranding a key, which would be the opposite of
  the intended effect.

  **`keys/set-exportability/0.1`** changes it. The substance is in Authorization,
  and it is one rule:

  > A consumer **MUST** require strictly stronger authorization to set
  > `exportable: true` on a key that currently carries `false` than it requires to
  > set `false` in the first place.

  That asymmetry is the whole value of the member. A restriction the party who
  imposed it can lift unilaterally protects against accident but not against a
  compromised caller holding that party's credentials — which is the case the
  restriction exists for. Because the directions are checked differently, reaching
  the authority that can impose it does not reach the authority that can remove it.

  What "strictly stronger" is made of is left to the consumer — a second approver,
  an operator with authority the ordinary administrator lacks, a
  re-authentication are all reasonable — because §7.3 item 13 forbids a
  specification from declaring that consent, approval or a step-up is required.
  What this spec constrains is the *relation* between the two entitlements, not
  the mechanism behind either.

  `exportable` is an absolute state, not a toggle, so a producer that retries a
  request whose reply was lost lands where it asked rather than the opposite; the
  task is idempotent and "already in this state" is explicitly not a conflict.
  One of the nine negative fixtures is a `toggle` member, and another is
  `"exportable": "false"` — truthy in several languages, and the most dangerous
  possible misreading of this task.

  Response wraps the record in `key` to match `keys/show` and `keys/create`;
  `keys:notFound` is the family code from the category conventions, and
  `permissionDenied` stays the standard one, named in prose as §3 of those
  conventions requires.

title: Draft the terminology and introduction chapters
body:
Continues filling the gaps listed in `STRUCTURE.md`. `npm run render` succeeds, and for the first time reports **no dangling definitions** — including the two template stubs that came with the boilerplate.

## Terminology

**29 term definitions** written with the Spec-Up-T glossary tooling, in `spec/terms-definitions/`: verifiable trust agent, trust context, context path, principal, operator, subject, access control entry, role, capability, act scope, approve scope, super-administrator, context administrator, approver, client, bootstrap identity, delegate, trust task, mediator, host service, trust registry, step-up, assurance level, consent, member, recognition, composition, composition-owned requirement, indeterminate.

They are **cross-linked to each other**, so the glossary reads as one model rather than an alphabetical list — a reader who lands on `approver` is one hop from `approve scope`, `act scope` and `consent`. Each definition carries the distinguishing rule rather than a paraphrase of the name: *act scope* records that an empty context set means everywhere for an administrative role and nowhere for every other; *bootstrap identity* records that it is low-trust by construction; *consent* records that it is never satisfied by elevating the requester's session.

The chapter also states the two distinctions that have produced defects when conflated: **delegation is not authority** — being able to execute an operation is evidence about capability and none about whether it was granted — and **an attribute is an attribute**, since the word means something else one layer down in at least one implementation's vocabulary.

## Introduction

What the specification covers and does not; a **vocabulary paragraph** that walks the whole model in the order a reader meets it (principal → VTA → contexts → client → entry → delegate → bootstrap identity → the two administrator shapes → step-up and consent → mediators and hosts → VTC, members, registry, recognition → composition and indeterminacy); the four-part structure with what each part binds; how requirements are identified and why identifiers are permanent; why rationale paragraphs are kept in a normative document; and a table routing a reader to the chapters their purpose actually needs.

## Remaining

Appendices A, B and C; the references; the minimum operation set; editors and the IPR working-group name.

title: chore(deps): align with the VTA on main — trust-tasks 0.19.4, tdk 0.13
body:
The gateway resolved `trust-tasks-rs 0.17.3`, two generations behind the
VTA it enrols with and calls. Two shapes had moved underneath it, both on
paths this crate uses and both fatal at the client rather than refused by
the agent, because every generated response type is
`#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`:

  - `auth/whoami/0.1` gained a REQUIRED `capabilities` member in 0.18.
  - `provision/integration/0.3`'s `ProvisionSummary` gained `adminScope`
    and `context`.

A VTA built from main emits all three unconditionally, so a 0.17 client
fails to deserialise a reply that is entirely well-formed.

The four crates move together because `trust-tasks-rs` is a *public*
dependency of `affinidi-messaging-sdk` — its version is part of that
crate's API — so a partial bump puts two `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in the
graph and fails on `expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`.
No semver check catches that; it arrives through a public dependency.

The target is the newest set the published `vta-sdk 0.35.0` admits, which
is not the newest that exists. Main has since moved to `trust-tasks-rs
0.20.1` / `affinidi-tdk 0.14`, but vta-sdk 0.35.0 requires `^0.19.4` and
`^0.13`, so pinning 0.20.1 beside it would reintroduce the two-node split
this bump closes. That gap is wire-safe: 0.19.4 -> 0.20.1 adds
`vta/contexts/secrets` and tightens `process-attestation`, and this crate
calls neither.

  trust-tasks-rs                      0.17 -> 0.19.4
  affinidi-tdk                        0.10 -> 0.13
  affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service   0.5 -> 0.7
  (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.23 arrives transitively)

Not one source file changes. Lockfile holds exactly one node of each of
the four. 28/28 tests pass.

title: chore(deps): align with the VTA on main — vta-sdk 0.35, trust-tasks 0.19.4
body:
The plugin resolved `trust-tasks-rs 0.17.3` / `vta-sdk 0.31`, two
generations behind the VTA it stores memories in. Two response shapes had
moved underneath it, both fatal at the client rather than refused by the
agent, because every generated response type is
`#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`:

  - `auth/whoami/0.1` gained a REQUIRED `capabilities` member in 0.18.
  - `provision/integration/0.3`'s `ProvisionSummary` gained `adminScope`
    and `context`.

A VTA built from main emits all three unconditionally, so enrolment and
every session check fail on a reply that is entirely well-formed.

Most of this is the lockfile rather than the manifests. `vti-secrets` was
pinned at 0.3.0 though the requirement already admitted 0.3.4, and it
dragged `vti-common 0.15` -> `vta-sdk 0.31` -> `tdk 0.10` in beside the
new set, which is the two-node `trust-tasks-rs` graph that fails on
`expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. `affinidi-tsp` was
likewise stale at 0.1.14, which does not carry the `advertises_tsp` that
`affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.23` calls.

  vta-sdk         0.31   -> 0.35
  vti-common      0.15.0 -> 0.18.2   (lock)
  vti-secrets     0.3.0  -> 0.3.4    (lock)
  affinidi-tsp    0.1.14 -> 0.1.16   (lock)
  trust-tasks-rs  0.17.3 -> 0.19.4   (transitive)
  affinidi-tdk    0.10   -> 0.13     (transitive)

One source change: `CreateAclRequest` gained `capabilities`, the ACL
narrowing member. It is set empty, which leaves the entry holding
everything `AGENT_ROLE` implies — exactly what it held before the member
existed. Narrowing it to what this plugin actually exercises is worth
doing and is deliberately not done here: it changes the grant, not the
pin.

Lockfile holds exactly one node of each. 95/95 tests pass, clippy clean.

title: chore(deps): @openvtc/trust-tasks 0.17.8 -> 0.19.1
body:
The binding was two minors behind the spec registry the VTA serves. This
is a correctness and coverage bump rather than a repair: unlike the Rust
consumers, nothing here was breaking.

Why the Rust side broke and this did not. `auth/whoami/0.1` gained a
REQUIRED `capabilities` member and `provision/integration/0.3`'s
`ProvisionSummary` gained `adminScope` and `context`. Every generated
Rust response type is `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`, so a stale client
fails to deserialise a reply that is entirely well-formed. TypeScript
types erase at runtime, so the same reply simply arrives with fields the
types do not name.

The one place that could have refused it is the validator seam in
`trust-tasks/validate.ts`, which does enforce `additionalProperties`
against a bundled `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`. It is wired only to the inbound
`task-consent/request/0.1` path, and that spec is byte-identical across
this range, so no validated document changed shape.

What the bump buys: `provision/integration/0.3` types that name
`adminScope` and `context`, so a caller can set the first and read the
second instead of hand-rolling them; and the task families added since
0.17 — `persona/facet/*`, `persona/claim-types/list` and the `rooms/*`
set — addressable by their generated Type URIs rather than by string.

Build and the full workspace test run are green. `dist/` is gitignored,
so nothing generated is carried in this commit.

title: Draft the operational, considerations and conformance chapters
body:
Stacked on #12. Completes the drafting sequence — with this merged, every chapter of the specification is drafted and the document holds **356 numbered requirements** across 17 areas, with no duplicate identifiers. `npm run render` succeeds.

## Operational and assurance (`OPR`, 19)

Bootstrap without a cleartext shared secret, with the unauthenticated first-authority path closed after use and its use audited. Protection at rest, including that the protecting material is not stored where obtaining the data obtains the means to decrypt it. Audit retention, and **VTI-OPR-032**: an auditor can reconstruct who held what authority at a past moment — which is what makes every other record interpretable, since an action recorded without the authority that permitted it can be read but not assessed.

**Containment does not depend on the cooperation of the component being contained** (VTI-OPR-022). An agent that must acknowledge its own kill switch is contained only while it is behaving, which is the state in which containment is not needed.

**VTI-OPR-050** lists the five questions a deployment must be able to answer about itself — who holds authority where; what each agent may do and has done; which operations need another human, who can supply it, and whether it can currently be satisfied; what stops working if this credential is withdrawn now; which policy version governed a past decision. Each is asked for the first time during an incident, and a deployment that cannot answer then will not acquire the ability while the incident runs.

## Considerations

All five ToIP-required sections, written as numbered items citing the requirements that carry them rather than introducing new ones (and carrying no RFC keywords, since they are informative).

Two are more than pro forma:

- **Internationalization** records *why* context segments are restricted ASCII compared octet by octet: confusability on an authorization boundary is prevented by restriction, and normalization is itself a source of confusability.
- **Accessibility** is substantive. Three normative requirements depend on a human understanding what they are authorising. An approval a person cannot perceive or comprehend is not consent, and a control built on one fails in the direction that looks like success — the record shows an approval, and what happened was someone clicking past something they could not read.

## Conformance (`CNF`, 18)

- **Five profiles** (`Core`, `Delivery`, `Community`, `Composition`, `Operations`) mapped to chapters, and a target-by-profile table.
- **A claim states** the spec version, the targets, the profiles, and any OPTIONAL behaviour a peer may rely on — and may not be made for a subset of a profile.
- **Coverage** (VTI-CNF-006): a requirement with no test is recorded as a defect *in this specification*, not as a shortcoming of an implementation. A requirement nobody can test is one nobody can be held to, and the gap is invisible from inside the document.
- **The assessment interface** (D4): cited requirement identifier, disposition of `supported`/`refuted`/`indeterminate`, method, artefacts, assessor, date — and for a composition property, the components and versions composed.
- **What an assessment cannot do**: no normative authority, no alteration of conformance status, only the WG converts an open proposition into a requirement, and **two assessments that disagree are both recorded** (VTI-CNF-023). Recording only the preferred disposition destroys the more useful of the two facts.

## STRUCTURE.md

Now carries a chapter status table and an explicit list of known gaps — editors and the IPR working-group name, Appendix A/B/C, the minimum operation set, the references, and the test suite's location and governance. Each is deliberate rather than overlooked.

title: spec(keys): a key can be marked as never leaving its custodian
body:
A custodian holds private keys and will release some of them to an entitled
caller — that is what `vta/contexts/secrets` exists for. For some keys that is
exactly wrong: the key signs something whose authority should never be
reproducible outside the custodian, and no future caller, however well
authorised, should be able to walk away with it.

Two parts.

**`exportable` on the shared `KeyRecord`.** `false` means the custodian refuses
every export of the key and serves only *uses* of it — signing, key agreement —
so the material never leaves.

Absence means the key may be exported. That is the permissive reading and it is
deliberate: it is what every record written before this member existed already
meant, so a custodian adding the member cannot silently retract access its
callers already have. Stated in prose, and **no JSON Schema `default` is
declared** — a declared default is materialised by the bindings, the field
becomes non-optional, and an absent member would reappear as an explicit `true`
on re-serialisation, breaking round-trip idempotence for every existing record.
The generated field is `Option<bool>`, which is the check that this was done
right. There is a `$comment` in the schema saying so, because the mistake is
easy to make twice.

The member also does not speak to recoverability: a custodian's whole-store
backup is a different mechanism from an export to a caller. If it did, operators
would avoid the flag for fear of stranding a key, which would be the opposite of
the intended effect.

**`keys/set-exportability/0.1`** changes it. The substance is in Authorization,
and it is one rule:

> A consumer **MUST** require strictly stronger authorization to set
> `exportable: true` on a key that currently carries `false` than it requires to
> set `false` in the first place.

That asymmetry is the whole value of the member. A restriction the party who
imposed it can lift unilaterally protects against accident but not against a
compromised caller holding that party's credentials — which is the case the
restriction exists for. Because the directions are checked differently, reaching
the authority that can impose it does not reach the authority that can remove it.

What "strictly stronger" is made of is left to the consumer — a second approver,
an operator with authority the ordinary administrator lacks, a
re-authentication are all reasonable — because §7.3 item 13 forbids a
specification from declaring that consent, approval or a step-up is required.
What this spec constrains is the *relation* between the two entitlements, not
the mechanism behind either.

`exportable` is an absolute state, not a toggle, so a producer that retries a
request whose reply was lost lands where it asked rather than the opposite; the
task is idempotent and "already in this state" is explicitly not a conflict.
One of the nine negative fixtures is a `toggle` member, and another is
`"exportable": "false"` — truthy in several languages, and the most dangerous
possible misreading of this task.

Response wraps the record in `key` to match `keys/show` and `keys/create`;
`keys:notFound` is the family code from the category conventions, and
`permissionDenied` stays the standard one, named in prose as §3 of those
conventions requires.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: Draft the credentials, VTC, membership and registry chapters
body:
Stacked on #11. Retarget down the stack as each merges. `npm run render` succeeds.

The community half of Part C, plus the credentials chapter it rests on. 58 requirements across four areas.

## Credentials and presentations (`CRD`, 16)

- **Status that cannot be determined is indeterminate** (VTI-CRD-012), not valid and not revoked.
- **A status query must not identify the credential or subject to the party answering** (VTI-CRD-013) — otherwise the issuer learns, on every use, which of its subjects is transacting and roughly with whom. The privacy cost is paid by the subject and collected by the issuer, precisely because the verifier did the responsible thing.
- **Presenter binding is established by the protocol, never declared in the payload** (VTI-CRD-021), with a single-use verifier-bound challenge (VTI-CRD-022). Without proof of possession a credential is a bearer token: whoever captures it — relayed exchange, audit log, compromised device — holds a replayable impersonation. The credential formats do not make this mistake; compositions do, by treating a valid signature over a valid credential as an authenticated session.

## The Verifiable Trust Community (`VTC`, 12)

Provisioned on a VTA, one-way dependency. **VTI-VTC-012 enumerates what the VTC owns** — admission, membership state, recognition, publication — and nothing else in this specification, which is the section that stops a decision having two plausible owners and no actual one.

VTI-VTC-013 says a VTC makes no key-custody decisions for members, and the rationale is the design principle behind the whole split: the VTA holds the material whose compromise is unrecoverable, the VTC holds relationships that can be re-established. A compromised community can wrongly admit, wrongly remove and wrongly recognise — all serious, all recoverable — and cannot take a member's keys.

Also: the community expresses its authority model using the common one rather than a parallel model (VTI-VTC-020), and records which policy version governed a decision (VTI-VTC-031).

## Membership lifecycle (`MEM`, 18)

- **Admission is a decision, not the completion of a join exchange** (VTI-MEM-011).
- **Paired credentials commit over the exact transmitted form** (VTI-MEM-021). A commitment computed over a parsed and re-serialized form covers only what survived the round trip — a status member the parser did not recognise, an ordering it normalised — so an artefact can be altered in exactly those members without disturbing the proof.
- **An erasure disposition community policy cannot downgrade** (VTI-MEM-032), and **batched publication must not delay status** (VTI-MEM-034): batching is a legitimate measure against timing correlation, but applying the same delay to status leaves a departed member's credentials being accepted.
- **Rotation is not a transfer** (VTI-MEM-042). Rotation and transfer are the same operation on the wire and differ only in whether the same person is on the other end; proof of control from the new identifier does not distinguish them, so the prohibition is stated separately. A community that permits transfer by rotation has a membership that can be sold.

## Registries and recognition (`REG`, 12)

- **Unavailability is not absence** (VTI-REG-012) — collapsing them either admits parties never recognised or refuses parties that were, decided by an error handler rather than by policy.
- **Recognition requires proof of possession** (VTI-REG-020), since recognition is the flow in which a bearer-shaped credential pair travels furthest from its holder, plus subject agreement, status checked with the issuing community, and explicit role mapping that cannot exceed the local equivalent.
- **Recognition is not transitive** (VTI-REG-024) — it would compose decisions each made about one counterparty into a reach nobody assessed, and the third community never appears in the second's decision.

## Remaining

Operational requirements, the considerations chapter, and the conformance profile detail.

title: Draft the credentials, VTC, membership and registry chapters (#12)
body:
Draft the credentials, VTC, membership and registry chapters (#12)

Credentials and presentations (16): issuance authority; status,
including that an undeterminable status is indeterminate rather than
valid or revoked, and that a status query must not identify the
credential to the party answering it; presentation binding established
by the protocol rather than declared, with a single-use verifier-bound
challenge, because without proof of possession a credential is a bearer
token; what verification does and does not establish; minimisation.

The VTC (12): provisioned on a VTA with a one-way dependency; owns
admission, membership state, recognition and publication, and nothing
else in this specification; creates no contexts, derives no keys and
makes no key-custody decisions for members — the VTA holds the material
whose compromise is unrecoverable, the VTC holds relationships that can
be re-established; expresses its authority model using the common one
rather than a parallel model; and records which version of a policy
governed a decision.

Membership lifecycle (18): states and audited transitions; admission as
a decision distinct from the exchange that requests it; paired
membership credentials committing over the exact transmitted form,
because a commitment over a re-serialized form covers only what
survived the parser; suspension reflected in status; an erasure
disposition that a community policy cannot downgrade; batched
publication that must not delay status; renewal and rotation, with
rotation prohibited as a route to transferring membership.

Registries and recognition (12): what an entry asserts and what it does
not; unavailability is not absence; recognition with proof of
possession, subject agreement, status checked with the issuing
community, explicit role mapping; and recognition is not transitive.

Adds the CRD, VTC, MEM and REG areas to the conformance area registry.

title: chore(deps): align with the VTA on main — vta-sdk 0.35, trust-tasks 0.19.4
body:
chore(deps): align with the VTA on main — vta-sdk 0.35, trust-tasks 0.19.4

The plugin resolved `trust-tasks-rs 0.17.3` / `vta-sdk 0.31`, two
generations behind the VTA it stores memories in. Two response shapes had
moved underneath it, both fatal at the client rather than refused by the
agent, because every generated response type is
`#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`:

  - `auth/whoami/0.1` gained a REQUIRED `capabilities` member in 0.18.
  - `provision/integration/0.3`'s `ProvisionSummary` gained `adminScope`
    and `context`.

A VTA built from main emits all three unconditionally, so enrolment and
every session check fail on a reply that is entirely well-formed.

Most of this is the lockfile rather than the manifests. `vti-secrets` was
pinned at 0.3.0 though the requirement already admitted 0.3.4, and it
dragged `vti-common 0.15` -> `vta-sdk 0.31` -> `tdk 0.10` in beside the
new set, which is the two-node `trust-tasks-rs` graph that fails on
`expected MediatorAcl, found a different MediatorAcl`. `affinidi-tsp` was
likewise stale at 0.1.14, which does not carry the `advertises_tsp` that
`affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.23` calls.

  vta-sdk         0.31   -> 0.35
  vti-common      0.15.0 -> 0.18.2   (lock)
  vti-secrets     0.3.0  -> 0.3.4    (lock)
  affinidi-tsp    0.1.14 -> 0.1.16   (lock)
  trust-tasks-rs  0.17.3 -> 0.19.4   (transitive)
  affinidi-tdk    0.10   -> 0.13     (transitive)

One source change: `CreateAclRequest` gained `capabilities`, the ACL
narrowing member. It is set empty, which leaves the entry holding
everything `AGENT_ROLE` implies — exactly what it held before the member
existed. Narrowing it to what this plugin actually exercises is worth
doing and is deliberately not done here: it changes the grant, not the
pin.

Lockfile holds exactly one node of each. 95/95 tests pass, clippy clean.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: Draft the keys, transports, sessions and VTA chapters
body:
Stacked on #10. Retarget down the stack as each merges. `npm run render` succeeds.

Completes Part B of the common model and adds the first node chapter. 82 requirements across four areas.

## Identity, DIDs and key management (`KEY`, 24)

D7 as normative text: `did:webvh` for the durable identity of a VTA, VTC or host; `did:key` for client bootstrap; everything else optional and never assumable of a peer. VTI-KEY-004 states the *properties* the durable position depends on — resolution by a stranger, verifiable update history, key rotation without identifier change, deactivation — so a future method is evaluated against the requirement rather than the name. Curve25519 mandatory to implement.

The caching rules carry a specific defect: **a resolver may not cache a negative result derived from a transport failure** (VTI-KEY-061). A transport failure is evidence about the network and none at all about the identifier, and the symptom of getting this wrong is an identifier that cannot be resolved long after it can — indistinguishable, downstream, from one that does not exist.

## Transports, messaging and delivery (`TRN`, 17)

- **Transport-independent authorization** (VTI-TRN-002/003): where transports carry different decisions, the weakest one is the node's real policy and nothing records which.
- **Truthful send** (VTI-TRN-030/031): a send resolves successfully only for a message transmitted or durably queued, and hop acceptance is not delivery. This is a defect that has shipped repeatedly in independent implementations for the same reason each time — it makes every layer above it wrong in the same direction.
- **Three classes of delivery evidence in descending strength** (VTI-TRN-040), with the class recorded (VTI-TRN-041): a receiving-layer receipt is the only end-to-end one; a protocol reply; transport evidence of collection. They close different windows, and a sender that records only "delivered" cannot say which window its claim rests on.
- **Escalate on an expired window** (VTI-TRN-042), re-resolving and trying an alternate binding before failing, because a dead mediator is not a dead peer.
- **Re-falsifiable reachability and honest health** (VTI-TRN-052/053): a connection state decided at boot reports green for as long as the process survives, so the signal designed to detect the outage is the reason nobody is looking.

## Sessions and authentication (`SES`, 21)

Challenge entropy, binding and single use; signer equals challenged subject, stated separately from the challenge's own binding because the two are enforced at different moments; **authority re-resolved at authentication and at every refresh**, so revocation takes effect on the timescale of a refresh rather than of the longest-lived session; atomic refresh claim, since a concurrently replayed credential otherwise yields two live sessions from one; assurance preserved across rotation with credential lifetime a function of it; and a maximum session lifetime refresh cannot extend.

## The Verifiable Trust Agent (`VTA`, 20)

- **Operations performed, not keys exported** (VTI-VTA-002) — the distinction that makes revocation meaningful: a caller holding a key keeps it after its authority is withdrawn.
- **Receiving and removing a credential separately gated** (VTI-VTA-011).
- **Sealed provisioning with an out-of-band verification value** (VTI-VTA-030/031): sealing protects the material from the relayer, but does not tell the holder that the bundle they opened is the one sealed for them — and the relayer is exactly the party positioned to substitute.
- **Agents get their own identifier and entry** (VTI-VTA-040): an agent under the principal's own credential cannot be revoked without revoking the principal and cannot be distinguished from them in any audit trail. It is a copy, not a delegate.
- **Restores recorded** (VTI-VTA-051), because a restore silently reinstates entries revoked since the backup.
- **The operator surface** (VTI-VTA-060–062): a control the operator cannot reach belongs to whoever operates the software rather than to the principal it acts for.

## Remaining

Credentials, the two VTC chapters, registries, operational requirements, and the considerations/conformance detail.

title: Draft the keys, transports, sessions and VTA chapters (#11)
body:
Draft the keys, transports, sessions and VTA chapters (#11)

Identity and key management (24): did:webvh required for durable node
identity and did:key for client bootstrap, with the properties the
durable position depends on written down so a future method can be
evaluated against the requirement rather than the name; Curve25519
mandatory to implement; key purposes; derivation bound to the context
tree; rotation; and the negative-cache rule — a transport failure is
evidence about the network and none about the identifier.

Transports and delivery (17): transport-independent authorization;
truthful send, where a send resolves successfully only for a message
transmitted or durably queued; the three classes of delivery evidence
in descending strength, with the class recorded, because acceptance by
a hop is durably-queued and not delivered; escalation on an expired
delivery window, re-resolving before failing because a dead mediator is
not a dead peer; bounded waits; and re-falsifiable reachability, since
a connection state decided at boot reports green for as long as the
process survives.

Sessions (21): challenge binding and single use; signer equals
challenged subject; authority re-resolved at authentication and at
every refresh; atomic refresh claim; assurance preserved across
rotation and credential lifetime a function of it; a maximum session
lifetime refresh cannot extend.

The VTA (20): custody, and operations performed rather than keys
exported, which is what makes revocation meaningful; receiving and
removing a credential separately gated; sealed provisioning with an
out-of-band verification value, because sealing protects the material
from the relayer but does not tell the holder the bundle is theirs;
agents with their own identifier and entry, since an agent under the
principal's credential is a copy rather than a delegate; backup and
restore recorded; and the operator surface.

Adds the KEY, TRN, SES and VTA areas to the conformance area registry.

title: Draft the composition-requirements chapter
body:
Stacked on #9. Retarget down the stack as each merges. `npm run render`
succeeds.

Step 5 of the drafting sequence: the chapter the RAHP composition work feeds.
38 requirements (`VTI-CMP-*`), each stating a property of the composed
interaction that no single component can establish.

## What frames the chapter

Two structural requirements do most of the work:

- **VTI-CMP-001** — a component's conformance to its own specification does not
  satisfy anything in this chapter. The failure this chapter exists to prevent
  is not a component behaving incorrectly; it is every component behaving
  correctly and the system built from them holding a property none of them
  held.
- **VTI-CMP-002** — a claim against the Composition profile states the evidence
  relied on, per requirement.

## The requirements

- **Composition integrity** — a property established by one component is not
  assumed to survive composition with another.
- **Semantic completion** — protocol success is not the trust outcome, and an
  implementation has to distinguish the two *in what it reports*, because a
  relying party told only "completed" will take the stronger reading.
- **Authority ≠ verification** — six steps kept distinguishable (identity,
  authentication, credential verification, authority, authorisation, trust
  decision); authority established at decision time from a source entitled to
  answer for it, never inferred from signature validity.
- **Currency of state** — evidence of currency carries the time currency was
  determined, with a stated freshness bound; beyond it the outcome is
  indeterminate rather than the last known state. Each component in a flow may
  be reading a different vintage of the same fact.
- **Delegation lineage** — no deriving authority from protocol capability;
  scope, lineage, expiry, revocation and re-delegation determinable; and
  **VTI-CMP-053**, that the acting delegate's identity reaches the point of
  decision. A component that substitutes principal for delegate produces a flow
  where every artefact is valid and "who actually did this" has no answer at
  the far end.
- **Privacy across composition** — evaluated over the whole interaction;
  durable correlators from naming, routing, lookup and session management
  identified, not just those from credentials. An unlinkable proof beside a
  stable agent name, over an observable route, after a revealing registry
  lookup, is a linkable interaction containing an unlinkable proof.
- **False independence** — the seven threat classes as one unsafe inference,
  with the table of what each wrongly upgrades. Independence established by
  evidence, not inferred from separate identification; completeness of a
  presentation considered separately from validity; and where neither can be
  established, indeterminate rather than corroborated.

  **VTI-CMP-074 carries the other boundary** — legitimate plurality,
  pseudonymity, shared infrastructure, coalitions, independent agreement and
  selective disclosure are not adversarial merely for resembling the patterns.
  It is specified as half of the property rather than as a caveat, because a
  system that reads every pseudonym as a sock puppet has not become safer, and
  only one of the two boundaries gets implemented unless both are normative.
- **Indeterminacy** — a first-class outcome, distinct from success and failure;
  a policy states what happens on it per decision class, and where the policy
  is silent the decision is refused. Insufficient evidence and evidence of
  absence are different conditions.
- **Configuration materiality** — same review and audit as a code change; the
  effective configuration that governed a past decision reconstructable; and
  semantics-altering configuration identifiable as such.
- **Component substitution** — properties re-established after a swap;
  conformance of the substituted part does not carry them.
- **Human control** — authorisation bound to the action it authorises, the
  human given enough to understand it, and a delegate unable to satisfy its
  principal's requirement. Restated here because a flow can satisfy every
  node's local rule and still complete without anyone having meaningfully
  decided.

## Appendix E

Now carries the record VTI-CMP-120 requires: the ownership vocabulary
(including why `JOINTLY-OWNED` is not a step toward moving a requirement into
this spec), the family-1 false-independence corpus with its seven preserved
judgments and its current `UNRESOLVED` disposition, and the shape of an
assessment submission — including that two disagreeing submissions are both
recorded.

## Note for the WG

Publishing unresolved propositions with their status visible is deliberate
(D8). Family 1 is recorded as `UNRESOLVED` with strong `COMPOSITION-OWNED`
evidence rather than being asserted as settled, and the informative references
for the source material still need filling in.

title: chore(deps): take the published 0.35 line and delete every patch entry
body:
`did-git-sign` 0.4.8 is published and requires `vta-sdk ^0.35`. That is the release six consecutive minors have been waiting on, and it makes the whole line resolvable from crates.io for the first time since 0.23.

## ⚠️ Upgrade the VTA before this ships

**`vta-sdk` 0.35 refuses an unsigned trust-task reply by default.** An agent predating VTI #1334/#1335 sends no proof, so a client on 0.35 refuses *every* answer it gets — a total outage in the pane, from a change that compiles clean and passes every test in this repo.

- #1334 / #1335 merged **2026-09-09 06:20–06:37Z**
- `vta-service` **0.24.1** published 05:13 that day — **before** the merge, does **not** sign
- `vta-service` **0.25.0** is the first release that does

The only API change between 0.34.1 and 0.35.0 is an *addition* — `VtaClient::trusting_unsigned_replies()` — which exists precisely as the staging hatch for this ordering. The manifest note beside the `vta-sdk` line carries all of it so the next reader does not have to re-derive it under pressure.

This is the same shape as the `provision/integration` 0.3 skew: both halves self-consistent, invisible to CI, fatal in the field.

## The moves

| crate | | |
|---|---|---|
| `vta-sdk` | 0.34.1 → **0.35** | git pin → crates.io |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.18.11 → **0.19.4** | |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.18.5 → **0.19.4** | |
| `affinidi-tdk` | 0.12 → **0.13** | |
| `affinidi-messaging-sdk` | 0.22 → **0.23** | |
| `did-git-sign` | 0.4.6 → **0.4.8** | git pin → crates.io |
| `vta-service` (dev) | 0.24 → **0.25** | |
| `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` (dev) | 0.5.2 → **0.6** | |

**Zero source changes.**

## Every patch entry is gone

`[patch.crates-io]` is **deleted, not emptied**, so reintroducing one is a visible decision rather than a line added to an existing block. `deny.toml`'s `allow-git` list — the other half of the same change, since `unknown-git = "deny"` — goes with it. Both keep a note saying what the block was for and what to do if it is ever needed again.

All three redirects became unnecessary at once:

- **`did-git-sign` / `vgi-core`** — 0.4.8 published on `vta-sdk ^0.35`.
- **`vta-sdk`** — 0.35.0 published carrying `persona/facet/*` (VTI #1338), which that entry existed solely to reach.
- and upstream of both, **`trql-client` 0.17** published, which is what let VGI release at all: `cargo publish` rejects a git dependency outright, so 0.4.7 could never have been cut while VGI held one.

## The edge that nearly got left behind

`trust-tasks-capability-client` declares its own `trust-tasks-rs` requirement, so the first resolve produced **two copies of both** while every other line in the manifest looked correct. `cargo tree -i trust-tasks-rs@0.18.11` named it in one read; `cargo outdated` would not have, because the crate reporting "latest" was not the one pulling the old copy.

Final state: one `vta-sdk`, one `trust-tasks-rs`, one `trust-tasks-capability-client`, no git sources.

## Prose refreshed, not just versions

The manifests carry a lot of load-bearing rationale keyed to specific versions — which line each crate is built against, why two copies break rather than merely duplicate, why the floor must name a patch. All of it is updated to the 0.35 line. The `did-git-sign` note now reads as *the rule has not changed, the cadence did*: VGI still has to move with every sdk minor, and what is new is that `trql-client` shipping let it publish again.

## Checks

`fmt`, `clippy` (default and `--all-features`, `--all-targets`), `test --workspace --all-features`, `test -- --include-ignored` (the MockVta e2es — the ones that actually exercise `vta-service` 0.25), `--no-default-features`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`, and `cargo deny check advisories licenses bans sources`. All green.

Not exercised against a live VTA — which is exactly what the warning at the top is about.

* test(tsp): stop asserting a property of the runner's DNS

`an_unresolvable_did_web_falls_back_rather_than_failing` resolved
`did:web:nothing-seeded.example`, which is a real DNS query. The assertion
holds only when that query fails *fast*: discovery is wrapped in a 5s
timeout, and a timeout reports `Unavailable` rather than the
`NotAdvertised` the fallback produces. A resolver that answers NXDOMAIN
instantly gives one outcome and one that hangs on an unknown TLD gives the
other, so the test was pinning the environment as much as the code.

It failed on a macOS runner in this PR and passes on every machine here,
which is the shape that costs an afternoon later. Nothing in the bump
caused it: `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` 0.8.36 and `affinidi-did-web`
0.1.4 are byte-identical across it, the only networking move is a
`reqwest` patch, and the sibling test — the one using `did:example:`, which
needs no network at all — passed.

Port 1 on 127.0.0.1 is refused by the kernel with no name to look up, so
resolution still fails, still fails fast, and reaches the same fallback
branch the same way everywhere. The comment says why the address is what it
is, because the obvious "tidy-up" is to put a hostname back.

title: Draft the client and operation-surface chapters
body:
Stacked on #8 (architecture + trust contexts), which is stacked on #7 (the
outline). Retarget down the stack as each merges. `npm run render` succeeds.

Chapters 3 and 4 of the drafting sequence: the client, and the operation
surface it calls.

## Client onboarding and lifecycle — `spec/07-clients.md`

40 requirements (`VTI-CLT-*`) across the four steps, written in sequence order
because the order is what carries the security properties.

**Step 1 — mint.** The client generates its own key pair; the private key never
leaves it and a node may not require its disclosure. `did:key` is required here
specifically because this happens before the client has standing, network, or
anywhere to publish. The identifier is recorded as a *bootstrap identity*,
distinguishable in local state from a long-term one.

**Step 2 — enrol.** Least-privilege at creation, enrolling administrator must
hold act authority over the target context, bootstrap identifier treated as
low-trust because it crossed a channel outside the trust system.

Two requirements here address a threat the outline didn't: **the enrolment
channel's weak point is substitution, not disclosure.** An attacker who can
modify the message carrying the identifier can have the administrator enrol an
identifier *they* control — and rotation in Step 3 does not help, since the
substituted identifier simply rotates onto another one the attacker controls.
So: confirm the identifier over a second channel (VTI-CLT-015), and require
that a client refused for want of an entry reports that condition
distinguishably (VTI-CLT-016), so the "legitimate client never got standing"
signal reaches a human instead of looking like an ordinary connection failure.

**Step 3 — roll.** SHOULD, per D2, with the rationale tied to exposure: a
sealed provisioning bundle is a defensible reason not to roll, a DID pasted
into chat is not. The mechanism is REQUIRED of a VTA either way. Then the
sequence: mint → **prove reachability before committing** (a liveness check,
not an authorization one — before the swap the new identifier has no entry at
all; committed to an unreachable identifier the rotation is unrecoverable) →
**atomic swap** with caller-is-current-subject and new-subject-is-proven-holder
bindings and authority preserved exactly → **persist before anything else**.

VTI-CLT-029 and VTI-CLT-030 are what make a self-service operation safe to
expose to the subject itself: without the first it is a self-service
escalation, without the second it is a way to take over someone else's grant.

**Step 4 and lifecycle.** Refresh rather than re-enrol; never treat a past
authorization as evidence for a later request; surface step-up to a human and
never satisfy a consent requirement on one's own behalf; distinguish a refusal
from a transport failure; hold an idempotency key stable. Plus **one identity
per instance, including via machine images** (VTI-CLT-052) — that is how
sharing actually happens, not by a decision to share but by cloning a template
captured after enrolment — and **no entry may be moved to a subject that hasn't
proven control** (VTI-CLT-054), so a lost key is recovered by re-enrolling.

Ends with a conformance checklist splitting the client's requirements from the
node's.

## Operation surface — `spec/08-operations.md`

33 requirements (`VTI-OPS-*`), implementing D3.

- **Precedence** — canonical Trust Task wherever one exists; private interfaces
  only where none does, namespaced so they cannot collide with a future
  canonical task, discoverable, and carrying a retirement path.
- **Extension not divergence** — payloads stay closed so a misspelled member is
  refused rather than ignored; a declared extension slot is the only local
  content, and it confers no authority.
- **The operation document** — and VTI-OPS-021, which records a defect rather
  than a preference: an implementation shipped the consumer half of the rule
  while its producer built unsigned, unaddressed documents on exactly the two
  transports whose sender authentication made the guard look unnecessary. The
  same defect reported a different condition on each transport and was
  diagnosed twice. Transport authentication says who opened the connection;
  document proof says who authored this and what it covers.
- **Responses conform too** (VTI-OPS-031) — a request-only check measures its
  own fixtures. And a condition with no defined code gets a machine-readable
  discriminator rather than a generic failure, "not found" being the recurring
  case.
- **Versioning** — no 0.x exemption (VTI-OPS-041), and **enum-value changes are
  breaking** (VTI-OPS-042). The concrete case: a set of enumerated values
  renamed across two minor bumps with the payload shape untouched — invisible
  to a schema comparison, fatal to every peer. An unsupported version is
  refused explicitly and never left to time out.
- **Policy gate in front of dispatch** (VTI-OPS-050/051) — a requirement
  enforced in handlers is enforced wherever it was remembered.
- **Retry and idempotency** — classify every operation by what a repeat costs;
  unclassified is treated as the most costly class; exactly one retry owner per
  failure domain, and no application-level loop, because a hand-written loop
  cannot hold a key stable and so converts one operation retried into several
  operations performed.

## Left open

The minimum operation set per profile is still an instruction — it needs the
canonical catalogue references settled first.

title: Draft the client and operation-surface chapters (#9)
body:
Draft the client and operation-surface chapters (#9)

Client onboarding and lifecycle: 40 requirements over the four-step
sequence. Mint client-side, with the private key never leaving the
client and the identifier recorded as a bootstrap identity; enrol
least-privilege, with the bootstrap identifier treated as low-trust
because it crossed a channel outside the trust system; roll the key
(SHOULD, per D2) with reachability proven before the commit, an atomic
swap that preserves authority exactly, and nothing optional between the
commit and the persist; then steady-state use and lifecycle.

Two threats are addressed explicitly. Enrolment-channel substitution is
not solved by rotation, so it is met with second-channel confirmation
and a requirement that a client refused for want of an entry says so
distinguishably. Shared client identity is prohibited including via
machine images, which is how sharing usually happens.

exists, private interfaces namespaced and temporary (D3); closed
payloads with a declared extension slot rather than local members; the
operation document, including the requirement that a sender-authenticated
transport does not relieve a producer of signing; response conformance
as well as request conformance; versioning with no 0.x exemption and
enum-value changes as breaking; the policy gate in front of dispatch;
and retry classification with exactly one retry owner per failure
domain.
