title: feat(console): hide sensitive fact values behind a per-fact Show
body:
The persona pane draws the holder's own facts, so a passport number, a mobile
number and a date of birth sit on screen for as long as the pane is open —
through a screen share, a screenshot pasted into an issue, and anyone walking
past the desk. Which of those is sensitive is a property of the claim type, and
the claim-type registry now says so.

## What this is, precisely

**Client-side masking is not a security control.** By the time any of this code
runs, the console has already called `persona/attribute/list`, the agent has
already answered, and the value is a string in a React tree that every script on
this origin, every screenshot and every screen recording can reach. Masking it
afterwards changes what is *drawn*, not what was *fetched*.

What it does defend against is the whole of what it claims: shoulder-surfing,
screenshots, a support call where the console is shared. Those are real, and
they are the entire scope.

**The control that would matter does not exist yet.** It is a read-path one — an
`includeSensitive` flag on `persona/attribute/list`, so a listing that did not
ask for sensitive values is answered without them and the console never holds
the string. `CLAIM-TYPES.md` §3.1 says the same thing in one sentence: *"Masking
a value already fetched is theatre. The control that matters is on the read
path; the mask is what makes the control visible."* Until that flag exists in
the spec and the agent, this PR ships the visible half of a control whose
enforcing half is missing. The module doc says so at length, so that nobody
reviewing this in six months mistakes one for the other, and no UI string in it
implies the console does not hold what it hides.

## The table is vendored

`packages/extension/src/manager/claim-sensitivity.ts` carries a hand-copied
`sensitivity` + `mask` table from
`dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/specs/persona/_shared/0.1/claim-types.json`
(`registryVersion` 0.1, draft/in review). Vendored because the agent does not
serve it: `persona/claim-types/list` is an open question in `CLAIM-TYPES.md` §6,
deliberately deferred until the first extension type ships, and clients ship the
table statically until then. The source file and version are named in the module
doc so a re-sync is a diff rather than a rewrite, and only the two members this
console reads are transcribed — a copy reproducing `release`, `oidc` and
`minimumSet` would look like a client that acts on them.

Mask styles are the registry's own: `none` / `last2` / `last4` / `emailLocal` /
`full`, rendered as the registry's own examples (`•••• 4242`,
`a•••@example.com`). Two decisions the registry leaves to the renderer:

- **The bullet run is fixed width, not one glyph per hidden character.**
  Per-character publishes the length of every value the mask exists to hide, and
  length is a real hint for a card number, a passport number or a postcode.
- **A value no longer than its own tail is masked in full.** "The last four of a
  four-character value" is the value, so honouring `last4` literally would
  render the whole secret and call it masked. Same for `emailLocal` over
  something that is not an address.

## The conservative default, and the prefix walk that isn't there

An unregistered or `x:`-prefixed token resolves to `high` / `full` — §4 rule 3,
because a vocabulary nobody has reasoned about is exactly the one where showing
the value is a decision nobody made. `x:` is tested before the lookup, so
`x:payment.card` cannot borrow `payment.card`'s `last4`.

There is deliberately **no prefix fallback**, and its absence is the registry's
rather than a shortcut here — see the findings below. Inventing the walk locally
would make this console *less* careful than the registry asks: an unregistered
`payment.giftCard` would pick up `last4` from a family rule instead of the
`full` that rule 3 gives it.

## How it renders

Every value the pane draws — the fact card, the detail strip, `ResolvedProfile`,
the guided setup's "what a stranger would receive" card and its facts-so-far
list — now goes through one `FactValue` component, and `formatValue` is no
longer exported so that is structural rather than a convention. A card that
hides a passport number while the strip below it prints the same number in full
has hidden nothing, and the second surface is always the one added later.

**Reveal is per value and lives in that component's own state.** Not lifted to
the pane keyed by fact id, which would be a store of "things the operator has
unhidden" — one that survives selection changes, outlives the card the person
was looking at, and is one refactor away from a *Show all*. Component state
cannot become that: it dies with the element, so leaving the pane, reloading the
console or navigating anywhere re-hides everything. Revealing the same fact in
two places is two deliberate acts. The reveal control calls `stopPropagation`,
because the card underneath is itself a click target and pressing *Show* must
not also move the selection.

**A masked value is visually distinct from an absent one.** The mask is drawn at
full strength in mono; `c.faint` stays this pane's word for "the agent did not
send a value". Greying the mask too would make a fact the holder *has* look
exactly like one they do not, which is worse than not masking.

## Tests

`packages/extension/tests/manager-claim-sensitivity.test.mts` (10, node:test +
assert/strict) pins the transcription where getting it wrong costs something,
the conservative default, the `x:` rule, the short-value and non-address
fallbacks, and the fixed-width run. Three more in
`persona-pane.render.test.mts` assert it *rendered*: nothing sensitive on screen
until asked for, one control per fact and never a global one, pressing *Show*
does not also select the fact, and a fresh mount comes back hidden — which
passes trivially for component state and fails for every way of making reveal
sticky.

`npm run lint` and `npm test` are clean from the repo root; the extension build
is clean too.

The render fixture moves from a bare `name` to `name.legal`: the registry has no
entry for the former, so it now resolves to the conservative default and those
assertions would have been reading a mask.

## Three things in the registry draft that looked wrong from here

Raised as findings against `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` rather than worked around:

1. **The hierarchy §2 argues for is not expressible in the data.** §2 says the
   token is hierarchical so `payment.*` "classifies as one family without
   enumerating its members, which is what makes a default table finite and a
   future token safe by construction" — but `claim-types.json` contains only
   leaf entries, declares no family or prefix entry, and §4's three resolution
   rules never consult a prefix. So an unregistered `payment.giftCard` is not
   safe by construction: it falls to the unregistered default. For masking that
   is harmless (`full` is stricter than `last4`), but **the `release` axis
   degrades the wrong way** — `stepUp`, which §3.2 says is the default for
   `payment.*` and `gov.*`, silently becomes `consent` for an unknown member of
   a gated family. That is a real hole for whoever implements release next, and
   it needs either family entries in the JSON or a fourth rule in §4.
2. **`email.*`'s mask style is unreachable under §3.1's own rule.**
   `email.personal` and `email.work` are `sensitivity: "normal"` with
   `mask: "emailLocal"`, and §3.1 defines masking as what `high` means. Under
   the registry as written, no rule ever applies `emailLocal` to anything — yet
   §1 motivates the whole registry partly with "masking needs to know that …
   `email.work` [is shown] as `a•••@example.com`". Either the email types should
   be `high`, or §3.1 needs a second trigger for a mask, or the §1 example is
   wrong. This console implements §3.1 (mask iff `high`), so email addresses are
   currently shown in full.
3. **There is no entry for a bare `name`,** and no rule that would route it to
   the `name.*` family, so a pool using that token — this repo's own fixtures
   did, and `persona-setup.tsx` still special-cases `f.type === "name"` — has
   every name masked in full. That is rule 3 working as specified, but it is a
   sharp edge for the first real pool that meets it, and it is the same missing
   prefix mechanism as finding 1.

Minor, not worth an issue on their own: `defaults` carries two keys,
`unregistered` and `extension`, with identical content and nothing in the JSON
saying which one `x:` maps to (§4 rule 3 treats them as one answer in prose);
and the registry does not say whether a mask applies to a value or to its
rendering, which only matters for the `object` value type — every object-valued
type is `full` today, so no consumer has had to decide yet.

title: spec(provision): separate where an admin lives from how far it reaches
body:
`provision/integration` writes the minted admin's ACL entry naming the target context, and there is no way to ask for any other shape. That is right for every integration-class consumer — a mediator acts where it was provisioned — and it makes one consumer unrepresentable: an **operator console**, whose whole job is administering the maintainer.

## The shape of the change

`adminScope` is a **second axis beside `context`**, not a replacement for it.

The obvious spelling — making `context` optional to mean "everywhere" — is the wrong one, and rejecting it is most of the design. A console still has to keep its own configuration somewhere, and that somewhere is one ordinary context; dropping `context` would leave it with nowhere to put that, and would collapse "provision me everywhere" and "provision me wherever you like" into the same document.

So:

* **`context` is where the admin lives.** The admin DID is minted under it, the authorization VC is issued in it, and it is the home a wallet-class producer stores its own configuration under. Resolved on every request, sent or inferred.
* **`adminScope` is how far the admin reaches.** `context` (default) writes an entry naming that one context. `unrestricted` writes an entry naming none, which an ACL reads as authority over every context the maintainer holds — including contexts created after this provisioning ran.

## Two MUSTs, not guidance

**A relayer may not confer what it does not hold.** `unrestricted` is refused with `provision/integration:forbidden` unless the relayer is itself a super-admin. This is the same rule an ACL applies to a direct grant; routing the request through a provisioning maintainer does not launder it.

**The outcome is echoed, not assumed.** A maintainer that predates the member ignores an unknown `adminScope` and writes a `context`-scoped entry, and a success response is otherwise indistinguishable from one that honoured the ask. `summary.adminScope` is what tells them apart; absent, a producer MUST read the outcome as `context`.

`summary.context` is echoed for the same class of reason: a producer that omitted `context` and let inference run currently has no way to learn where it landed except by guessing at the maintainer's layout — precisely the thing the inference rules exist because it cannot do.

## Scope

* `payload.adminScope`, `summary.context`, `summary.adminScope` on `specs/provision/integration/0.3/payload.schema.json`.
* An `## Admin scope` section, plus the conformance items that change: producer MAY ask, consumer MUST bind the entry accordingly and MUST refuse an unrestricted ask from a scoped relayer.
* One invalid example — `adminScope: "superAdmin"`, the word an operator says, which the wire deliberately does not use: it names the shape of the entry, not the informal name of the role that shape produces.
* Both binding generators re-run (`build-ts-bindings`, `trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt`). `check-bindings` reports all 403 specs agree; `trust-tasks-rs` is green (786 tests).

Additive to a `draft` spec, per the Status section's allowance.

## Consumers

Landing this unblocks two dependent PRs, in order — the VTA rejects `adminScope` at its dispatch spine until it ships a `trust-tasks-rs` carrying this schema:

* OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure — honours `adminScope`, gated on the relayer being a super-admin.
* OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin — the wallet's setup flow asks for it, so a management console can be granted what it needs.

title: ci: fail fast when Cargo.lock does not satisfy the manifests
body:
`main` was red for three merges today, and the failure kept arriving under other jobs' names. This is the check that would have said so in one second, on the merge that caused it.

## What it catches

A dependency requirement with **no matching version in `Cargo.lock`**, so every `--locked` command refuses to run:

```
error: cannot update the lock file /build/Cargo.lock because --locked was passed to prevent this
```

## How that reaches main with every check green

Two dependency PRs, each correct alone and incompatible together:

| | |
|---|---|
| **#1297** | pins the workspace to `jsonschema = "0.47"` |
| **#1295** | bumps regorus to 0.12, which requires `jsonschema ^0.49.9` |

#1295 was opened before #1297 merged, so its merge commit resolved against a main that still said `0.46` — and was green, honestly. Merging it never re-ran against the main that existed by then, and nothing afterwards checked the combination.

## Why it needed its own job

The cost was **misattribution** — the same one #706 and #711 paid for the sibling lockfile invariant, which the `lockfile self-pins` job right above this one already documents.

Later PRs inherited the broken lock through their own merge commits, and it surfaced under whichever job touched it first. For #1296 that was **MSRV**, which sent the diagnosis chasing a Rust-version problem that did not exist: the dependency it appeared to accuse declares `rust-version = "1.85"`, well under this workspace's 1.95 floor. That PR needed no code change at all.

`check` and `msrv` already pass `--locked` and would eventually fail on the same thing. They fail **slowly, inside a compile job, wearing the wrong name.** This runs in about a second and says the true thing.

Like `lockfile self-pins`, it is deliberately **not PR-only** — it runs on pushes to `main`, which is the moment this class of breakage is actually created.

## The message

It tells the reader which side is at fault, because that was the expensive part:

```
If you changed no dependency, and especially if this is failing on
main: a pull request was merged while stale. Its lock was resolved
against an older main and no longer matches the manifests it landed
beside. Fix it on main rather than in the branch that inherited it —
the branch is not what broke.
```

## Verification

I ran the extracted step itself, in both directions:

- against the broken commit `95877dc9` — **fails**, with the message above
- against `main` post-#1301 — **passes** (`Cargo.lock satisfies every manifest.`), in ~0.8s

`cargo metadata` because it resolves the whole graph without compiling: no system libraries, no cache, no toolchain-specific behaviour.

## What this does not fix

This detects the breakage; it does not prevent it. The root cause is that a PR can merge without being up to date with `main`, and GitHub does not re-run its checks against the main that exists at merge time. **"Require branches to be up to date before merging"** in branch protection is what actually closes that, and it is a repo setting rather than something CI can assert. Worth considering alongside this — the two are complementary, and dependabot PRs touching a shared transitive dependency will collide again.

title: feat(setup): ask what the wallet is for, and where it keeps its settings
body:
feat(setup): ask what the wallet is for, and where it keeps its settings

Setup asked one muddled question — a "Workspace" toggle between letting
the agent choose a context and naming one — and never asked the question
that actually decides what the wallet can do. Two things came out of that.

**The wallet could not know where its own configuration lives.** Picking
"let the agent choose" omitted `payload.context`, the agent ran its
inference rules, and its reply does not have to name what they picked. So
onboarding could finish successfully with the wallet holding no answer to
"which context are my vault entries and personas landing in". `context` is
now required on the whole path, which also makes
`provision/integration:contextRequired` unreachable — inference never runs
— so the picker that recovered from it is deleted rather than kept for a
case that cannot arise.

**And the management console could not be granted what it needs.** The
agent wrote the minted admin's ACL row scoped to one context
unconditionally, so no answer to any question here could produce the
unrestricted admin a console has to be. That is fixed on the VTA side by
`adminScope` on `provision/integration/0.3`; this is the half that asks
for it. The two are deliberately separate fields rather than one: a
console needs authority over every context *and* one ordinary context to
keep its state in, so expressing "everywhere" by leaving the context blank
would have left it nowhere to put that.

The order of the two questions differs by scope, and it is forced rather
than chosen. An unrestricted grant is `pnm acl create … --role admin` with
no `--contexts`, so the home context can be asked afterwards — from the
list the now-authorised ephemeral reads off the agent, which is a picker
of real contexts instead of a slug typed from memory. A context-scoped
grant carries `--contexts <id>`, so it has to be asked first.

`grant-command.ts` exists because that command is a security decision
wearing a display string's clothes, and both ways of getting it wrong are
silent: omit `--contexts` and the operator grants the whole agent while
the screen says one context; include it for an unrestricted wallet and the
provisioning is refused after they ran a command they were told was right.
It also ends a live bug — the flow printed `--role super-admin` whenever
inline context creation was ticked, and `pnm acl create` has no such role
(admin, initiator, application, reader; super-admin is the shape of an
admin grant, not a name), so that command could not run at all.

What gets stored is the agent's account, not the ask. An agent that does
not implement `adminScope` ignores an `unrestricted` request and writes a
context-scoped entry while replying success — indistinguishable from
having honoured it except by `summary.adminScope`. A wallet that recorded
its own request would show a console the holder cannot drive.

Two harness bugs surfaced while writing the rendered test, both silent.
Node's strip-only TypeScript refuses a constructor parameter property, so
any component transitively importing `webauthn-prf-wrap.ts` failed to load
with a parse error naming a file the test never mentions; `.ts` now goes
through esbuild alongside `.tsx`. And `react-dom` decides `canUseDOM` and
probes `isEventSupported("input")` at module scope, so importing it before
a window existed left its change plugin on an input-event polyfill: clicks
worked, typing did nothing, and a filled field left component state empty.
It is now imported after a DOM exists, and `type()` clears React's value
tracker.

Requires the VTA change ("let a caller ask for an unrestricted admin") and
the registry release under it; below that floor the agent rejects
`adminScope` at the dispatch spine.

title: fix(deps): align jsonschema with what regorus 0.12 requires
body:
**`main` is currently red.** `cargo check --workspace --locked` fails on the tip, and with it every Docker image build and every PR whose merge commit inherits the state. This is two lines.

## What happened

Two dependabot PRs were individually fine and mutually incompatible:

- **#1297** pinned the workspace to `jsonschema = "0.47"`.
- **#1295** bumped regorus to 0.12 — which requires `jsonschema ^0.49.9`.

#1295 was based on a main that predated #1297, so its lock regeneration wrote `jsonschema 0.49.9` while `Cargo.toml` kept saying `"0.47"`. The result is a requirement that **no version in the lock satisfies**, which is exactly what `--locked` exists to catch:

```
error: cannot update the lock file /build/Cargo.lock because --locked was passed to prevent this
```

Neither PR was wrong. They were incompatible, and merged in an order that hid it until the next `--locked` build ran.

## The fix

Align the direct pin forward to the version regorus already pulls in, so one jsonschema serves both:

```diff
-jsonschema = "0.47"
+jsonschema = "0.49"
```

plus the single lock entry that follows (`vtc-service` moves from `jsonschema 0.47.0` to `jsonschema 0.49.9`, which was already in the lock for regorus).

The alternative was reverting regorus to 0.11, which undoes a merged PR. Aligning forward is the smaller move, and `vtc-service` — the only consumer of the direct dependency — compiles and passes against 0.49 unchanged.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-features` — clean
- `cargo check --workspace --locked` — **satisfied**, which is the thing that was broken
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --all-features` — green

## What this unblocks

| PR | Was failing | After this |
|---|---|---|
| #1294 (ulid 3.0) | Docker ×2 | needs only its own `Ulid::new` → `Ulid::generate` rename, already pushed |
| #1296 (getrandom 0.4.3) | MSRV, Docker ×2 | **no code change needed** — the "MSRV" failure was this `--locked` error, not a rustc-version problem (getrandom 0.4.3 declares `rust-version = "1.85"`, well under our 1.95). `@dependabot rebase` will clear it |

Both were fine at their branch head and failed only at the merge commit — confirmed by fetching `refs/pull/N/merge` and reproducing locally.

## Worth a follow-up

Nothing in CI checks that a *merged* result stays lock-consistent — each PR was green on its own head. A `cargo check --locked` on the merge commit, or requiring dependabot PRs to be up to date with main before merge, would have caught this at the point of merge rather than three PRs later.

title: spec(persona): the step-up approval is the maintainer's state, not the request's
body:
A correction to my own rule in #377, found by trying to implement it.

## What was wrong

#377 said `present` MUST refuse a `stepUp` claim when "no fresh approval bound
to that previewId **accompanies the request**".

`present`'s payload is `contextId`, `previewId`, `challenge`, `mint`, `ext`.
There is nowhere to put an approval, so the rule was unimplementable as written.

## Why the fix isn't a new member

The obvious repair — add an `approval` member — is the wrong one. **An approval
a producer carries is a bearer token**, and a bearer token authorising a
disclosure is replayable by whoever holds it. That is precisely the property the
single-use `previewId` exists to deny; re-introducing it one member along would
undo it.

So the rule now says what it should have said in the first place: **the
maintainer holds the approval, bound to the preview.** It shares that preview's
lifetime — consumed with it, expired with it, unable to outlive the decision it
belongs to. A maintainer implementing this has a natural home for it (the
preview record itself) and no new token to protect.

Also stated explicitly, since it was only implied by the error's own
description: the refusal MUST NOT consume the preview. Refusing for want of an
approval must not cost the holder the decision they already made.

## Note

This is the fourth round of gaps found by implementing this family rather than
reading it, and the first that was a straightforward error rather than an
omission — I wrote a MUST about a request member that does not exist.

Prose only; no schema member moves, so the bindings are unchanged.

title: spec(persona): say what kind of prefix rule 3 means
body:
The VTA implementation (verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1299) asked a question
§4 did not answer: is the "longest registered prefix" matched over **bytes** or
over **dot segments**?

## Why the omission was worse than ambiguous

The same task answers the same question differently a few lines away.
`attribute/list`'s `typePrefix` is explicitly a byte comparison and says so:

> compared over the UTF-8 encoding … a prefix that ends mid-segment is a byte
> comparison like any other

An implementer meeting that first would reasonably carry it into §4 — and
`paymentology.card` would become a member of the `payment` family.

**Consequence, stated accurately:** rule 3 can only ever tighten, so the wrong
reading produces *spurious strictness*, not a leak — an unrelated token gated
behind a step-up nobody asked for. Wrong and worth fixing; not a hole, and I'd
rather say so than dramatise it.

Now stated: **dot-segment boundaries, proper prefixes.** A token is not its own
prefix, since rule 2 has already answered for an exact match and comparing one
against the floor would contradict "an exact entry is used as written".

## A note for whoever extends the table

**"Longest" is not currently observable.** No two nested families in the shipped
table disagree on any axis, and the floor is already maximal on `sensitivity`
and `mask` — so today rule 3 can only move `release`, and a *shortest*-prefix
implementation passes every outcome these entries can express.

The rule is written for the table that adds `payment.crypto` with a treatment of
its own. An implementation should be tested on the mechanism rather than on a
result the current entries happen to make unobservable — which is the sort of
thing a green test suite will not tell you.

## Standing back

This is the third round of gaps found by *implementing* this registry rather
than reading it: the prefix walk and the sensitivity/mask tangle (#377), the two
rendering edges (#380), and now the shape of the prefix itself. Every one came
from a consumer, none from review.

Documentation only — no schema member moves, so the bindings are unchanged.

title: fix(rooms)!: a room stays readable across a membership change (#1300)
body:
fix(rooms)!: a room stays readable across a membership change (#1300)

Adding or removing one member made every record already in the room fail to
open — for every member, including the one who wrote it.

Records are sealed under the MLS exporter for the epoch current when they were
written, and `SealedRoom::open_record` used the group's *current* key regardless
of the record's own epoch. Every membership change is a commit and every commit
advances the epoch, so the first add or remove silently destroyed read access to
the room's entire contents. The failure surfaced as `DidNotOpen`, which reads
like corruption rather than like a key the caller no longer has.

Nothing caught it because every test in the crate sealed and opened inside one
epoch, and the end-to-end demo never advanced one either.

# The fix: an epoch key chain

At each commit the committer seals the outgoing epoch's storage key under the
incoming one — an `EpochLink`. A holder of the current key walks the chain
backwards to any retained epoch. Backwards only: a member holding epoch 2's key
derives nothing at epoch 3, so removal stays forward-only and a removed member
still reads nothing written after them.

This is the upper tier of the retention system in the Encrypted Spaces
architecture whitepaper (§4.2), linearised — we have no directory hierarchy for
a lower tier to align to.

Links are ciphertext, so a host stores them and learns only that an epoch
happened, which `Room.epoch` already told it.

# What it costs, and why it is a policy

Post-compromise security for record content: once the chain exists, a
compromised current key reaches every retained epoch. MLS's own PCS is
untouched — a compromised leaf still heals at the next commit — but the storage
layer above it no longer inherits that healing. That is the trade a library
makes and a message stream does not, so it is `RetentionPolicy::{Chained,
FromJoin}`, fixed at creation beside `visibility`.

`Chained` is what every host creates. `FromJoin` is the old behaviour kept
deliberately, and deserialising defaults to it — a room stored before this
change genuinely has no links, and no policy field can conjure keys that were
never sealed.

# Cryptographic deletion

`storage::prune_epoch_links_before` severs the chain below an epoch. Unlike
`purge_record`, which asks a host to erase bytes and trusts it, this destroys
the only path from a key any member holds to the keys that material was sealed
under — a host retaining every byte retains ciphertext nobody can open again.

# What is not finished

A **newly joined member** still reads only from their joining epoch. Their
Welcome carries the current epoch and nothing below it, and the links reach them
over a task that does not exist yet. The crate supports the backfill
(`SealedRoom::{links, add_links}`, exercised in the demo and in tests); the wire
does not. Same for choosing `FromJoin` at creation and for a prune verb — all
three need `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` first, because every `rooms/*` request schema
is `additionalProperties: false`. Design note §12.2 has the table.

# Breaking

- `Room` gains `retention_policy`.
- `MembershipChange` gains `link`; `RoomGroup::apply_commit` returns it.
- `SealedRoom::group_mut` is gone — it let a caller advance the epoch behind the
  chain's back, which reintroduced this defect one call site at a time. Replaced
  by `add_member`/`remove_member`/`apply_commit` on `SealedRoom`.
- `SealedRoom::open_record` takes `&mut self` (it memoises the walk).
- `vta_service::operations::room_groups::RoomGroupRecord` gains `links`.

title: feat(persona): withhold sensitive values from a listing that did not ask for them (#1299)
body:
feat(persona): withhold sensitive values from a listing that did not ask for them (#1299)

`persona/attribute/list` honours `includeSensitive`, the half of
`sensitivity` that is not cosmetic. A listing that asked for values still
omits the plaintext of anything resolving to `sensitivity: high`; the row,
its type, its label and its version come back regardless, because this is
withholding a value and not hiding a fact. `includeSensitive` on its own
introduces no plaintext — it widens `includeValues` and is never a request.

Resolution follows CLAIM-TYPES.md §4, per axis: a holder's override wins,
then an exact registry entry used as written, then the more protective of
the longest registered family and the unregistered floor, then the floor.
A family entry can only ever tighten, so `payment.giftCard` inherits
`payment`'s gate while `name.somethingNew` inherits none of `name`'s
permissiveness; an `x:` token is unregistered by construction and borrows
neither an entry nor a family.

The table is embedded from specs/persona/_shared/0.1/claim-types.json at
registryVersion 0.1, because no `persona/claim-types/list` task exists yet
to serve it.

`attribute/put` stores the holder's `sensitivity` override, which it
previously accepted and dropped. The audit trail tells the three listings
apart through `detail` — metadata only, values with N sensitive withheld,
values with sensitive included — carrying counts and claim types and never
a value.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(console): the persona pane no longer locks out the recommended setup
body:
Found while sweeping the persona vocabulary across the three repos. This one is
not cosmetic — the console currently disables itself for the configuration the
stack now recommends.

## The stale claim

`holderGate` disabled every button on the persona pane unless the caller was an
unscoped admin, and said so:

> Your identity sits above every trust context, so this needs an unscoped holder
> credential — Admin at this agent with no context restriction.

True when written. Not true since `Capability::PersonaHolder`
(verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1286): a **context-scoped** entry granted that
capability reaches the holder-scoped tasks too — and it is now the recommended
shape, because OpenVTC's setup asks for exactly it (`--admin-holder`).

So an operator following the documented path saw a dead pane and a message
telling them to widen their agent credential, when a capability grant is the
better answer and the one they already had.

## What it does now

`isUnscopedHolder` is *sufficient* and no longer *necessary*. `auth/whoami`
reports roles and scopes but not capabilities, so this console cannot tell which
a caller holds — and the thing it must not do is claim to know.

The caution now names both ways to satisfy the agent, says plainly that the
console cannot see which you have, and **stands aside** rather than disabling.
The agent decides on every task regardless — `isUnscopedHolder`'s own comment
said as much before this change.

It also speaks `design-docs/persona-vocabulary.md`: *your facts*, not "the
holder's attribute pool".

## Where it lives

Moved to `manager/holder-gate.ts` with `isUnscopedHolder` beside it — one
decision, one module — following the precedent the consent view already sets:
what the screen says here is a security property, and nothing tests a
component's reasoning. Concretely, the pane's test runner cannot load a `.tsx`
file, so a decision left inside one is a decision no test can reach. `use-vta.ts`
re-exports the predicate; importers are unaffected.

`manager-holder-gate.test.mts` pins all four cases, including that the caution
names `persona-holder` *and* the unscoped credential — naming only one is what
made the old message wrong — and that it carries no word the vocabulary keeps
off the screen.

## Follow-up

Making this certain rather than cautious means `auth/whoami` returning
capabilities: a spec change, then trust-tasks-rs, then the VTA. Worth doing, and
not worth guessing in the meantime.

`npm run lint` (tsc -b) clean; `npm test` 851 passing across the three
workspaces.

title: feat(auth): whoami reports the capabilities it enforces (#1298)
body:
feat(auth): whoami reports the capabilities it enforces (#1298)

A client could see a caller's roles and scopes and not whether that caller held
a capability its role does not imply. Since `persona-holder` (#1286) that is a
real gap rather than a theoretical one: the capability is additive, no role
derives it, so a client computing a role's own set can never see a grant of it.

The console met this immediately. Unable to tell a granted entry from an
unauthorised one, it disabled the persona pane for every caller that was not an
unscoped admin — which, after OpenVTC's setup started asking for exactly the
scoped-plus-granted shape, meant disabling itself for the configuration the
stack recommends. It now explains and stands aside instead
(vta-browser-plugin#183), because standing aside was the best answer available
to a client that cannot see the answer. This is the answer.

**Effective, not stored.** An entry that narrows nothing is the commonest entry
there is, and its stored list is empty; reporting that would answer "what has
this been narrowed to" and read as "you may do nothing" for a full
administrator. `effective_capabilities` is the same function the enforcement
path uses, so the report cannot drift from the decision.

**One read, not two.** `check_acl_full` returned two members of an entry it read
whole. A second read for the third could straddle a concurrent ACL edit and
answer with a role from before it and a capability set from after — so
`check_acl_entry` returns the entry and `check_acl_full` is now a thin wrapper.

Two tests, and the second is what makes the first mean anything: an ungranted
entry must NOT report `persona-holder`, or a handler returning every capability
that exists would pass the granted case.

title: feat(secrets)!: cache seed reads so KMS traffic scales with time, not requests
body:
## Why

The BIP-32 master seed is read on **every** key-touching request. `load_seed_bytes` has ~25 call sites — the signing oracle, key mint/rotate/list, the holder-key paths, every `did:webvh` lifecycle operation — and each one calls `SeedStore::get` with no memoization.

On the local backends that is free. On AWS Secrets Manager every read is a `GetSecretValue`, and every `GetSecretValue` is one **billed KMS `Decrypt`** against the key protecting the secret. So KMS request volume tracked request volume.

This started from an observed bill: **58,101,221 KMS requests in a month** (~22/sec sustained, USD 174.30) on a single region. The VTA's *direct* KMS use is boot-only and bounded — four call sites, all in `vta-tee/src/kms_bootstrap.rs`, 1–2 requests per enclave boot — so it was never the enclave. It was the seed store, re-reading a value that never changed, once per signature.

## What

`[secrets] cache_ttl_secs` — default `60`, `0` disables — bounds how long a successfully-read seed is reused from memory. A `CachingSeedStore` decorator applied at the single `create_seed_store` chokepoint, so every backend gets it and no arm can be silently missed.

Same VTA: **~43k backend reads a month instead of 58M.** The read now scales with wall-clock time, not traffic.

## Why reuse is safe

The seed for a generation is immutable — it changes only on rotation — so the cache skips a re-read of a constant rather than gambling on a moving value. Four invariants hold it up, each with a test:

- **Writes invalidate.** Load-bearing, not hygiene: `operations::seeds::rotate_seed` writes the new seed and then *immediately* re-reads it to re-encrypt every imported secret. A cache surviving the write would re-encrypt them under the wrong key.
- **A read that raced a write is discarded** via a generation counter, so it can never install a superseded seed for a full TTL. Signing requests run concurrently with rotation, so this case is real.
- **`Ok(None)` and every error pass straight through.** Caching "absent" would make a transient backend outage indistinguishable from an unprovisioned VTA for the whole TTL, and would race first-boot provisioning.
- **The cached copy is zeroized** on eviction and drop (P0.7); the TTL doubles as the bound on how long the seed sits resident.

Nothing here defends against an *out-of-process* writer, because there is no supported topology with one: runtime rotation is in-process under `ROTATE_LOCK`, and the offline `vta` CLI surfaces require the daemon stopped.

## The trade-off

Documented rather than glossed, in both the config doc and the module docs: the seed is now resident in process memory for up to the TTL, where previously it was resident only per-operation. On a busy VTA that is a distinction without a difference — at 22 req/s it is effectively always resident anyway. On a quiet one it is a real if small widening of the window a memory-scraping attacker has to hit. `cache_ttl_secs = 0` restores the old behaviour at the cost of a backend read per request.

## Also: the same defect one layer down (R1.2)

The AWS, GCP, Azure and Kubernetes backends each built a client — and re-resolved credentials — on **every** call: an IMDS/STS round trip, or a kubeconfig/ServiceAccount re-read, on top of the API call itself. Each now builds once via `OnceCell`, which is what the Vault backend already did and is the model the others now follow.

## Deliberately untouched

- **The TEE path.** `KmsTeeSeedStore` is constructed directly by `vta-enclave` and already holds the seed in enclave memory, so it is not wrapped. No behaviour change for Nitro deployments.
- **The VTC.** It reads its key bundle once at boot (`vtc-service/src/server.rs:1647`) into process state; its other reads are backup/status/emergency operator paths. It has no per-request read, so it never had this problem.
- **BIP-32 root derivation.** `load_seed_bytes` still re-derives `ExtendedSigningKey::from_seed` per request. That is pure CPU, not KMS, and caching derived key material is a bigger security conversation — separate change.

## Breaking change

`SecretsConfig` is now `#[non_exhaustive]`, so struct-literal and functional-update construction are no longer available outside `vti-secrets`. Build from `SecretsConfig::default()` and assign — the 8 in-tree sites in `vta-service/src/setup/from_toml.rs` are converted here.

Taken deliberately while a break was already being made: this struct has grown a field per backend and will keep growing, so marking it now makes every future field additive. Note this reaches further than the diff — any *external* consumer constructing one with a struct literal breaks on upgrade.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — 0 failures
- `cargo test -p vti-secrets --all-features` — 20/20, including 6 new cache tests; re-run after the Kubernetes change since it sits behind a non-default feature

## Note for whoever is chasing the bill

This fix only moves the needle if the 58M is actually the seed store. Confirm with CloudTrail before assuming — KMS calls made on behalf of another service carry `invokedBy` naming it:

```sql
SELECT eventname, useridentity.invokedby AS called_by, count(*) AS n
FROM cloudtrail_logs
WHERE eventsource = 'kms.amazonaws.com' AND eventtime >= '2026-08-01'
GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 20;
```

`secretsmanager.amazonaws.com` means this PR is the fix. `s3.amazonaws.com` means the cause is outside this repo and the answer there is S3 Bucket Keys, not this change.


---

## `semver report` — what it flagged, and what is attributable to this PR

The check is red. Two of its findings are this PR's, two are pre-existing on `main`. Per `RELEASING.md` the fix is **not** a version bump in this branch — release-plz reads the `!` and puts the bump in the Release PR.

**From this PR** (`vti-secrets`):

- `constructible_struct_adds_field` + `struct_marked_non_exhaustive` on `SecretsConfig` — intended, and the reason this PR carries `!`.
- `auto_trait_impl_removed` — `AwsSeedStore`, `GcpSeedStore`, `AzureSeedStore` and `K8sSeedStore` are **no longer `UnwindSafe` / `RefUnwindSafe`**, because `tokio::sync::OnceCell` holds a mutex internally.

  That second one was a consequence I did not anticipate when proposing the client-reuse change. It only affects a caller putting one of these stores inside `catch_unwind`, which nothing in this workspace does and which would be a strange thing to do to a secret store — but it is a real public-API break, not a false positive, and the major bump this PR already requires covers it. Flagging it explicitly rather than letting it be discovered in the Release PR.

**Pre-existing on `main`, unrelated to this branch** — a merged breaking change keeps this check red for every later PR until the Release PR lands:

- `struct_pub_field_missing`: `vta_persona::correlation::Finding::shared_with_profile_count`
- `function_parameter_count_changed`: `vta_service::operations::acl::create_acl`, `vta_cli_common::commands::acl::{cmd_acl_create, cmd_acl_update}`

title: feat(rooms)!: read mirrors — a host that serves a copy and writes nothing
body:
§7.3's optional half, and the last of the data-room gaps that was buildable. A room has one write-primary; another host can now hold a read-only copy of it, fed by `sinceVersion` pulls, serving reads and refusing every write.

### The decision the design left implicit

It says mirrors are "fed by `sinceVersion` pulls" without saying *by whom* — and reads are authorized. So this makes a call, and states it rather than burying it: **a mirror pulls as a member**, presenting a room-issued chain conferring `read`, exactly as any other reader does. No mirror-shaped exemption at the primary, no new verb. The room admits a mirror the way it admits a person, and can stop admitting it the same way.

Two consequences, both in the module docs and the guide:

- On `attributed` / `private` a mirror only ever holds **ciphertext** — mirroring gives its operator nothing the primary's operator lacks.
- On `open` it reads **cleartext**, because everything on that tier is cleartext to whoever holds it. Mirroring an `open` room to a host you would not let read it is not a thing this can do, and pretending otherwise would be the dishonest option.

Worth a look in review — if a mirror should instead hold something narrower than a member's `read`, that needs a new grant upstream.

### What a mirror cannot do

Tamper. Records are signed and AEAD-bound to `roomId | key | version | epoch`, so an altered or renumbered copy does not verify and does not open. Its only failure modes are **stale** and **silent**, and a client watching the version watermark sees both.

That shapes `store_mirrored_record`:

| | |
|---|---|
| Keeps the **primary's version** verbatim | Renumbering breaks the AEAD binding *and* gives the watermark a different meaning from the one every `sinceVersion` pull compares |
| Refuses a version **at or below** the mirror's watermark | Records only gain versions, so a lower one is a replayed pull or a rolled-back primary; accepting it would serve a fresh member an older room than the copy already had (R2‑5) |
| **Skips** the primary's visibility/epoch validation | Deliberately. Re-running it would mean a mirror refusing to copy a record its primary accepted — a copy silently diverging, the one failure mode a mirror must not have |

### The write refusal covers `admin`

`authz` refuses every non-read action on a mirror and names the primary. `Admin` is **not** exempt here, unlike the lapse gate: a mirror that accepted an epoch mint would fork the lifecycle clock its primary owns — live on the copy, lapsed at home.

### Operating one

```bash
room-host --mirror-config mirrors.json --mirror-interval-secs 300
```

The config holds a private key and the room's credentials, so it is hardened to owner-only on load and read from a file rather than a flag — a credential on a command line is a credential in the process table. One sequential pass per interval rather than a task per room: a mirror is not latency-critical, and a task per room turns one unreachable primary into unbounded concurrent retries. A failed pull is logged and the loop carries on, because stale is a state the design allows a mirror to be, and stopping would make every other mirror stale too.

### Tests

Four on the storage invariants, two on the authorization gate, three on the config shape, and two end to end **against a real socket**: two hosts, records written at the primary, pulled, and served from the copy under the primary's own numbers; an unreachable primary leaving the mirror serving what it has rather than losing it; and the write refusal naming the primary over the wire.

`clippy --all-targets` and `fmt --check` clean across `vti-rooms`, `room-host` and `vtc-service`; the `data_room` example still runs end to end.

### Breaking

`vti_rooms::Room` gains `mirror_of`, so struct literals need the field (every in-tree one is updated). It is `#[serde(default)]`, so every stored room deserialises as a primary — which is what they all are.

title: feat(rooms): a member's CLI surface, driven through the oracle
body:
Rooms had no CLI. Using one meant writing Rust against `vtc-client` or hand-building signed Trust Task documents — not a surface an operator has. This is the **member's** half: `pnm rooms {create,list,get,put,curate,renew}`.

### Two parties, never confused

Every command talks to both and keeps them apart: the operator's **VTA** mints a presentation (`rooms/keys/present`) and opens sealed records (`rooms/keys/open`), and the room's **host** stores the bytes. The credentials the presentation is derived from, and the group key that opens a record, stay inside the VTA — **this CLI holds neither at any point**.

That makes the CLI the room oracle's first real consumer, and the model holds up: a member who holds less than an action needs is refused *by their own VTA*, before anything reaches the host — the earlier and clearer of the two refusals.

Each command mints its own presentation for exactly the action it performs — `read` for list/get, `write` for put, `curate` for curate, `admin` for renew. Caching one across commands would mean re-binding it (impossible without the VTA) or sending it unbound, which is a bearer token.

```bash
pnm rooms list --room <room-did> --host https://rooms.example.org --host-did <host-did>
pnm rooms get  decision/pricing-2026 --room <room-did> --host …
pnm rooms put  decision/pricing-2026 "Agreed not to reprice." --room <room-did> --host … \
               --title "Pricing holds" --expected-version 0
pnm rooms renew 3 --room <room-did> --host …
```

`--host-did` binds the presentation to that host; omitting it warns, because an unbound presentation is usable by anyone who observes it for its four-hour life.

### Where the pieces had to live — a cycle forced the shape

`vta-sdk` gains `room_present` / `room_open`, since those are calls to *your own* VTA. It **cannot** gain the room wire types: `vti-common` re-exports `vta_sdk::acl`, so `vta-sdk → vti-rooms → vti-common → vta-sdk` is a dependency cycle.

So `vta-cli-common` takes `vtc-client` — which, despite its name, is the host-neutral room client (`room-host`'s own example drives itself with it). Worth a look in review: the alternative was a second copy of the `rooms/*` wire types in the CLI, which is exactly the duplication that crate deleted when the group-key layer moved out.

`vtc-client` also gains `curate_record` — nothing had implemented it, and it's the shared surface a mirrors PR would build beside.

### What it deliberately cannot do

| | |
|---|---|
| Write to a **sealed** room | Sealing needs the room's group key, which lives in the VTA, and no task seals on a caller's behalf. Refused with that reason rather than writing cleartext into an encrypted room |
| **Issue credentials** | Minting a VIC/VMC/VAC needs the *room's* signing key — the owner's, a different party with different custody. It belongs in an owner surface and is absent rather than half-present |

`get` also translates the epoch-mismatch failure into *"your VTA has not been given the room's latest commit"* — which is what it means, and not what it reads like.

### Tests

Five, on the two pure decisions worth pinning: rebuilding a session from what the VTA minted (every missing member refused rather than defaulted; a private room's subject binding surviving the rebuild; a non-string chain link refused rather than silently shortening the chain, since a shorter chain confers less than was minted); and the pin/unpin tri-state, where absence must stay distinct from `false` or a status-only curation would silently unpin the record.

`clippy --all-targets` and `fmt --check` clean; `vta-sdk`, `vtc-client` and `vta-cli-common` suites green.

title: fix(console): the map shows where you are known, not everywhere you could be
body:
From the first real screenshot of #176: twelve contexts, one persona, and eleven cards saying *"Nobody yet. This context knows nothing about you."* around the one that mattered.

The band's own label promises **where you are known, and as whom**. A context where nobody is known is not that, and on an agent with many contexts the empty cards were the whole page.

## What changed

Empty contexts fold into a single row:

> Not known in **11** other contexts. They hold nothing about you. — *Be known somewhere else…* · *Show them*

- **Be known somewhere else…** asks which context first (offering the empty ones, since that is what the row is about) and then opens the same binding form a card's own button opens.
- **Show them** reveals the cards as before, with a *Hide* in the band header to fold them back.
- A holder known nowhere sees *"You are not known anywhere yet. Nothing below the line holds a copy of anything."* instead of a grid of identical empty cards.

**A context the agent would not answer for stays visible in either state.** "Could not ask" is not "nobody is known here", and folding it away would draw a picture that reads as complete when it is not — the one wrong answer the map must never give.

## Not done here

A tree of contexts (the shell already knows parent/child) was the other option raised. It would organise the *known* ones better once there are many, but the problem in the screenshot was the empty ones, and a tree of twelve nodes with one lit is still twelve nodes. Worth revisiting when the known set is what's crowded.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test` — 836 across four workspaces; all six `ci.yml` assertions against the real build.

title: feat(console): the persona pane is a picture — guided first, then the map
body:
Direction B for the first run, Direction A after it — from the [UX review canvas](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/95be07ae-4417-4bbd-952c-d50f02e0f51c).

## What changed

The five stacked admin panels are gone. `persona.tsx` now loads the pool, the faces and every context's bindings, builds a model in `identity-graph.ts`, and shows one of two things.

**While the holder has no face — the guided setup** (`persona-setup.tsx`). Three steps in the order the model runs, each saying what it changes before it is done. Beside the second, the exact card a stranger would receive, updating as facts are ticked — the thing a tick list cannot convey, and where the teaching happens: *"Nothing here is proven"* / *"a credential carries the same signature to everyone who sees it, so it links you wherever it goes."*

**Otherwise — the identity map** (`persona-map.tsx`). Facts on top, faces in the middle, contexts below, with the one-way line drawn between them: *Copies go down. Nothing reads up.* Edges run from each fact to the faces that select it and from each face to the personas wearing it. Select anything and everything it reaches lights up. Two arrows from one face to two personas are drawn red and dashed, because they **are** a link — every wearer shows the same values. The strip beneath answers the selected thing's three questions (where it reaches, whether it links, when it last left) and opens the same editors the guide uses.

## What lights up is computed, not drawn

`reachOf` in `identity-graph.ts` runs a fact's reach **down** to the contexts it goes to, and a context's reach **up** to the facts it holds. The asymmetry is the model — a fact's reach is where it *goes*, a context's is what it *holds* — and getting it wrong means a context claiming a fact it was never given, or a fact appearing to reach nowhere when it does. Twelve tests, every negative paired with a positive, because a reach function that lights nothing satisfies every "does not light" assertion there is. The component measures card positions after layout and draws curves; it decides nothing.

## One flow bug caught by reading, not clicking

Deriving "guide or map" from `profiles.length === 0` on every render switched to the map the instant step two created a face — before step three, which is the step the whole guide leads to. The mode is decided once when data arrives and changed only by the guide finishing or being skipped.

## The words are fixed

On screen: a **fact**, a **face**, a **context**, a persona that **wears** a face. Provenance in plain words: *you said so · credential · ‹issuer› · made per verifier*. History is *what has left*. The table lives in `design-docs/persona-vocabulary.md` (the shared design-docs directory, outside this repo) with why each word won — **face** because "profile" is already three things in this product, including the wallet's per-site `first-use-profile`; **context** kept rather than "room" because Data Rooms already own that word. `CLAUDE.md` points at it. The spec's words stay in code and off the screen.

## Removed

The attributes, profiles, bindings and correlation panels; `profile-bindings.ts` and its eight tests, superseded by the graph, which confirms every face by `binding/get` in the same way. Correlation analysis survives as *Check values with your agent* in the map header; structural links (one face, two wearers) need no call at all.

## Not exercised — read this before merging

**This is a large UI change built without a browser.** The model is tested; the drawing is not. Specifically:

- Edges between cards that wrap onto a second row will cross other cards. Fine for a handful of facts; a pool of thirty needs grouping by vocabulary prefix, which the model already supports and the layout does not yet.
- The stranger card in the guide mirrors the face editor's ticks by watching its checkboxes in the DOM. That keeps one editor rather than two drifting copies, but it depends on the checkboxes rendering in `attributes` order — which they do today.
- Nothing renders a pane in a test. That gap predates this PR and is larger after it.

I'd suggest loading the unpacked build and walking the guide end-to-end on an agent with an empty pool, then the map on one with a bound persona, before this goes anywhere.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test` — 836 across four workspaces (extension 240: −8 scan tests, +12 graph tests). All six `Assert*` steps in `ci.yml` pass against the real build; the ten holder-scoped URIs are still confined to, and present in, `manager.js`.

title: spec(persona): say what a mask does at its two edges
body:
Fallout from implementing the registry twice in parallel — and the most useful
kind, because both implementations met the same two gaps and neither was
specified.

## What was missing

**A value shorter than the tail a style keeps.** `last4` of a four-character
value is the value. A four-digit card number printed whole is not a masked card
number, but nothing said so.

**Whether a mask tracks the value's length.** Both clients drew a fixed run, and
the reasoning deserves to be written down rather than rediscovered: a run of one
bullet per hidden character publishes the *length* of a passport number, a date
of birth or a card — which is exactly what the mask was drawn to withhold, and
is frequently enough to identify the format on its own. The exact width is the
client's; that it does not vary with the value is not.

Also: `emailLocal` on a value with no local part or no `@` masks in full rather
than guessing.

## Why bother, given both got it right

They guessed **alike**, which is luck rather than a specification. The third
implementation is the one that would have differed, and a registry whose whole
purpose is that two surfaces treat a card number the same way should not leave
its own rendering rules to inference.

This is the second round of gaps the parallel client work has found — the first
was #377's prefix walk and the sensitivity/mask tangle. Being the registry's
consumer rather than its author turns out to be how its holes surface.

Documentation and table comments only; no schema member moves, so the bindings
are unchanged.

title: feat(persona): mask sensitive facts in the identity pane (#282)
body:
feat(persona): mask sensitive facts in the identity pane (#282)

* feat(persona): mask sensitive facts in the identity pane

A fact's claim type says how carefully its value is shown to its own
holder, and the identity pane now reads that: `high`-sensitivity types are
painted reduced, and `s` shows the selected fact and only that one.

The table is a vendored copy of the masking half of the persona claim-type
registry (`specs/persona/_shared/0.1/claim-types.json`), because the agent
serves no such table — there is no `persona/claim-types/list` task, and the
registry's own §6 lists adding one as an open question. Unregistered tokens
and the open `x:` namespace resolve to the conservative default the registry
specifies: masked entirely.

Sensitivity, not the mask style, decides whether to mask; the style decides
how. `email.work` is `normal` with an `emailLocal` style, and is shown whole
to its own holder — masking everything would teach the reveal key as a
reflex, and a reveal pressed by reflex protects nothing.

Masking here is not a security control and nothing in the code says it is.
The value has already been fetched, decrypted by the agent and parked in
this process; the mask defends against someone reading the terminal over a
shoulder and against a screenshot. The control that would matter is on the
read path — an `includeSensitive` flag on `persona/attribute/list`, so a
listing that did not ask is never sent sensitive values — and it does not
exist.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(persona): the vendored table is private, so link it as prose

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(persona): follow the registry's revised masking rules

The claim-type registry draft was revised while this was being written, in
two ways that this vendored copy has to follow.

**Masking is no longer gated on sensitivity.** §3.3 now makes the two
independent: any type whose style is not `none` is masked on screen,
whatever its sensitivity, and `sensitivity: high` means the value is
additionally withheld from a listing that did not ask for sensitive values.
That was the tangle worth untangling — the first draft left `email.*`
carrying an `emailLocal` style that no rule could ever apply, while the
registry's own §1 used `a•••@example.com` to motivate the table. An email
address is worth hiding from the person behind you without being worth
withholding from every listing.

It also puts the honesty caveat on firmer ground rather than softer: the
half of the registry that is not cosmetic is now named as a read-path
control, and it is exactly the one that does not exist. Nothing here can
act on `sensitivity`; it is carried so a caller can read it.

**Families resolve by longest registered prefix.** §4 adds a rule this copy
previously argued against: a token with no exact entry takes the longest
registered prefix together with the unregistered floor, most protective per
axis. Without it a gated family is leavable by inventing a token —
`payment.giftCard` resolved to a floor whose `release` is weaker than every
registered member of the family it plainly belongs to. Because the more
protective answer wins, a family can only tighten: an unregistered
`name.somethingNew` still lands on the floor. `x:` never inherits a family.

Prefixes match on `.` boundaries, so `paymentx.token` is not in the
`payment` family.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(persona): the mask is a rendering, and the words say which axis

Two follow-ups to the registry's revised §3.3, where `mask` and
`sensitivity` became independent decisions.

The registry now states that a mask applies to a rendering, never to what is
stored or sent. The editor already fills from the value rather than from
`display_value`, so nothing was wrong; the failure it avoids is quiet enough
to be worth a test, because a form filled from the masked form would save
eight bullets over a card number and the write would be perfectly
well-formed.

The rest is wording. "Sensitive" is now a specific claim about one axis —
withheld from a listing that did not ask — and using it loosely for "masked"
is the conflation §3.3 exists to end. The comments and test names that meant
the mask now say the mask.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

title: feat(acl): grant authority over the holder's own identity without granting every context
body:
## The sentence this removes

> To manage your own identity from a client, you must give that client authority
> over every context on the agent.

The ten holder-scoped `persona/*` tasks — the attribute pool, the profiles over
it, correlation, cross-context disclosure history — were reachable only by an
`Admin` with unrestricted scope. Correct as a boundary; wrong as an
authorization model.

**OpenVTC is the case that found it.** Its setup provisions a context-scoped
admin (`contexts create --admin-did` → `allowed_contexts: ["openvtc"]`), so the
identity pane shipped in openvtc#277 has its Attributes, Profiles and
Disclosures tabs refused on every install — by a gate it cannot satisfy without
becoming a super admin. Bindings (context-scoped) work today; nothing above them
does.

## `Capability::PersonaHolder` — the first additive capability

No role derives it. An entry holds it only where it was granted by name.

Every other member of `Capability` is a subset of what some role carries, and
`effective_capabilities` intersects, never unions — a property the ACL's display,
audit trail and role checks all lean on. Holder authority cannot be expressed
that way, because it is not *within* what a context-scoped admin may do. The two
alternatives were:

- derive it from `Admin` — which hands the pool to **every context-scoped
  administrator that already exists**, silently, on upgrade. That is the exact
  breach the persona gate was written to prevent; or
- let it stand outside a role, which is what this does.

`ADDITIVE_CAPABILITIES` is a `const` list so each future exception has to be
argued for in one place a reviewer can find.

### Two consequences worth reviewing closely

- **The narrowing is computed from the non-additive names alone.** Otherwise
  granting an entry holder authority and nothing else — a list of one name no
  role contains — intersects its role's set down to empty. An operator granting
  a capability would have silently revoked the entry's vault access in the same
  command. Pinned by `granting_only_an_additive_capability_narrows_nothing`.
- **`capabilities_beyond_role` cannot gate it**, because no role carries it, so
  the gate is a privilege check on the *granter*:
  `validate_additive_capability_grant` refuses anyone who is not an unscoped
  holder, on **both** create and update. Without it the escalation is one command
  long — an admin of one context grants a DID it controls `persona-holder`, and
  reads the holder's entire cross-context identity. Pinned by
  `a_scoped_admin_cannot_grant_holder_authority{,_by_update}`.

## At the gate

`persona::authorize` satisfies `Reach::Holder` two ways and only two: an unscoped
holder credential, or an entry granted the capability.

- The ACL read happens **only where it can change the answer** — a holder task,
  for a caller not already unscoped — so context tasks and the super-admin path
  cost what they did.
- The decision is split into a pure `decide(claims, uri, ctx, holder_granted)`,
  so the reach matrix stays testable without standing up a store. The reach table
  is the thing most likely to be got wrong, and a test needing an `AppState` is a
  test nobody extends when they add a task.
- The grant is read **per call, not from the token**: a grant in a JWT outlives
  its revocation for that token's life. (The narrowing gate reads per call for the
  mirror-image reason.) A store error is answered "no" and logged — an unreadable
  ACL must not become permission.

## Granting it

```
pnm contexts create --id openvtc --admin-did <did> --admin-holder   # a client that is the holder's own
pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities persona-holder            # an existing entry
```

Being additive, naming it alone *adds* authority rather than narrowing the entry
to nothing — the CLI help for both flags now says so, since "every name must be
one the role already carries" is no longer the whole truth.

## Deliberately not done here

- **No role gate on holding it.** A personal agent running as `application` can
  be given holder authority, by a super admin, on purpose — that is the Cierge
  shape. What is gated is who may *confer* it.
- **No `Role::Holder`.** A new role means auditing every `match claims.role` in
  the workspace for a concept that is orthogonal to role, not a point on it.

## Follow-up

openvtc's setup flow needs to emit `--admin-holder` in the `pnm` command it shows
the operator, and its pane should name the grant when it meets the refusal.
That's a separate PR in that repo.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new(); no new outbound clients (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4) — no retries added
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*) — `Capability` gains a kebab-case variant;
      the enum is already #[non_exhaustive], so downstream matches are unaffected
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*) — no entry ⇒ no grant; store
      error ⇒ refuse; no role derives the capability
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*) — the refusal now names
      both ways to satisfy the gate
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered (R2.1) — grant is one ACL write,
      already atomic
- [x] Deviations flagged — the "capabilities only narrow" invariant is now
      "role-derived capabilities only narrow"; stated at effective_capabilities,
      bounded by a const list, and pinned by no_role_derives_an_additive_capability
```

`cargo test -p vta-service --lib` 1040 pass, `-p vti-common` 419 pass, clippy
`--workspace --all-targets` clean.

title: Trust Task Context Binding on published mechanisms, taskContext re-anchoring, and W3C proof/digest alignment
body:
Consolidated Working Draft 01 batch from the task force's working fork, superseding #15 by carrying it: the first commits are @bmiller59's #15 restructuring (authorship preserved), with three further changes built on top of it and the #15 first-pass review addressed. Closes #11. Resolves #17.

## What's inside, in order

**1. The #15 restructuring** (@bmiller59) — Trust Task Context Binding depends only on mechanisms already defined in the Trust Tasks core specification; the "qualifying specification" profile; outcome evidence travels with the presentation.

**2. `taskContext` re-anchoring and framework-0.4 alignment** — the outcome of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#173: `taskContext` carries the **`id` of the originating exchange's initiating document** (globally unique per the core specification's §4.3; the innermost exchange that attests the event, per §4.9.1), retiring the issuer-side uniqueness workaround. The qualifying profile is reworded against framework 0.4 (per-variant proof; the error variant honestly excluded — a task specification cannot strengthen `trust-task-error`'s own declaration; the no-`#response` escape hatch dropped). Outcome Interpretability cites the core specification's reply-disposition classification (§8.6) rather than hand-rolling the terminal/non-terminal split, and states the verifier's pairing checklist for retained evidence. A `trust-task-error` is failure evidence only, attributable to third parties when it carries `inResponseTo` (§8.2).

**3. W3C proof and digest alignment** (#17, all three items) — the VWC digest becomes `digestMultibase` (multibase multihash over the JCS canonical form the definition already named); multibase headers restricted to `z`/`u` per CID 1.0 §2.4 with alphabets enforced; proofs move from `Ed25519Signature2020` to the `DataIntegrityProof` envelope with `eddsa-jcs-2022` as the RECOMMENDED default suite (offline-verifiable; one canonicalization shared with `digestMultibase`) and `bbs-2023` named as the selective-disclosure path.

**4. The #15 first-pass review, addressed** — normative citations are commit-pinned permalinks (framework 0.4, `fbe196a`) so "pinned" is literally true; the stray subsection marking is removed; the per-issuer-uniqueness comment is mooted by the re-anchoring; and the term **"Trust Tasks core specification"** is now defined (`spec/terms-definitions/`), stating the core-vs-individual-specification architecture, explaining the upstream document's own "framework 0.4" version labels, and explicitly disclaiming the ToIP governance-framework sense.

## Evidence

The pairing checklist and the anchoring rule are executable: [`tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange`](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06w-witnessed-exchange) runs the witnessed exchange end-to-end — the VWC's `taskContext` lands on the ceremony's initiating document `id` structurally, and the retained `submit#response` passes exactly the checks the text states. The digest change is encoding-only for implementations already canonicalizing with JCS (verified against the Keyring witness implementation's own digest function).

Spec-Up-T render verified locally: every `[[ref:]]` resolves, no unresolved terms. Review history: Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#2, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#3, Mickens-Lab/dtgwg-cred-spec#4.

title: spec(persona): a claim-type registry, and the two axes that key on it
body:
Attributes carry a type, a value and a provenance, and nothing saying how
carefully to handle either. So every consumer decides for itself whether a card
number renders in the clear — which is to say nobody decides.

## The gap that turned out to be underneath everything

Four separate things wanted somewhere stable to attach to — a mask format, a
sensitivity default, a release requirement, and any mapping to an external
vocabulary. All four key on the claim type, and `ClaimType` had a **pattern**
but no **registry**: nothing distinguished `phone.mobile` from `mobile.phone`,
and both validated.

So the registry comes first, not last. It's also the cheapest of the five
artefacts — a table and a document, no protocol change.

`claim-types.json` names 26 core tokens, each with expected `valueType`,
sensitivity, release requirement, mask style, minimum-set membership, and the
OIDC standard claims it answers. `CLAIM-TYPES.md` carries the reasoning.

It doesn't reopen the decision `ClaimType` already records — **the token stays
ours**, external vocabularies are mappings applied at presentation. It *records*
those mappings rather than adopting one, and keeps the two properties no flat
vocabulary has: a hierarchy (`payment.*` classifies a family without
enumerating it) and an open `x:` namespace, which exists because CardSpace's
fifteen fixed claim types is the specific way the prior art failed.

## Three axes, and they are not the same axis

| axis | question | where |
|---|---|---|
| **sensitivity** | how carefully shown **to the holder** | registry default, holder override |
| **release** | what it takes to let it **leave** | registry default, holder override |
| **linkability** | what it **costs** once gone | already computed — `correlation/analyze` |

A payment card is highly sensitive, release-gated, and barely linkable: every
card number is unique, so knowing one tells a second verifier nothing about the
first. A passport number is all three. Reading any one as a proxy for another
builds a consumer that hides the wrong things and warns about the wrong things.

## Store the override; derive the default

`sensitivity` and `release` are optional and their absence means *the holder did
not decide* — not `normal`. `attribute/put` MUST NOT persist a resolved default
in their place: an attribute recording one would keep it after the registry
tightened, so a reclassification would protect new attributes and leave existing
ones exposed.

An unregistered or `x:` token resolves conservatively. **That** is where
"absence is most restrictive" belongs — applied to a vocabulary nobody has
reasoned about, not to an unset field on a known type, where it would mask every
legal name and teach holders to hit reveal reflexively.

## The half that isn't cosmetic

`attribute/list` gains `includeSensitive`: a listing that asked for values still
omits the plaintext of a `high` attribute unless it asks for those too. Separate
from `includeValues` because the escalations answer different callers — a picker
wants every name and no card number, and shouldn't have to choose between
plaintext for everything and plaintext for nothing.

Masking a value you've already received defends a screen. It's no defence at all
against a log, a crash dump, or the memory of the process holding it.

## Release, enforced where it can be

`disclosure/present` MUST refuse a `stepUp` claim without a fresh approval bound
to **that `previewId`** — binding to the session would turn "each time" into
"once per login", which is the whole of what the requirement asks for. The new
`stepUpRequired` is retryable and does **not** consume the preview: refusing for
want of an approval must not cost the holder the decision they already made.

## Also: whoami reports capabilities

Effective, not stored — the question is "what may I do", and an entry that
narrows nothing means everything its role implies.

Without it, a client seeing only roles and scopes can't tell whether a caller
holds a capability its role doesn't imply, so it must either refuse a caller the
service would honour or offer everything and let the service refuse. Not
hypothetical: the console did the former until vta-browser-plugin#183.

## The rule the new persona conventions state

> **A response may name identity; it may not carry identity.**

A persona's label, a face's name, an attribute's type — names. Values are
content, returned by exactly three tasks. whoami is worth naming because it's
the one a maintainer is most tempted to extend: a convenience display-name
member would make an authority endpoint an identity endpoint, and every consumer
already logging its response would begin logging identity.

## Scope note

Existing stored attributes are expected to be lost — we're the only implementer
and still in active development — so the 1.0 schemas are amended in place rather
than versioned. Shout if you'd rather I minted `/2.0`.

## Open questions in the doc rather than decided here

- Should `release: "never"` exist — held for reference, never disclosable? It's
  useful and honest, but makes the pool partly a password manager, and that's
  easier to add later than remove.
- Should the agent *serve* the registry (`persona/claim-types/list`, the shape
  `renderers/list` already has)? Clients can ship it statically today; worth
  doing when the first extension type ships.

## Checks

`npm run validate` — 403 specs, 68 shared schemas, clean. Rust and TS bindings
regenerated (`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen`, `npm run build-ts-bindings`)
and committed; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` 14 suites green.
