title: feat: replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope (pairwise | directed | public)
body:
Closes #22. Closes #23.

Implements **[#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22)**, which offered to write the text if the WG considered it in scope for WD02. Here it is, so the change can be judged as spec prose rather than as a proposal.

**Updated** to carry the resolution reached in [cred-tf discussion #41](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/41) and in [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22): **three** scope values, not four, and the four acronyms retired outright rather than kept as shorthand. What changed since the first push, and since review, is summarised at the bottom.

## The problem

Each of the four VID types encodes **two independent things in one name**: what the identifier is attached to, and how widely it may be correlated. Only the second is what implementers and users need to reason about — and the first is already carried by the credential the identifier appears in. A VMC's subject is a member; a VRC's issuer is a party to a relationship. The credential says so.

Naming the identifier again duplicates that, and the duplication is where the ambiguity lives: put an M-DID in a VRC — which §VRC explicitly permits — and both names apply.

## The change

One axis, ordered, declared by the holder:

| Scope | Known to | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `pairwise` | exactly one counterparty | R-DID; M-DID where the community is the only counterparty |
| `directed` | a set of counterparties the holder chooses | P-DID; M-DID where the member is deliberately correlatable |
| `public` | unbounded; ordinarily published so that it can be found | C-DID |

Plus the principle: **roles are conferred by credentials, scope is declared by the holder.**

### Why three and not four

Per [@talltree](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460210235) and [@geoffturk](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460754153). A `community` value was the only one whose bound came from **structure** (the VMC) rather than from the holder's choice — a role smuggled back onto the scope axis, which is precisely what this change exists to remove. It is also a distinction no verifier can act on: `pairwise` is falsifiable by contradiction, `public` is observable, and everything between them is an unverifiable holder assertion, so splitting the middle gives a verifier two values it cannot tell apart.

A membership identifier is therefore `pairwise` when the community is its only counterparty, and `directed` when the member also uses it with other members. The join-time choice becomes a three-way one a person can actually be asked to make:

1. `pairwise` — known to the VTA only (**single-counterparty pseudonym**, lasting as long as the membership)
2. `directed` — known to the VTA and whoever the person chooses, including other members (**private persona**)
3. `public` — known to anyone (**public persona**)

### The four acronyms are retired

Not kept as informal shorthand. R-DID / M-DID / C-DID / P-DID leave the normative model *and* the glossary; their four term files are deleted. The shorthand is where the confusion lived. The 42 dangling references this would once have created are gone — the body no longer refers to the types at all.

## What the change moves rather than removes

Three things a community-bounded scope value was quietly carrying now have explicit homes:

**1. New normative subsection — "Scope the holder cannot declare alone."** A member can declare their membership identifier `pairwise`, but that stays truthful only if the community keeps it so: a VTC that publishes a member directory, or presents a member-issued VMC to a third party (which Privacy Consideration 8 permits), has widened the exposure without the member choosing it. So: **a VTC that issues VMCs MUST publish, in its governance framework or trust registry, whether member identifiers are disclosed beyond the VTA, and to whom** (bound on the VTC as an Issuer under Conformance Target 1), and a verifier MUST NOT infer from a member's `pairwise` declaration that the community treats it as such. This is what `community` appeared to capture — a property of the community, which belongs in its governance. A matching item is added to §Governance Considerations and to §Privacy Considerations.

**2. Intra-community relationships.** Under strict `pairwise` the identifier toward the VTC and the one toward a counterparty differ by construction, so the community-anchored ZKP must establish common control across two identifiers rather than read one out of both credentials. Stated in both §Correlation Scope and §Community-Anchored Zero-Knowledge Proof, along with the fact that `directed` is the honest default for intra-community use. The ZK protocols themselves remain out of scope, so this is not a new hole — it just stops being invisible.

**3. Durability and scope are chosen independently.** §DID Method Considerations no longer groups methods by VID type. A `pairwise` identifier toward a community must survive key rotation for the life of the membership, so "pairwise ⇒ disposable" is false. Durability follows the lifetime of the credentials issued under an identifier; scope follows the holder's disclosure choice; a method is judged against both.

## The uniqueness rule becomes a check

§Unilateral Relationship Identification currently requires *"each entity MUST generate a new, unique R-DID for every single entity they connect with."* Under a declared scope that becomes the check #22 agreed: an identifier declared `pairwise` MUST NOT be used with more than one counterparty, a verifier that observes reuse MUST treat the declaration as false and MUST NOT rely on it, and implementations SHOULD default to a fresh identifier per relationship. `pairwise` is the one value falsifiable on evidence.

**The public community stops being an anomaly.** A community that wishes to be found declares `public` and is done. No bootstrapping exception, because `public` is an ordinary value on the axis rather than a departure from a pairwise default.

## What is deliberately unchanged

**Membership is still established by the VMC pair. A persona is still asserted by the VPC.** Those mechanisms have real machinery and it is untouched. Only the claim that the identifiers are distinct *types* is retired — which is the part that collides.

Mechanically, credential field constraints reduce to plain DIDs throughout: VRC, VMC, VIC, VPC and VWC no longer name identifier types in their issuer and subject rules. One exception is stated rather than implied — a witness identifier is `directed` at minimum, since it must be recognizable to both parties to the edge and to the community whose policy it is issued under.

## Where the declaration is carried: in the credential, by elimination

The first push left this open between the credential and the DID document. Review closed it on a technical fact rather than a preference: `did:key` and `did:peer` numalgo-0 documents are *derived* from the identifier value, so there is no document to add a property to — and those are exactly the methods §DID Method Considerations recommends for `pairwise` and `directed`. Encoding scope into a `did:peer:2` value would put the declaration into the identifier itself, which the section forbids a verifier from reading as a declaration. §Declaring scope now records option 1 and the two consequences that come with it (one scope per identifier across all its credentials; a first-party declaration covers only the issuer's own identifier, so the subject's scope in VPCs, VWCs, VICs and VECs is undeclared).

**Still open, deliberately:** the property name and `@context` term. Until they are named, the section binds a declaration that has been made and does not require one, so no credential is non-conforming for the absence of a declaration this version cannot yet carry. The examples carry none.

## Migration note

Implementations built against the first draft of #22 used a **four**-value vocabulary. The `ref-07-dtg-edge-semantics` fixtures in Keyring Wallet declare `community`, and that value does not map onto one scope: each `community` has to be re-decided as `pairwise` (the community is the only counterparty) or `directed` (the member also uses it with other members), per fixture. `rDid` is also a DIDComm wire field in the VRC reference implementation, so retiring the name there is a peer-compatibility change rather than a comment edit. The acronym rename is cheap; the re-decision is the substance of this change and no script can make it.

## Changed since the first push

- `community` dropped; `linked` renamed `directed` — per #41 and [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5460754153).
- The four acronyms retired outright; `relationship_did.md`, `membership_did.md`, `community_did.md` and `persona_did.md` deleted rather than rewritten as shorthand.
- Added §Choosing a scope (informative — the three-way HTX choice, and when intentional correlation needs a ZK proof at all, per [@talltree](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22#issuecomment-5465297803)).
- Added §Scope the holder cannot declare alone (normative — the VTC disclosure requirement), with matching Governance and Privacy items.
- Added the durability-vs-scope rule to §DID Method Considerations.
- Credential field constraints reduced to plain DIDs; witness identifier stated as `directed` at minimum.
- Privacy Consideration 1 (M-DID reuse / migration) deleted; a new item covers what a community does with a member's identifier.
- `CONTEXT.md` updated so the repo's own vocabulary note no longer teaches the four types.

## Changed since review

Per [@bmiller59's review](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/30#issuecomment-5515992393) and the sequence in #31:

- **Rebased over #27 and #26.** #26's Edge Verifiability section is reworded from the retired vocabulary and gains one sentence naming the cross-VTN and no-VTN cases #24 asked for. #27's Privacy Consideration 9 is shortened to the one-line max-of-halves rule its description anticipated.
- **Item 1.** §Correlation Scope opens by binding only a declaration that has been made; a role may rule out declarations it would make false (the VTC and witness cases), stated in the section and in the `correlation scope` term; the VTC disclosure MUST binds the VTC as issuer, §Governance item 3 is a pointer, and Conformance Targets 1 and 3 pick up correlation scope.
- **Item 2.** The reuse check, as a plain normative paragraph in §Unilateral Relationship Identification; the "definitional rather than normative" paragraph is gone.
- **Item 3.** The ordering paragraph no longer contradicts the witness minimum; "ordered" replaces "monotonic" throughout.
- **Item 4.** Carriage settled on the credential, per the section above.
- **Item 5.** A supporting party — VWC witness, IDVP, resolver — is not a counterparty and does not widen scope.
- **Item 6.** The DID method sentence about the examples is now true, and the examples carry a note that the reused member identifier is `directed`.
- **Item 7.** §Roles are conferred by credentials is cut to the principle and the retired-acronym list.
- **Item 8.** `pairwise` is a single-counterparty pseudonym, not one-time; `public`'s intent column reads discoverability as a consequence.
- `directed` stays, per #41.

Spec-Up-T renders clean with no dangling references introduced.

## Related

- Implements [#22](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/22) — the structural proposal; carries the three-value resolution reached there.
- Carries the naming resolution from [dtgwg-cred-tf#41](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/41).
- [#21](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/21) was closed by [#26](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/26), now on `main`; this PR rewords its Edge Verifiability section from the retired vocabulary.
- Closes [#23](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/23) together with [#27](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/27), now on `main` — an asymmetric edge is nameable once each half declares its own scope; §Scope the holder cannot declare alone states that a declaration binds only its own holder, and Privacy Consideration 9 states the max-of-halves rule.
- Supersedes the C-DID amendment in [#29](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/29) and resolves its service-identifier editor's note — under a scope axis a mediator's identifier is simply `public`, with no new type needed. The two are otherwise independent.
- Independent of [#28](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/28), which reorders the credential-category sections. No overlap in substance — this PR does not touch the taxonomy — but both edit `spec/body.md` in the same neighbourhood, so whichever merges second will need a textual rebase.

title: feat: replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope (pairwise | directed | public) (#30)
body:
feat: replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope (pairwise | directed | public) (#30)

* spec: replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope

Implements issue #22, incorporating the working group's resolution in
cred-tf discussion #41.

The four VID types each encode two independent things in one name: what
the identifier is attached to, and how widely it may be correlated. Only
the second is what implementers and users need to reason about, and the
first is already carried by the credential the identifier appears in. A
VMC's subject is a member; a VRC's issuer is a party to a relationship.
Naming the identifier again duplicates that, and the duplication is where
the ambiguity lives - put an M-DID in a VRC, which the VRC section
explicitly permits, and both names apply.

Replaces them with one axis, monotonic from narrowest to widest, declared
by the holder: pairwise, directed, public. New normative section
Correlation Scope, and the accompanying principle - roles are conferred
by credentials, scope is declared by the holder.

Three values, not the four originally proposed. A community-bounded value
was the only one whose bound came from structure (the VMC) rather than
from the holder's choice, which is the same conflation this change exists
to remove, and no verifier can tell it apart from directed anyway. A
membership identifier is pairwise when the community is its only
counterparty and directed when the member also uses it with other
members. The HTX choice at join time is correspondingly three-way: a
one-time pseudonym, a private persona, or a public persona.

R-DID, M-DID, C-DID and P-DID are retired outright rather than kept as
informal shorthand, and their glossary entries are deleted. The shorthand
is where the confusion lived.

What the change moves rather than removes:

- New normative subsection, Scope the holder cannot declare alone. A
  member can declare their membership identifier pairwise, but that
  declaration only stays truthful if the community keeps it so. A VTC's
  governance MUST state whether member identifiers are disclosed beyond
  the VTA, and a verifier MUST NOT infer from the member's declaration
  that the community treats it as such. This is what a community-bounded
  scope value appeared to capture; it is a property of the community, and
  belongs in its governance.
- Intra-community relationships. Under strict pairwise the identifier
  toward the VTC and the one toward a counterparty differ by
  construction, so the community-anchored ZKP must prove common control
  across them. Stated plainly in both places rather than left implicit,
  along with the fact that directed is the honest default for
  intra-community use.
- Durability and scope are chosen independently. The DID method section
  no longer groups methods by VID type: durability follows the lifetime
  of the credentials issued under an identifier, scope follows the
  holder's disclosure choice, and a method is judged against both.

Two pieces of text delete themselves:

- The uniqueness MUST in Unilateral Relationship Identification becomes
  definitional. An identifier declared pairwise and used with a second
  counterparty is not pairwise; the declaration is false. That is more
  useful to a verifier than a requirement it cannot check, and pairwise
  is the one value a verifier can falsify on evidence.
- The public-community case stops being an anomaly. A community declares
  public and is done - no bootstrapping exception.

Credential field constraints reduce to plain DIDs throughout: VRC, VMC,
VIC, VPC and VWC no longer name identifier types in their issuer and
subject rules. The witness identifier is directed at minimum, since it
must be recognizable to both parties and to the community. Privacy
Consideration 1 (M-DID reuse and migration) is deleted, and a new item
covers what a community does with a member's identifier.

Membership is still established by the VMC pair, and a persona is still
asserted by a VPC. Those mechanisms are untouched. Only the identifier
types leave.

Where a scope declaration is carried - in the credential by the party
whose identifier it is, or in the DID document - is still deliberately
left to the WG. The vocabulary and the principle can be adopted
independently of the carriage.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Apply review feedback to correlation scope

Adds the pairwise reuse check that #22 agreed and the vocabulary
retirement had dropped, restates the ordering rule so a stated minimum
scope is not contradicted by the holder's freedom to declare narrower,
and settles carriage on the credential by elimination: did:key and
did:peer documents are derived from the identifier, so there is nowhere
else to put it. The property name is left to the WG.

Also: the section is conformable only against a declaration that has
been made; the VTC disclosure requirement binds the VTC as issuer and
Conformance Targets 1 and 3 pick up correlation scope; disclosure to a
supporting party (witness, IDVP, resolver) does not widen scope; the
rationale subsection is cut to what a WD02 reader needs; labels for
pairwise and public are corrected; the DID method sentence about the
examples is made true and the examples carry a note that the reused
member identifier is directed.

The Edge Verifiability section from #26 is reworded from the retired
vocabulary and gains a sentence stating the cross-VTN and no-VTN cases
that #24 asked for. Privacy Consideration 9 from #27 is shortened to
the one-line rule its description anticipated.

Per review feedback on #30.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.17.10
body:
### Specifications

- **persona**: Attribute.value is OPTIONAL, so the default listing is representable ([#367](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/367))

The schema required `value` while its own description said the member is
  absent in two situations. That contradiction made the DEFAULT path of
  persona/attribute/list unrepresentable: `includeValues` defaults to false
  precisely so a picker can render the pool without decrypting every fact in it,
  and a maintainer taking that path had to choose between disclosing every value
  in bulk and emitting a non-conformant response.

  The same contradiction blocked the other documented case — a credential-backed
  value that could not be re-derived, which is returned carrying `stale` so the
  holder learns a claim has stopped being presentable rather than seeing a pool
  that looks smaller than it is.

  Found by a conformance witness in verifiable-trust-infrastructure while wiring
  the family: the witness for the default listing would not round-trip. Which is
  what witnesses are for — the defect was in the schema, not the implementation,
  and nothing else would have caught it before the first non-disclosing read
  went out.

  Both bindings regenerated; conformance checks 403 specs against 403 TypeScript
  and 398 Rust modules.

title: Edge verifiability across VTN contexts: different VTNs, or none at all
body:
## Summary

The VRC and VMC glossary entries make edge verifiability conditional on the
issuing VTCs being recognized as trust anchors *in a specific VTN*. Neither
entry says what happens when the two peers' VTCs anchor in **different** VTNs,
or when one anchors in **none** — which is the deliberate posture of a private
community. The condition is silent on precisely the case a spanning layer exists
to serve.

This is the fourth question in #21 seen from the cross-community direction. It
is filed separately because #21 asks whether the condition should exist at all,
while this asks what it means if it survives.

## Detail

The VRC entry (`spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_relationship_credential.md`):

> A VRC is only verifiable as a DTG edge in the context of a specific VTN if:
> a) it contains M-DIDs for both peers, b) both peers have signed the VRC using
> their M-DID private keys, c) both M-DIDs are verifiable via VMCs issued by
> VTCs, and d) **those VTCs are recognized as VTN trust anchors in that VTN**.

The VMC entry carries the same construction in one clause.

Condition (d) is stated as though one VTN context governs the whole edge. Three
cases it does not cover:

**1. The two VTCs anchor in different VTNs.** Each half traces to a VTC that
some VTN recognises, but no single VTN recognises both. Is the edge verifiable
in either context? In neither? The text gives no rule, and the natural readings
disagree — "in the context of a specific VTN" could mean *the verifier's* VTN or
*an* agreed VTN, and those produce different answers.

**2. One peer's VTC anchors in no VTN, deliberately.** A community that exists
precisely so its membership is not discoverable has no reason to seek anchor
status anywhere. Under condition (d) every edge it forms with the outside world
is, permanently and by construction, not a verifiable DTG edge — not because
anything is unproven, but because a party chose privacy.

**3. The verifier is outside both.** An external verifier can check that both
halves are authentic and that each traces to *some* VTC. Condition (d) does not
let it conclude anything, because it asks about recognition rather than about
what the verifier can check.

## Why it matters

Under condition (d) as written, verifiability is a property of the *network the
issuers joined*, not of what a verifier can establish. Two edges with identical
cryptography and identical proofs get different answers depending on registry
membership neither peer controls at verification time.

The cross-community case is where the spanning layer earns its name. If an edge
between two communities can never be a verifiable DTG edge unless both
communities' VTCs happen to anchor in the same VTN, then the answer for the
motivating case is "no", and that should be stated deliberately rather than
arrived at by silence.

## Requested clarification

1. For an edge whose peers' VTCs anchor in different VTNs, which VTN's context
   governs?
2. Is an edge with one deliberately unanchored peer intended to be permanently
   unverifiable as a DTG edge?
3. Should edge verifiability be defined **per verifier** — what this verifier
   can establish — rather than per VTN?

**Proposed answer**: resolve alongside #21 Q1 and Q2. If edge verifiability
survives as a defined property, define it per verifier and in terms of what must
be checkable, not which registry the issuers appear in. A verifier that trusts
both VTCs by any route should reach the same conclusion whether or not a VTN
mediated that trust.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. Set out as item X3 in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html). Directly
dependent on #21; related to #22.

title: VRC edge-verifiability conditions exist only in the glossary and contradict the body
body:
## Summary

The glossary definition of the VRC states conditions for edge verifiability that
appear nowhere in the body, contradict the body's Privacy Considerations, and
contradict the body's own bidirectional edge model. The VMC definition carries
half of the same construction.

The VRC entry (`spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_relationship_credential.md`)
has not been revised since the Working Draft 01 migration (#3), while the body's
treatment of R-DIDs, M-DIDs and the ZKP constructions has moved on. An
implementer reading the two together gets opposite instructions.

## Detail

The glossary entry reads:

> A VRC may contain either R-DIDs or M-DIDs. A VRC is only verifiable as a DTG
> edge in the context of a specific VTN if: a) it contains M-DIDs for both
> peers, b) both peers have signed the VRC using their M-DID private keys,
> c) both M-DIDs are verifiable via VMCs issued by VTCs, and d) those VTCs are
> recognized as VTN trust anchors in that VTN.

Three problems.

**1. It inverts the body's identifier guidance.** The body recommends the
opposite of condition (a):

- §VRC: "R-DIDs are RECOMMENDED for privacy; M-DIDs are allowed for
  bootstrapping (see Privacy Considerations)."
- §Unilateral Relationship Identification: "The valid application of this
  specification requires that each entity MUST generate a new, unique R-DID for
  every single entity they connect with, even within the same community."
- §Privacy Considerations 1: "Migration from M-DID-based to R-DID-based edges is
  recommended post-bootstrapping for enhanced privacy."

So the body tells an implementer to migrate to R-DID edges, and the glossary
tells the same implementer that an R-DID edge is not verifiable as an edge. Read
together, the privacy-preserving construction the body recommends is the one
that forfeits VTN-level edge verifiability.

**2. It is not reconciled with the Community-Anchored ZKP.** §Community-Anchored
Zero-Knowledge Proof states plainly that "Community membership is **not** a
precondition for issuing, holding, or presenting a VRC," and then defines a
construction in which the holder proves that "the VRC issuer possesses a VMC
from the *same* C-DID" *without revealing the specific DIDs*. That is the same
predicate the glossary's conditions (c) and (d) express by disclosure. If the
ZKP construction satisfies VTN-level edge verifiability, the glossary's
requirement for M-DIDs in the credential is unnecessary; if it does not, the
body should say so, because the ZKP section currently reads as though it does.
(Related: #9, on whether the linkages those constructions require are encoded at
all.)

**3. Condition (b) contradicts the bidirectional edge model** — and the first
sentence of the glossary entry itself. §VRC: "two VRCs (one each direction) form
a complete DTG edge," and the schema has a single `issuer` and a single `proof`.
The glossary entry opens by calling a VRC "one half of a bidirectional peer-to-
peer trust relationship" and then requires that "both peers have signed the VRC"
— which describes a single dual-signed credential, not two.

**4. The VMC entry carries the same unsourced construction.**
`verifiable_membership_credential.md`: "A VMC is only verifiable as a DTG edge in
the context of a specific VTN if the issuing VTC is recognized as a VTN trust
anchor on that VTN." Whether or not that one is correct, "only verifiable as a
DTG edge in the context of a specific VTN" is a normative-sounding constraint
that exists in no normative section. `grep` for it returns only these two
glossary files.

## Why it matters

This is not theoretical. In `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054` we are
deciding whether relationship credentials published to a community should carry
pairwise R-DIDs or membership M-DIDs, and the current VTC policy requires both
parties to be identifiable current members — which is the glossary's rule.
Choosing correctly requires knowing whether an R-DID edge is a first-class DTG
edge or a degraded one, and the specification currently answers both ways
depending on which file is read.

## Requested clarification

1. Is VTN-level edge verifiability intended to be a defined property of the
   specification at all? If so, it belongs in a normative section, not only in
   the glossary.
2. If it is: does a VRC carrying R-DIDs, presented with a community-anchored
   ZKP, satisfy it? Our reading of §Community-Anchored ZKP is that it should,
   and that condition (a) is a bootstrapping-era artifact.
3. Should condition (b) be struck as inconsistent with the two-VRC edge model,
   or does it describe an alternative single-credential form that the body does
   not define?
4. Should the VMC entry's edge-verifiability sentence be moved to the body or

title: Define edge verifiability normatively and strike it from the glossary (#26)
body:
Define edge verifiability normatively and strike it from the glossary (#26)

* Define edge verifiability normatively and strike it from the glossary

Fixes the contradiction reported in #21: the conditions under which a
VRC is verifiable as a DTG edge exist only in the glossary, contradict
the body, and one of them cannot be satisfied by any credential.

Add a normative Edge Verifiability section to Edge Credentials, and
reduce both glossary entries to a pointer at it.

The section defines edge verifiability with respect to a verifier
rather than in the abstract: a credential is an edge to a verifier when
its proof verifies and the verifier can establish that the issuer holds
a VMC from a VTC in the anchor set that verifier accepts. A VTN is the
common case of such an anchor set, but no VTN need exist. This is the
per-verifier phrasing the ZKP task force reports the reference circuits
already use.

Q1 — the property is now stated in a normative section rather than
only in the glossary.

Q2 — the anchor predicate may be satisfied by disclosure or by a
community-anchored ZKP, and the two are equivalent. A VRC carrying
R-DIDs with a valid proof is an edge on the same terms as an M-DID
edge presented by disclosure. Glossary condition (a), requiring M-DIDs
in the credential, is dropped: it would have excluded the construction
the specification recommends on privacy grounds, and would have made
the specification's own VRC example — did:peer to did:peer, no
membership credential — not an edge. A note records that the linkage
the proof route depends on is not yet encoded, so that route states an
intended design goal until it is; that bears on the proof's witness
data, not on whether the edge counts.

Q3 — condition (b), requiring both peers to have signed the VRC, is
struck. The schema defines one issuer and one proof, so no credential
could satisfy it, including the M-DID edges the condition existed to
bless. The new section states instead that each half is signed by its
own issuer and evaluated independently, and that the halves need not
satisfy the section by the same route.

Q4 — the VMC entry carried the same unsourced construction and travels
with it.

Reported independently by two implementations. The framing of M-DID
edges as a bootstrapping state, also raised in #21, is a separate
question and is deliberately left alone here.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Align edge verifiability with Membership Edge Completion

Condition 2 now points at the completion rule that #12 added rather
than restating a looser 'holds a VMC' version of it, the disclosure
route names the VMC pair (or the issuer's own demonstration) it relies
on, and the equivalence claim records that the community-anchored proof
currently establishes the counterparty's membership only as attested,
not acknowledged, matching what main already says at statement 3.

Per review feedback on #26.

title: `vtc-service` recompiles in full on every `cargo build`, even with no changes
body:
## Summary

`cargo build -p vtc-service` is never a no-op. Two consecutive builds with
nothing touched in between both recompile the crate from scratch — about 4m17s
each on a 32-core machine. `build.rs` writes into the source tree, and what it
writes is registered as an input to the very build it just ran, so the
fingerprint is dirty the moment the build finishes.

This affects every `cargo build`, `cargo test`, `cargo clippy` and
rust-analyzer check-on-save for anyone whose workspace graph includes
`vtc-service`. It is invisible in cold-cache CI, which is likely why it has gone
unnoticed.

`admin-ui` is in `default = [...]`, so the plain default-feature build
reproduces it.

## Reproduction

```bash
cargo build -p vtc-service          # 4m17s
cargo build -p vtc-service          # 4m16s  <- expected: Finished in 0.0s
cargo build -p vtc-service          # 4m17s
cargo build -p vtc-service          # 4m19s
```

Each run prints `Compiling vtc-service v0.11.58`.

## Cause 1 — `build.rs` watches a file its own `npm install` rewrites

`build.rs` declares:

```rust
println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=admin-ui/package-lock.json");
```

and then runs `npm install` in `admin-ui/`, which rewrites `package-lock.json`.
The content is unchanged (`git status` stays clean) but the mtime is not. After
a build completes, the lockfile is consistently *newer* than the build-script
output cargo just stamped:

```
target/.../build/vtc-service-<hash>/output   11:34:33.451153013
vtc-service/admin-ui/package-lock.json       11:34:33.585155173   <- 134 ms newer
```

`CARGO_LOG=cargo::core::compiler::fingerprint=info` confirms this is what cargo
acts on:

```
fingerprint dirty for vtc-service v0.11.58 .../RunCustomBuild
    dirty: FsStatusOutdated(StaleItem(ChangedFile {
        reference: ".../build/vtc-service-<hash>/output",
        stale:     ".../vtc-service/admin-ui/package-lock.json" }))
```

So the build script reruns every time, which reruns npm, which rewrites the
lockfile again.

This also contradicts the intent stated in `build.rs`'s own comment:

> `cargo:rerun-if-changed` directives are scoped to admin-ui sources only, so
> building unrelated parts of vtc-service doesn't re-trigger npm.

## Cause 2 — `dist/` is a compile input and is rewritten on every build

`src/admin_ui.rs` does:

```rust
pub static ADMIN_UI_DIR: Dir<'_> = include_dir!("$CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/admin-ui/dist");
```

`include_dir!` registers every file under `admin-ui/dist/` as a compile input of
the lib — all 78 of them appear in `target/release/deps/vtc_service-*.d`. The
build script's `npm run build` regenerates that whole directory on each run, so
those inputs get fresh mtimes after the lib was compiled against them.

This is independent of cause 1: backdating `package-lock.json` to 10 seconds
older than the build-script output still produced a full 4m19s rebuild. A fix
that only adjusts the `rerun-if-changed` lines will not resolve the issue.

## Suggested fix

The underlying rule is that a build script must not write into the source tree
— only into `OUT_DIR` (see the [Cargo build-script
docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html)). Pointing
vite's `outDir` at `$OUT_DIR` and reading from there closes both loops at once,
because nothing under the manifest directory is rewritten any more:

```rust
// build.rs
let out = PathBuf::from(std::env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("admin-ui-dist");
run_npm(&admin_ui, &["run", "build", "--", "--outDir", out.to_str().unwrap(), "--emptyOutDir"]);
```

```rust
// src/admin_ui.rs
pub static ADMIN_UI_DIR: Dir<'_> = include_dir!("$OUT_DIR/admin-ui-dist");
```

Two narrower options, if moving the output is unattractive:

- Use `npm ci` rather than `npm install`. It installs from the lockfile and
  does not rewrite it, which closes cause 1 — but leaves cause 2 open.
- Have `build.rs` skip npm entirely when `dist/` is newer than the `admin-ui`
  sources, so the steady state does no work and rewrites nothing.

`VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` with a pre-built `dist/` is an effective local
workaround today.

## Environment

- `vtc-service` v0.11.58, upstream commit `f17bd628`
- cargo 1.97.1 (c980f4866 2026-06-30), rustc 1.97.1 (8bab26f4f 2026-07-14)
- node v25.9.0, npm 11.12.1
- Linux (not verified on macOS, though cause 2 does not depend on filesystem
  timestamp granularity, so it should reproduce there too)

title: fix(vtc-service): stop build.rs writing to the source tree, so cargo build is a no-op (#1254)
body:
fix(vtc-service): stop build.rs writing to the source tree, so cargo build is a no-op (#1254)

* fix(vtc-service): stop build.rs writing to the source tree, so cargo build is a no-op

`cargo build -p vtc-service` was never a no-op. Two consecutive builds
with nothing touched in between both recompiled the crate, so every
local build, test, clippy run and rust-analyzer check-on-save paid for
it. Cold-cache CI never builds the same tree twice, which is why it went
unnoticed. `admin-ui` is a default feature, so the plain build reproduces
it.

Both causes are `build.rs` writing into the source tree, which is exactly
what the Cargo build-script docs say not to do — what a script writes
there feeds the next build's staleness check.

`npm install` rewrites `admin-ui/package-lock.json`: identical bytes, new
mtime, so `git status` stays clean and nothing looks wrong. But the
lockfile is one of the script's own `rerun-if-changed` inputs, so the
script was dirty the instant it finished and re-ran on every build. Of
the six watched paths it is the only one npm moves, which makes it the
whole pump.

`npm run build` then regenerated `admin-ui/dist`, and `include_dir!`
expands to one `include_bytes!` per file, so all 78 of them are compile
inputs of the lib (312 entries across `vtc_service-*.d`). Each re-run
refreshed their mtimes and turned a cheap script re-run into a full
recompile.

So: `npm install` goes through `run_npm_preserving_lockfile`, which
restores the lockfile's mtime when npm left the content byte-identical —
a real lockfile update still changes content, so it still triggers a
rebuild. That is the fix that closes the loop; with the script no longer
re-running, nothing regenerates the bundle either.

Vite's `--outDir` now points at `$OUT_DIR` and `include_dir!` reads
`$OUT_DIR/admin-ui-dist`. That is the Cargo rule rather than the bug fix,
but it earns its keep independently: `admin-ui/README.md` tells
developers to run `npm run build` by hand, and while the bundle lived in
the source tree doing so refreshed 78 compile inputs and rebuilt the
crate. `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` keeps its documented contract — a
pre-built `admin-ui/dist/` is copied into the baked directory, so
air-gapped builds are unaffected.

Deliberately not included: keeping the baked files' mtimes stable across
a re-run so the lib could survive one. That was implemented, measured,
and removed — cargo rebuilds a build script's dependents whenever the
script re-runs, whether or not its output changed. Not re-running the
script is the only lever, and the comments now say so.

Measured on the same tree, four consecutive builds:

    before   1m02s, 6.31s, 6.31s, 6.16s
    after    6.81s, 0.23s, 0.21s, 0.21s

A real SPA source edit still rebuilds and re-bakes; the reporter's
release-profile figure was ~4m17s per build.

Guarded two ways, because nothing existing could catch a regression
here. `tests/no_rebuild.rs` pins the two structural properties on every
`cargo test`: the baked bundle is outside the manifest directory, and no
watched input is left newer than the build script's own output stamp —
which is literally the comparison cargo makes. CI adds a "vtc-service
rebuild is a no-op" step that builds twice and fails if the second
compiles.

Reported with a full fingerprint-level diagnosis in #1243. That report
also concluded the two causes were independent and that moving `outDir`
alone would fix it; retesting showed the opposite, and the fix here
follows the retest.

Closes #1243

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc-service): assert the lockfile guard from build.rs's own verdict, not from mtimes

The `no_rebuild` regression test asserted that no `rerun-if-changed`
input was left newer than the build script's output stamp — cargo's own
staleness comparison. That failed in CI, correctly reporting
`admin-ui/package-lock.json (newer by 9.874s)`, but for a benign reason:
on a fresh checkout the runner's npm re-resolves the lockfile, which is a
genuine content change, so `build.rs` deliberately does not restore the
mtime and the build legitimately rebuilds once before settling.

An mtime comparison cannot tell that apart from the #1243 bug, because
both look identical from the test's side: the lockfile is newer than the
stamp. The distinguishing fact — whether npm changed the content — is
known only inside `build.rs`, which is where the decision is made.

So `build.rs` now records what it did (`restored`, `content-changed`,
`not-run`, or `restore-failed: <err>`) to `$OUT_DIR/lockfile-verdict` on
every path, and the test asserts on that. It fails only on
`restore-failed`, which is the case that actually means the crate
rebuilds on every `cargo build`, and rejects an unrecognised verdict so a
new variant has to teach the test rather than silently pass.

The end-to-end property is unchanged and still covered by the
"vtc-service rebuild is a no-op" CI step, which absorbs a one-off
lockfile re-resolution with settle builds.

Verified by reproducing the CI condition locally — reindenting
`package-lock.json` so npm rewrites it with different bytes yields
`content-changed` and the test passes, where the previous assertion
failed; the steady state still records `restored`, and three consecutive
builds are 9.99s / 0.54s / 0.24s.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: Add a privacy consideration for the effective disclosure of an edge
body:
Addresses #23. One paragraph, one file.

The rule proposed in #23 and supported by both @mitchuski and @albertoleon7794: **a choice of identifier constrains only its own holder's disclosure, and an edge's effective disclosure is the wider of its two halves.**

## Why it is missing today

Privacy consideration 2 covers R-DID reuse — an issuer's own failure, which the issuer can avoid. This is the other case: a *correctly* unique R-DID that is correlated to a named party because the counterparty published the opposing half under an M-DID into a readable graph. The party who loses privacy is the one who followed the specification's recommendation, through an action it neither controls nor can discover. Nothing currently warns an implementation that computing an edge's privacy from the half it issued gives the wrong answer.

## Two corrections to the framing in #23

I filed #23 as a cross-community problem. Two people have since improved on that, and the text reflects them rather than my original framing:

- @albertoleon7794's classifier returns **no answer** — not a wrong one — when asked whether a mixed edge is an R-DID or an M-DID edge, and, more usefully, showed the same failure is reachable **inside a single community** passing through the migration consideration 1 recommends. So it is not a cross-community special case, and the text says so.
- @mitchuski's observer reading generalises past two-party edges, so the paragraph closes on joint presentation: what a set of credentials discloses together may exceed what any of them discloses alone.

## Scope

Stated as a consideration rather than a normative requirement: it describes a property an implementation must compute correctly, not behaviour a credential can be checked against.

Written to stand **independently of #22**. If the declared-scope model lands, this falls out of the vocabulary and the paragraph can be shortened to the one-line rule; until then it needs saying in prose. It also does not depend on #26.

`npm run render` clean, dangling-definitions list unchanged from `main`.

title: Add a privacy consideration for the effective disclosure of an edge (#27)
body:
Add a privacy consideration for the effective disclosure of an edge (#27)

Addresses #23. An edge is two halves, each issued by its own party
under an identifier that party chose. The specification says what a
party's own identifier choice achieves, but not what happens to it
when the opposing half is published under a different one.

State the rule: a choice of identifier constrains only its own holder's
disclosure, and an edge's effective disclosure is the wider of its two
halves. An R-DID that is correctly unique to one counterparty is still
correlated to a named party if that counterparty publishes the opposing
half under an M-DID into a readable graph. Privacy consideration 2
addresses R-DID reuse, which is the issuer's own failure; this is the
case where a conforming issuer loses the privacy the recommendation was
supposed to give it, through an action it neither controls nor can
discover.

The halves may legitimately differ. That is reachable across two
communities with opposing disclosure policies, and also inside a single
community passing through the migration item 1 recommends, so it is not
a cross-community special case.

Generalised to joint presentation on the ZKP task force's observer
reading: what a set of credentials discloses together may exceed what
any of them discloses alone.

Stated as a consideration rather than a normative requirement, since it
describes a property implementations must compute correctly rather than
behaviour a credential can be checked against. It stands independently
of the vocabulary question in #22.

title: fix(ci): the semver report broke the first time every crate had a baseline
body:
Follow-up to #1252, found by running the script minutes after `vti-rooms` and
`vti-rooms-dtg` were published.

```
scripts/semver-report.sh: line 175: unpublished[@]: unbound variable
```

`"${unpublished[@]}"` on an **empty** array under `set -u` is an
unbound-variable error in bash 3.2. That array is empty precisely when every
publishable library has a crates.io baseline — the healthy state the script
exists to reach. So it worked while the two crates were unpublished and broke
the moment they were not, which is the reverse of what a guard should do.

Bash 4.4+ made the plain expansion safe, so CI on ubuntu would never have shown
it. The bash-3.2 portability added in #1252 so the script could be run on a
laptop is the only reason this surfaced before it mattered — the same property
that caught that PR's other bug (expecting binary-only crates).

Fixed with `${arr[@]+"${arr[@]}"}` on both empty-capable expansions.

Also adds the case this bug's shape suggests: if the expected set ends up empty
— everything excluded or unpublished — that is now an error rather than a run
that checks nothing and exits 0. A report covering nothing should never be
green.

## Verification

Real run on the workspace with both crates now published:

```
publishable libraries: 20   excluded for runtime: 12
checking: vta-cli-common vta-sdk vta-service vtc-client vti-common vti-rooms vti-rooms-dtg vti-secrets
coverage: all 8 expected crates were checked
```

The "NOT CHECKED — no crates.io baseline yet" line is gone and the two new
crates joined the checked set with no edit here, which is the self-healing
property #1252 claimed and could not yet demonstrate.

title: ci(semver): stop the report aborting on an unpublished crate, and assert its coverage
body:
`cargo semver-checks --workspace` does not skip a workspace member that has
never been published — it aborts the whole run with exit 101. A declared API
break also exits non-zero, so the job's red said nothing about which had
happened. Since `vti-rooms` entered the workspace, every run has ended in that
abort, and the red has been read as the expected break because that is what the
job's own warning says.

**Being exact about the damage**, since I first overstated it: the abort lands
*after* the six library crates are checked, not partway through. I pulled the
real CI log and extracted every crate that completed — `vta-cli-common`,
`vta-sdk`, `vta-service`, `vtc-client`, `vti-common`, `vti-secrets` — which is
all of them. Nothing was silently skipped. The defect is that the job cannot
say so, not that it lost coverage.

## What changes

The exclusion logic moves to `scripts/semver-report.sh`, which **derives** what
to check rather than trusting a hand-written list: publishable workspace members
with a library target, minus the runtime exclusions, minus the ones with no
crates.io baseline yet (looked up in the sparse index and named in the output
rather than passed over). Unpublished crates are excluded rather than fatal, so
the run finishes and the exit status reflects API breaks alone.

It then asserts the tool reported on every crate in that set. Both existing
guards ask *why did it stop*; neither asked *did it cover everything*, which is
why a truncating abort would have been invisible had it landed a few crates
earlier. That assertion is insurance against the next one, not a repair of this
one.

Because the set is derived, it self-heals when `vti-rooms` and `vti-rooms-dtg`
first publish: they drop out of the "no baseline yet" line and into the checked
set with no edit here.

## Why it is a script and not inline

So it can be run before it is pushed — and that immediately paid for itself. The
assertion's own first bug was expecting `pnm-cli` and `cnm-cli`, which are
binary-only and expose no API for cargo-semver-checks to compare, so it printed
nothing for them. Inline, that would have failed CI on every run. The expected
set now comes from crates with a library target.

## Verification

- Stubbed cargo, all three paths: truncated run (names the missing crates, exit
  1), clean run (exit 0), genuine break (warning, passes cargo's status through).
- Real end-to-end run: `coverage: all 6 expected crates were checked`, exit 100
  from the genuine `vta-sdk` and `vti-common` breaks rather than 101 from the
  abort.
- Portable to bash 3.2 and BSD sed, so it runs on a laptop. GitHub forces colour
  even through a pipe, so the coverage grep has to match logs with and without
  ANSI escapes.

## Not addressed here

`vta-sdk` and `vti-common` both genuinely report `semver requires new major
version`, from new variants on exhaustive enums (`AuditEvent::RoomOperation`,
`Capability::{MemoryRead, MemoryWrite, RoomPresent, RoomOpen}`). Those are
pre-existing and are release-plz's to resolve in the Release PR. This PR only
makes the report say which kind of red it is.

title: fix(persona)!: Attribute.value is OPTIONAL, so the default listing is representable
body:
The `Attribute` schema required `value` while its own description said the member is absent in two situations. The contradiction made the **default path of `persona/attribute/list` unrepresentable**.

`includeValues` defaults to `false` precisely so a picker can render the pool without decrypting every fact in it — that is the common case and the non-disclosing one. A maintainer taking it had to choose between disclosing every value in bulk and emitting a non-conformant response.

The same contradiction blocked the other documented case: a credential-backed value that could not be re-derived, returned carrying `stale` so the holder learns a claim has stopped being presentable rather than seeing a pool that looks smaller than it is.

## How it was found

A conformance witness in `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`, while wiring the family: the witness for the default listing would not round-trip through the generated types. Which is what witnesses are for — the defect was in the schema rather than the implementation, and nothing else would have caught it before the first non-disclosing read shipped.

## Breaking

Marked `!` because `value` becomes `Option<_>` in the generated Rust, which is a source break for anything already matching on it. The family published hours ago in 0.17.9 and has one consumer, unreleased — so this is the cheapest moment it will ever be.

## Checks

- `npm run build` — 403 specs validated
- Both bindings regenerated; `npm run check-bindings` — 403 specs against 403 TypeScript and 398 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- DCO signed

persona/attribute/list unrepresentable: `includeValues` defaults to false
precisely so a picker can render the pool without decrypting every fact in it,
and a maintainer taking that path had to choose between disclosing every value
in bulk and emitting a non-conformant response.

The same contradiction blocked the other documented case — a credential-backed
value that could not be re-derived, which is returned carrying `stale` so the
holder learns a claim has stopped being presentable rather than seeing a pool
that looks smaller than it is.

Found by a conformance witness in verifiable-trust-infrastructure while wiring
the family: the witness for the default listing would not round-trip. Which is
what witnesses are for — the defect was in the schema, not the implementation,
and nothing else would have caught it before the first non-disclosing read
went out.

Both bindings regenerated; conformance checks 403 specs against 403 TypeScript
and 398 Rust modules.

title: fix(tee): make allow_kms_reinit explicit authorization for reinit regardless of KMS failure type (#1249)
body:
fix(tee): make allow_kms_reinit explicit authorization for reinit regardless of KMS failure type (#1249)

* fix(tee): make allow_kms_reinit explicit authorization for reinit regardless of KMS failure type

Signed-off-by: Yaroslava Kurash <yaroslava.k@affinidi.com>

* fix(tee): clear the integrity manifest on an authorized reinit, refuse transient classes

Review follow-ups on the fail-closed change.

The reinit path this PR promotes to the only recovery route did not
produce a bootable VTA. The clear dropped the four KMS-protected rows but
left `tee:integrity-manifest`, which lives in the same bootstrap keyspace
and is MAC'd with a key derived from the storage key — itself derived from
the seed the reset discards. First boot then minted a new seed, so
`boot_verify_and_install` found a manifest whose MAC no longer verified
and aborted with "tampered with or the storage key changed": the operator
followed the error message, lost the identity, and still could not start,
with the failure pointing at parent-host compromise rather than the reset
they had just authorized. The manifest is now cleared with the ciphertexts
it is sealed against.

`allow_kms_reinit` is still the sole authorization, but it is no longer
sufficient on its own. `KMS_INTERNAL` and `NETWORK` mean KMS never
answered, so the ciphertexts have not been shown to be undecryptable;
destroying a recoverable identity on "no answer" would reopen the same
denial of service through a config that still carries the flag from an
earlier deliberate reset. Those two classes fail closed even with the flag.

The decision is extracted as `resolve_reinit(class, allow_kms_reinit) ->
ReinitDecision` (plan P3.6) and every cell of the truth table is asserted;
the branch had no test coverage at all before. `clear_reinit_state` is
likewise a named function with a test over a real store, so the manifest
cannot silently drop out of the clear list again.

An in-place reinit is still not a full reset — the discarded seed is what
every other keyspace is encrypted under — so the log lines, config doc
comment, security model and Nitro README now say so, and point at the
data-volume wipe instead. `deploy/nitro/README.md` still documented the
removed auto-recovery as the way to get a fresh identity; it now describes
the fail-closed behaviour, and its ciphertext-deletion note is corrected
for the same reason (deletion is caught by the manifest, not silently
re-minted). The tee-architecture.md justification for excluding the
ciphertexts from the manifest was circular — a parent-host deletion
consults no flag at all — and now names the manifest as the control that
actually catches it.

title: test(trust-tasks): fix doc() helper ignoring issued_at, cover the unboundable-window case
body:
## What

Fixes a bug in the `freshness_bounds::doc()` test helper: it always seeded a fresh default `issuedAt` regardless of its `issued_at: Option<&str>` argument, so `doc(None, None)` never actually built a document without one, and the test that name implied went unexercised for as long as it existed.

## What this PR does

With the helper fixed to genuinely omit `issuedAt` when `None` is passed, replaces the one test that relied on the broken helper with three that cover the actual behavior:

- a truly timestamp-less document is refused under a bounded `FreshnessPolicy` (`max_age.is_some()`) with `RejectReason::Stale { detail: Unboundable }` — SPEC §7.2 *Bounding the record*: a consumer retaining a bounded window has nowhere to place a document it can't measure the age of.
- `expiresAt` alone is sufficient without `issuedAt`.
- the same timestamp-less document is accepted under a policy with no window at all.

All six `freshness_bounds` tests pass with nothing ignored. `cargo test`, `cargo clippy`, and `cargo fmt --all --check` are clean.

## History

The first version of this PR mischaracterized the wire-level `expired` code on this path as a §7.2 item 13 violation. [@stormer78 corrected this](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1229#issuecomment-5490325599): the `expired` code here is `trust-tasks-rs`'s mapping of an internal `Stale { detail: Unboundable }` reason (there's no narrower standard code for it), governed by §7.2's *Bounding the record* clause, not item 13 — and it's driven by this VTA's own `freshness_policy()` choosing a bounded 10-minute window, not by a defect in the crate. Verified directly against the `trust-tasks-rs` 0.17.3 source (`freshness.rs:216-228`, `error.rs:525`). No upstream report needed.

title: feat(rooms): succession, so a room outlives one person's availability
body:
Implements `rooms/owner/transfer` and `rooms/owner/claim` (specs #359, #361,
published in trust-tasks-rs 0.17.9) across `vti-rooms`, `vti-rooms-dtg`,
`vtc-service`, `room-host` and `vtc-client`.

Ownership is load-bearing for liveness, not just administration: a room's owner
is its sole committer, so a room with no reachable owner cannot advance an epoch
— and one that cannot advance an epoch cannot be renewed, cannot admit anyone,
and lapses to read-only. Without succession, one person becoming unreachable
ends a shared space.

Transfer is the owner acting while present, gated on `admin`. Claim needs three
things at once: a nomination the room itself issued naming this claimant, a room
that has gone *dormant* rather than merely lapsed, and the claimant's own
membership. Each closes a different route to a takeover.

A nomination is a VAC granting `succeed` — deliberately a word no room task
accepts, so it confers nothing at all while the owner is present. Keeping it out
of the `Action` enum is what makes that structural rather than a matter of
discipline: `authorize` cannot be handed it, so no later edit there can quietly
turn a nomination into a working grant. Verification goes through
`authority::verify_chain` so the property that matters — the chain reaches *the
room* — comes from the library rather than a second hand-rolled copy.

The defence against a hostile claim is the same act as ordinary use. An owner
who was merely away defeats every pending claim by minting an epoch, which is
what they would have done anyway; nothing has to be revoked and no dispute has
to be raised. Hence dormancy rather than lapse — a window that opened the moment
an epoch expired would make every holiday one.

A claim does not renew the room. `set_owner` hands over a dormant room and
leaves it dormant, so the new owner's first act is the one that proves they can
perform it. A claim that silently renewed would hand the room to someone who
might turn out to be unable to commit, with the room looking healthy until the
next lapse a year later.

Neither host checks that an incoming owner is a member of the MLS group, because
neither can: a host holds no roster and no group state. Refusing what it cannot
verify would fail every correct transfer, and treating its own ignorance as
evidence would convert "I don't know" into "no". On claim the host uses the one
signal it has — the VMC the room issued — and the spec is exact about what that
proxy is worth.

Three defects found on the way, fixed rather than worked around:

`audit::action_name` mapped `Admin` to `room.epoch.mint`, so a transfer would
have been logged as an epoch mint — least informative exactly when someone reads
the log after an unexpected ownership change. Replaced the `(Action, bool)` pair
with a `RoomOperation` enum from which the required action is derived, so a
handler cannot gate on one thing and log another.

`wire::ROOMS_DISPATCHED_URIS` had no consumer, so `rooms/records/curate` was
dispatched by the VTC while appearing in neither the declared-URI census nor the
schema-conformance suite. Both censuses now read that constant, `room-host` gains
the routing census it never had, and curate gains its conformance entries.

Those censuses could only ever check that two of our own lists agreed, which says
nothing if both are wrong — a URI is matched as a string, so a drifted version
segment produces a service answering `unsupportedType` to a document the registry
says it serves, with nothing in Rust noticing. Now that the bindings have
published, `every_dispatched_uri_is_the_published_one` pins each constant against
its generated `TYPE_URI`, so the chain reaches the registry.

`vti-rooms-dtg`'s signed tests compiled only when another workspace member
happened to enable `test-support` and cargo unified the feature — `cargo test -p
vti-rooms-dtg` alone failed to build. A self dev-dependency fixes it.

`storage::set_owner` and `create_room` now validate the owner DID. The owner is
what a host addresses about quota, abuse and lifecycle, and the party who could
correct a bad value is the one it replaced.

The `data_room` example gains Act IV, which transfers a room, shows the same
nomination stop working the instant its owner renews, and claims an abandoned
one. §10 of the data-rooms design note gains the reasoning.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --all-features` — clean, 165 test binaries
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features` — clean
- `cargo run -p room-host --example data_room` — runs end to end, Act IV included

## Pre-merge checklist (cross-service)

- Wire types are camelCase and `deny_unknown_fields`; both new bodies validate
  against their published schemas in `vti-rooms/tests/schema_conformance.rs`.
- No new retry loop; neither verb is wrapped in one.
- No `version =` field edited. The semver report will go red on `vti-rooms` and
  `vti-rooms-dtg` — `RoomOperation` replaces `audit::action_name`, and there are
  new public items. That is the report working; release-plz puts the bump in the
  Release PR.

* docs(rooms): write the §10.5 both §5.4 and §14.2 point at

Two cross-references in this note asked the reader to see `§10.5 DID
rotation` for an answer, and no §10.5 has ever existed. Numbering the

about a party, never on who they are — so the dependency is not assumed

title: spec(rooms): the Consent/purpose section six specs shipped without
body:
The Security & Privacy lint landed **2026-08-26** (#273). These six specs landed between **3 and 5 September** — after it — each carrying `Data carried`, `Correlation` and `Retention` but not `Consent/purpose`:

| Spec | Added |
|---|---|
| `rooms/records/curate/0.1` | Sep 3 (`bb106e85`) |
| `rooms/keys/commit`, `key-package`, `welcome` `/0.1` | Sep 4 (`18cfa47f`) |
| `rooms/owner/claim/0.1`, `rooms/owner/transfer/0.1` | Sep 5 (`361cb210`) |

That distinction is the reason this is a writing job rather than an allowlist entry: the allowlist holds 307 specs as pre-existing debt and its own message says it is "only for content predating this lint". These six are not that.

## What the sections say

Each names the purpose, what records the basis, and where the purpose stops. The limit is the interesting half in all six:

- **`rooms/records/curate`** — `curate` changes what a record *counts for*, not what it says, which is why it is a grant separate from `write`. The `reason` is addressed to the room, not to the record's author, who is neither asked nor notified — no member exists through which they consent or contest. And no consent withdrawn here reaches an export taken before the retraction.
- **`rooms/owner/claim`** — the consent authorizing a claim was given in advance, by the previous owner, in the nomination. Consent given in advance decays: a nomination with no expiry is a right its issuer cannot withdraw by stopping, and stopping is definitionally what a dormant owner has done. The room's other members are not party to it and the host is not an arbiter of whether the room wanted it.
- **`rooms/owner/transfer`** — the outgoing owner's consent is contemporaneous and needs no credential. The **incoming** owner's is not recorded at all: nothing evidences that they agreed to a role carrying quota, abuse and lifecycle obligations, and afterwards the only correction is another transfer that only they can perform.
- **`rooms/keys/commit`** — there is no per-commit decision. A member who does not apply one has declined nothing; they have stopped being able to open what comes next. Consent operates at the boundaries of membership, not on each epoch inside it.
- **`rooms/keys/key-package`** — minting is not joining; the expiry is a purpose bound rather than housekeeping; and reuse across rooms joins two rooms' observers into one view of the same party, a disclosure the party never made and cannot detect.
- **`rooms/keys/welcome`** — consent reaches the member's own key-holding agent and no further. Accepting an invitation is not consenting to the host learning you are in the room, which is why a `private` room's Welcome is not routed through it.

Prose only — no front matter, schema, or generated code moves. `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings` clean.

## The second half is a policy change — strip it if you'd rather

The PR also sets `TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY: '1'` on the CI build step. **This is separable** — one `env:` block in `deploy.yml` — and it is a decision about every future PR, so it should be a deliberate yes rather than a rider.

The case for it: with these six written the non-allowlisted count is **zero**, so strict mode passes today and can only ever fire on a spec added *without* the section. The allowlist is closed to new content by definition, so this does not put the 307 legacy specs on anyone's critical path. And six specs in three days is the evidence that the warning alone does not work — it was invisible in a green build, and nothing else would have caught them.

Negative-tested: removing one `### Consent/purpose` and running the build gives

```
Security & Privacy: 95/403 spec(s) carry the section and all four sub-headings;
307 allowlisted as pre-existing debt, 1 not allowlisted (STRICT: failing the build)
Build failed with the following problems:
  - rooms/keys/commit/0.1/spec.md: is missing the sub-heading `### Consent/purpose`
```

One judgment call worth your eye: these are `rooms/*` specs and I am not their author, so the consent stories are read off each spec's own Security & Privacy prose and payload rather than out of design intent I was party to. `rooms/owner/transfer`'s "the incoming owner never consents" in particular is a claim about the design, not just about the text — if that gap is deliberate and documented elsewhere, say so and I will reword.

title: test(trust-tasks): fix doc() helper ignoring issued_at, cover the unboundable-window case (#1229)
body:
test(trust-tasks): fix doc() helper ignoring issued_at, cover the unboundable-window case (#1229)

* test(trust-tasks): expose validate_freshness rejecting a timestamp-less document

The freshness_bounds::doc() test helper always seeded a fresh default
issuedAt regardless of the issued_at: Option<&str> argument, so
doc(None, None) never actually built a document without one --
a_document_without_issued_at_is_not_refused_here silently passed
without exercising the case its own name and comment describe.

With that helper bug fixed, validate_freshness rejects a genuinely
timestamp-less document as expired, contradicting the adjacent
comment's characterization of Framework 0.5.0 Consumer Requirements
item 13 ("it does not require one"). Marked #[ignore] rather than
flipped to assert the observed behavior, so this stays a live,
re-enable-when-fixed regression test instead of silently encoding
the discrepancy as intended behavior.

Signed-off-by: Marat Shakirov <marat.s@affinidi.com>

* fixup: replace ignored test with three assertions per review

@stormer78 correctly identified that this isn't a spec violation: the
wire-level `expired` code is a mapping (RejectReason::Stale { .. } =>
StandardCode::Expired, trust-tasks-rs error.rs:525) for an internal
`Stale { detail: Unboundable }` condition, distinct from item 13's
malformed-timestamp cases. It fires from freshness.rs:216-228 when a
policy has a bounded window (max_age.is_some()) and the document has
neither issuedAt nor expiresAt to place it in that window -- governed
by SPEC §7.2 "Bounding the record", not item 13. Confirmed directly
against the trust-tasks-rs 0.17.3 source.

Replaces the single #[ignore]d test with three that assert the actual
behavior and why: a truly timestamp-less document is refused under a
bounded policy (Stale/Unboundable, not a malformed-request path);
expiresAt alone is sufficient without issuedAt; and the same
timestamp-less document is accepted under an unbounded policy. All six
freshness_bounds tests pass with nothing ignored.

Signed-off-by: Marat Shakirov <marat.s@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta)!: require issuedAt, and cap replay retention at the acceptance window

The window #1127 gave `freshness_policy` bounds a document that carries an
`issuedAt`. It leaves two shapes a consumer keeping a duplicate-execution
record cannot answer honestly, and fixing the `doc()` helper is what made the
first of them visible.

**A document with no timestamp at all was answered `expired`.**
`validate_freshness` refuses it as `Stale { detail: Unboundable }`, which the
library maps to the wire code `expired` because §8.3 defines no narrower one.
That check runs at the top of `dispatch_trust_task_validated`, ~250 lines
before `schema_index::spec_policy_for(..).enforce(..)` — so for the 105 of 209
indexed specs that declare `IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED`, the spec's own rule, the
one that names the missing member, was unreachable. `expired` names a document
that was once acceptable and tells the producer to wait; this one was never
acceptable, so the producer waits, reissues the same shape, and loops. It is
the principle `a_future_dated_document_is_malformed_not_expired` already pins,
and the crate says the same on `IS_ISSUED_AT_REQUIRED`: `expired` "would
misdescribe a document that was never acceptable".

**A document carrying only `expiresAt` had no bounded acceptance window.** It
was accepted — an `expiresAt` does bound the record — but the bound was then
whatever instant the producer chose. `expiresAt = now + 10 years` is accepted
for ten years, and §7.2 makes the replay record's retention that same bound,
so the producer decided unilaterally how long this VTA must remember its `id`.

`requiring_issued_at` closes both, and makes the last instant any accepted
document can return provable: `issuedAt + max_age + skew`. `retain_until` then
caps on it, because `record_expiry` takes a producer-supplied `expiresAt`
verbatim — an entry held past the last moment it could be needed crowds out
the ones that are, which is the load-dependent eviction horizon #1127 set out
to close. The cap only ever moves retention earlier than the producer asked
for, never earlier than the window; shortening it below the window is the
direction §7.2 forbids.

This is a consumer posture stricter than most specs, and the cost is worth
stating: 104 of the 209 indexed URIs — the read-shaped ones, `acl/list`,
`auth/whoami`, `config/show`, `device/heartbeat` — leave `issuedAt` OPTIONAL.
For all but one shape that costs nothing, because the refusal already happens
and only the code changes. The one shape that moves from accepted to refused
is `expiresAt` present with `issuedAt` absent. It is the posture
`FreshnessPolicy::consequential` describes, scoped by the crate to "any
specification whose execution is consequential, which is exactly the set for
which item 11 applies" — and this spine applies item 11 to every document it
dispatches, `whoami` included.

Tests: `without_a_window_a_timestampless_document_is_accepted` validated
against a `FreshnessPolicy::default()` this service never uses, so it passed
whatever `freshness_policy` did — including its deletion. Replaced with
`the_services_policy_bounds_both_the_window_and_the_member`, which pins the
service's own policy, plus a `record_retention` module covering the cap in
both directions. Every one of them fails when the corresponding fix is
reverted.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(sdk): stamp issuedAt on messaging/ping, which a bounded VTA refuses

`TspPingSession::ping`, `TspPingSession::probe_send` and
`TspSession::announce` each built a `messaging/ping/0.1` document carrying
neither `issuedAt` nor `expiresAt`. A consumer that keeps a
duplicate-execution record bounds acceptance by the same window it retains
that record over (SPEC §7.2, *Bounding the record*), and a document with no
timestamp cannot be placed in any window — so from #1127, when the VTA set a
10-minute window, the probe was refused before it reached the handler.

Refused as `expired`, which reads as a transport delay rather than a
malformed document, so the failure looked exactly like the timeout it is not.
A liveness probe that a live peer refuses is worse than no probe: it reports
the transport broken when the transport is fine.

The three call sites are now one `ping_document` builder, because the thing
they had in common was the member they all left out. `issuedAt` alone is the
right bound for a client to carry — an `expiresAt` would put the consumer's
retention obligation in the client's hands.

`ping` reads its correlation nonce back off the built document rather than
keeping it alongside; the two have to be the same value for `correlates` to
mean anything.

The test asserts against `FreshnessPolicy::consequential` rather than
`issued_at.is_some()`: the latter passes on a document the consumer still
refuses, so it would not have caught this.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(sdk): gate ping_document on tsp, its callers' feature

`TspPingSession` and `TspSession` are both `tsp`-only, so under `session`
alone the shared builder has no consumer and `-D warnings` fails the
`vta-service rest only` feature combo on dead code. Gate it and its tests with
the callers.

Exactly what that CI step exists to catch: `cargo test --workspace` unifies
features across the graph, so `tsp` is on there and the build is green. Only a
narrowed combo compiles the function without its callers.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(ci): the two SDKs' error Type URI is a hand-edited constant in two languages
body:
Third of the same class as #362 and #363, and the one with no defect behind it yet — which is the point of adding it now.

## The unguarded invariant

`trust-task-error` is in the codegen's `SKIP_SLUGS`. The Rust side is hand-modelled in `error.rs`, the TypeScript side in `_runtime/document.ts`, so the version each SDK stamps on every error document it emits is a hand-edited constant, once per language:

| | |
|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs/src/document.rs` | `trust_task_error_type_uri()` → `TypeUri::canonical("trust-task-error", 0, 5)` |
| `trust-tasks-ts/src/_runtime/document.ts` | `TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI = "…/trust-task-error/0.5"` |

CLAUDE.md already tells you to point **both** at a new version when a standard error code lands. Nothing checked that you did. Update one and not the other and the two libraries disagree about the `type` of every error document they produce — and **no drift check can see it**, because both constants are hand-written, so regenerating reproduces them exactly as they stand and the diff is empty. That is precisely the "a generator that is consistently wrong" row of CLAUDE.md's own CI table.

They agree today — both `0.5`, which is also the newest published. I'd rather add the check while that's true than after it stops being.

## The check

Lives in `check-bindings-conformance.mjs`, whose job is already "generated Rust and TS agree with each specification and with each other". It does not touch, or DRY up, the deliberately duplicated policy derivation that file's comment warns about.

- **The two disagreeing fails the build.** There is no reading under which two SDKs emitting different error document types is intended.
- **Both lagging the newest published version prints a note, not a failure.** A published version may be deliberately unadopted, so lagging is a decision; disagreeing never is.
- Naming a version that does not exist under `specs/trust-task-error/` fails.

Negative-tested both branches:

```
- trust-tasks-rs / trust-tasks-ts: the two SDKs emit different error documents:
  trust-tasks-rs sends trust-task-error/0.5 (document.rs, trust_task_error_type_uri)
  and @openvtc/trust-tasks sends trust-task-error/0.4 (_runtime/document.ts,
  TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI). A new error specification version must be adopted in
  both or neither.

  note: both SDKs emit trust-task-error/0.4; specs/trust-task-error/0.5 is published.
  Adopt it in trust_task_error_type_uri() and TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI together, or
  leave both.
```

## CLAUDE.md

Adds rows for this check **and** for #363's two, and writes up the fourth instance of the hand-maintained-list failure mode next to the three already recorded there. That means this PR documents checks that #363 introduces — **merge it after #363**, or the table names two functions that do not exist yet.

Script and docs only; no specs, schemas, front matter or generated code move.
