title: fix(bindings): four bindings advertised one framework target and described another
body:
Follow-up to #362, which fixed this in `didcomm-v1/0.2` while it was open for other reasons. This is the rest of the sweep, plus the two checks that stop it recurring.

## Two drifts, neither visible to anything

**1. The framework target.** #308 moved `targetFrameworkVersion` to `0.5` in the five current bindings and updated no prose. Four of them have been advertising one target to the registry and describing another to the reader ever since:

| Binding | Front matter | Prose said |
|---|---|---|
| `didcomm/0.2` | `0.5` | `0.3` |
| `https/0.2` | `0.5` | `0.2` |
| `push/0.1` | `0.5` | `0.2` |
| `tsp/0.1` | `0.5` | `0.2` |

**2. A pinned error-specification version, one instance of which is an outright defect.** Three current bindings still named `trust-task-error/0.2` after the error spec reached `0.5`. In `didcomm/0.2` that produced a sentence an implementer cannot follow:

> The framework's `errored` state is carried by a `trust-task-error/0.2` document, which names the reported-on document by `inResponseTo`.

`inResponseTo` landed in `trust-task-error/0.3` (#185, from the #173 thread). `0.2`'s payload schema does not define it, so a consumer following that sentence literally emits a document that fails payload validation.

A binding should not pin the error specification's version at all — SPEC §8.1 routes an error response to the current one, so the pin is never what a consumer emits and can only rot. All 19 references across the four current bindings now name `trust-task-error` unversioned, which is what `didcomm-v1/0.2` already did. `didcomm/0.1` and `https/0.1` keep theirs: they target framework `0.2`, where `trust-task-error/0.2` *was* current, and they are superseded.

## Two checks, because this is the fourth instance of one failure mode

CLAUDE.md already documents three: the category taxonomy, the reserved-slug allowlist, the binding registry. Each is a hand-maintained list that nothing compared against the tree, and each shipped a defect before it was guarded. This is the same shape — the registry publishes front matter, the reader reads prose, nothing compared them.

- **`checkBindingFrameworkTarget()`** compares each binding's bold `Targets **framework `X`**` claim against its front matter and fails on disagreement; warns where a binding states no target in prose at all. It matches only the **bold** form on purpose — prose comparing versions in passing ("targets framework `0.5` rather than `0.3`") is history, not a claim about the current target, and sweeping it in would make the check unusable.
- **`checkBindingErrorSpecPin()`** fails on any `trust-task-error/<MAJOR.MINOR>` reference in a current binding. A superseded binding — one with a higher `MINOR` of the same slug on disk — is exempt and counted in a summary line, the same treatment §5.3 retired specs already get in this build (`Error spec pins: 7 frozen in superseded binding(s) (exempt, not debt); 0 in current bindings`).

Both were negative-tested by reintroducing each drift into `push/0.1` and confirming the build fails with the message that names the fix:

```
- bindings/push/0.1/spec.md: prose says "Targets **framework `0.4`**" but front matter
  declares targetFrameworkVersion: "0.5". …
- bindings/push/0.1/spec.md: names trust-task-error/0.4 (1 reference(s)). A binding does
  not pin the error specification's version: SPEC §8.1 routes an error response to the
  current one… Name it `trust-task-error` unversioned, as bindings/didcomm-v1/0.2 does.
```

Prose and build script only — no front matter, schema, or generated code moves. `npm run validate`, `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings`, `npm run test:infra` and `npm run validate-ceremonies` all clean.

title: DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its taskContext binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)
body:
# DTG Core Credentials now cites this framework normatively for its `taskContext` binding (pinned to existing mechanisms; one small optional ask)

## Context

[trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#11](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/11) flagged that DTG Core Credentials placed normative requirements on `taskContext`-bearing credentials (outcome evidence, terminal states, etc.) that depended on "the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification" — which doesn't exist yet, so the requirements were untestable.

Resolution ([dtgwg-cred-spec#15](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/15)) restructures that section to depend only on mechanisms **already defined in this framework's current editor's draft**, rather than on any future spec:

- **Terminal state** = presence of a `#response`-variant document ([§4.4.1](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#441-request-and-response-variants)) or a `trust-task-error` document ([§8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#8-error-responses)), correlated by `threadId` ([§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member)).
- **Outcome integrity** = the existing per-specification `proof`-required declaration ([§7.3 item 8](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Outcome artifact structure** = the existing per-specification `#response` payload schema ([§7.3 item 7.6](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements)).
- **Evidence discovery / retrieval authorization / confidentiality** — sidestepped for cred-spec's v1.0 by requiring the outcome document to travel *with* the credential presentation, rather than be discovered/retrieved asynchronously by a verifier who wasn't party to the original exchange. (This framework's bilateral, transport-bound request/response model doesn't naturally support that kind of later, third-party retrieval, so cred-spec isn't relying on it.)

cred-spec now requires that any Trust Task specification a VTC/VTN designates as the referent of a DTG credential's `taskContext` — a "qualifying" specification — declare `proof` REQUIRED on its response/error variants and define a `#response` schema (or rely on `trust-task-error`). That's it; no framework behavior change required for this to work.

**No action needed on your side for cred-spec's fix to land.** Filing this mainly so you're aware of the cross-reference (per the coordination cred-spec's Governance Considerations already calls for between the two task forces), and to flag one small, genuinely optional framework enhancement that would make part of this more robust.

## Optional ask: let a Trust Task specification declare `threadId` as REQUIRED-and-unique

cred-spec needs `taskContext` (its own name for a `threadId`) to reliably name *one specific* exchange. Right now `threadId` is framework-wide `MAY`, and [§4.9](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#49-the-threadid-member) is explicit that it "carries no normative validation semantics" — no presence guarantee, no uniqueness guarantee, and consumers can't reject on it.

cred-spec works around this by putting the uniqueness burden entirely on DTG *issuers* (its own conformance target), which is sufficient for cred-spec's purposes but means the framework's own consumer-side machinery can't enforce it — a misbehaving issuer's threadId reuse isn't independently rejectable the way, say, a missing required `proof` is (`proofRequired`, [§7.2 item 7](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

Proposal: add a declarable property to [§7.3](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#73-specification-requirements), mirroring item 8's Proof requirement pattern:

> **Thread requirement** — an explicit statement of whether `threadId` is OPTIONAL or REQUIRED for documents implementing the specification, together (where REQUIRED) with the uniqueness scope it MUST satisfy (e.g., "unique per exchange instance for the life of the specification's use"). A conforming consumer MUST reject a document lacking a REQUIRED `threadId` with `malformedRequest`, consistent with the existing `recipient`-required pattern ([§7.2 item 5](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/blob/main/SPEC.md#72-consumer-requirements)).

This is additive only — it doesn't touch `threadId`'s existing general-purpose, loosely-specified behavior for specifications that don't opt in. It would let a future DTG-ceremony Trust Task specification (or any other specification with the same need) get framework-level enforcement instead of relying on the depending spec's issuer-side discipline alone.

Happy to draft this as a PR here if it's wanted, or to help co-author a worked-example Trust Task specification for a DTG ceremony (e.g. relationship witnessing) satisfying the "qualifying" profile above, as a joint appendix in either repo — similar in spirit to your own Appendix A. Let us know which is useful.

title: spec(didcomm-v1): the three implementer findings the 0.2 carriage left unwritten
body:
Closes the tail of #173. Three findings from @albertoleon7794's Credo 0.6.3 measurements ([ref-06v1e](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06v1e-type-shape), [ref-06v1c](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06v1c-task-layer)) arrived after `didcomm-v1/0.2` merged and were never written into the binding. Three edits since (#276, #294, #308) passed over them.

Prose only. No front matter moves, so no schema, codegen or registry impact — `npm run validate`, `npm run build` and `npm run check-bindings` are clean.

### §2.2 — the two discover-features findings

**Registering a handler advertises nothing.** In Credo, registering the message class and its handler makes an agent able to *receive* this binding's messages; it does not make it *discoverable* as speaking it. An agent that expects to be found by negotiation **MUST** register the RFC 0031 protocol as a separate step. This matters because the bullet above it already tells producers to negotiate first: an agent that skips the registration answers nothing, and the producer concludes — correctly, on the evidence available — that the peer does not speak the binding.

**Query by document-URI wildcard.** Because the binding version sits in the document URI, a query naming an exact protocol matches one binding version only. `https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm-v1/*` is the sole form that spans them.

### §3 — case 2 changed homes with the carriage

Under `0.1`'s `basic-message`, Credo rejected an envelope whose sender bound to no known DID inside its own module, before any application code ran. Under the dedicated type the same envelope reaches the registered handler **with no connection attached**.

Nothing normative changes, and this is arguably the better home for it — the three-way split of §3 is the *consumer*'s decision, not the transport's. But the rules are now the consumer's to enforce rather than something filtered beneath it, and an implementer trusting the old description skips the unauthenticated-sender mapping on exactly the messages that need it. The new paragraph says so, and closes the fallback explicitly: a message delivered with no connection **MUST NOT** fall back to the document's in-band `issuer` for want of a transport-derived sender.

`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` already gets this right — `unpack_trust_task` distinguishes `AuthcryptUnknownSender` from the unauthenticated cases and never constructs a handler for either — so this is the spec catching up to the implementation, not a behaviour change.

### §1 + new §7.2 — the reach question, answered slightly against the report

The measurement reported that each binding bump mints a new protocol identity, so a `0.2` handler never sees `0.3` traffic and the producer never learns — "recurring at every future bump".

That holds only if the `@type` is re-minted at each version, which §1 already said it is not: the value is minted at `0.2` and pinned, exactly as `binding/didcomm/0.2` keeps `binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope`. So the loss is not recurring — but §1 stated the pin as description rather than obligation, which is how it came to be read as one that would drift. It is now normative (**MUST NOT** re-mint), with the RFC 0020 routing reason spelled out.

New **§7.2** states what the pin does *not* buy, which is the sentence that was asked for: reach across a change of spelling is not a property of the version number, **MUST NOT** be inferred from one, and belongs to capability negotiation. §2.3 is the same obligation discharged from the receiving side.

### Two stale lines fixed while here

- Front matter has said `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.5"` since #308, but the Status section and §7.1 still said `0.4`. **The same drift is in the other four current bindings** (`didcomm/0.2`, `https/0.2`, `push/0.1`, `tsp/0.1` all say `0.2` in prose against `0.5` in front matter) — #308 moved front matter only. Left for its own `fix(bindings):` PR rather than widening this one; nothing here depends on it.
- §8 described `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` as implementing the `0.1` carriage and needing updating. It doesn't — `ENVELOPE_TYPE` is the dedicated type and `basic-message` sits behind the `legacy-basic-message` feature. That was the last "still yours" item from the #173 thread, done but never written down.

/cc @albertoleon7794 @bmiller59

body:
### Added

- **persona**: A holder's own identity, composed once and disclosed under control ([#360](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/360))

* feat(persona): attribute pool — shared schema and attribute/put

  First slice of the persona family: the holder's own identity attributes,
  agent-scoped above the context boundary.

  The shared schema carries the family's load-bearing definitions — the three
  provenance kinds, the four profile-entry forms, the proof-rung ordering, and
  the two-scope rule that keeps a context-scoped caller from reading the pool.

  attribute/put establishes the pattern: holder-authorized and unscoped,
  value validated against its declared type, credential-backed provenance
  resolved at write time so an attribute cannot read back stale forever, and an
  advisory correlation count returned on the write so a builder can warn while
  the holder is still composing.

- **rooms/owner**: Transfer and claim, so a room outlives one person ([#359](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/359))

§10 of the data-rooms design was the last part with no specification.
  Ownership there is load-bearing for liveness, not just administration: a
  room's owner is its sole committer, so a room with no reachable owner
  cannot advance an epoch, cannot be renewed, and lapses to read-only. One
  person becoming unreachable ends a shared space.

  Two tasks, not one with a flag. They end the same way and differ in
  everything else - who initiates, what authorizes, and whether the room
  has to have lapsed. Collapsing them would mean either a transfer that
  waits for a lapse or a claim that works while the owner is still
  renewing, and both are wrong.

  There is deliberately no nominate task. A nomination is a credential the
  room issues and the claimant presents, the same shape as an invitation
  and for the same reason: a host keeping a roster of successors would hold
  part of the room's authority structure, and the room could no longer move
  hosts without rebuilding it. The consequence is that 'no successor' and
  'the successor has not claimed yet' are the same observation to a host -
  which is fine, because both resolve identically when retention runs out.

  A claim is an ACT, never an automatic promotion, and that is not
  ceremony. An automatic one is an ownership change nobody performed: no
  actor to audit, no moment to point at, and an owner who returns finds the
  room changed hands with no event to examine.

  Three conditions, all required, each closing a different route to a
  takeover: a nomination the room itself issued naming this claimant; the
  room dormant rather than merely lapsed, so the grace window has passed
  and the owner has had their notice; and the claimant already a member,
  because a successor who cannot commit inherits a room they cannot renew.

  Renewing cancels a pending claim, and that is the property worth
  noticing: the defence against a hostile claim is the same act as ordinary
  use. An owner who was merely away fixes it by doing what they would have
  done anyway - nothing revoked, no dispute raised.

  Transfer requires the incoming owner to be a member for the same reason.
  Handing someone a room they cannot renew looks like success and produces
  a room that lapses on schedule a year later with nobody able to save it.

  Three things the Security sections say plainly. A transfer does NOT
  remove the outgoing owner - they keep whatever their credentials confer,
  usually still admin, so handing over and leaving are two more acts. Every
  credential stays valid because the room's identifier does not change,
  which is the whole reason a room has an identifier of its own rather than
  borrowing its owner's. And the host is not an arbiter: it records what an
  authorized party told it, and ownership of an identifier is settled by
  whoever controls that identifier, not by a service that stores
  ciphertext.



### Documentation

- Base every example on the registered acl/change-role task ([#356](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/356))

SPEC.md, both READMEs, the loopback example and the framework unit tests
  all illustrated themselves with `kyc-handoff/1.0`, a slug that has never
  been registered. Three consequences, in increasing order of cost:

  - `https://trusttasks.org/spec/kyc-handoff/1.0` is a live URL in the
    Abstract and in five worked examples. It resolves — the registry site
    serves the SPA for any /spec/ path — and rendered `acl/change-role`,
    the alphabetically first entry, because SpecPage fell back to
    `TT_TASKS[0]` for an unresolvable slug. A reader following the URL in
    §1 got a complete, confident page for a different task.
  - No example could be checked against anything. The build validates every
    fenced JSON block against the framework envelope schema; a payload
    naming a slug with no schema was structurally unverifiable.
  - The `trust-task-error` extended-code example was non-conforming: it
    answered an ACL request with a `kyc-handoff:`-namespaced code, which
    §8.5 forbids in the same breath as it defines namespacing.

  Everything now names `acl/change-role/0.1`, whose payloads validate
  against its published schema, whose error codes are the two it declares,
  and whose REQUIRED `proof` the examples honour. Appendix A is reproduced
  from that registry entry rather than invented. The framework parser tests
  that used the slug as an arbitrary string now use real ones —
  `trust-task-discovery` and `trust-task-control` where a single-segment
  slug is the point.

  SpecPage is strict as a result: an unregistered slug, or a known slug at
  an unknown version, renders a not-found page offering the versions that
  do exist, the way BindingSpecPage and CeremonyPage already did. The
  lookup moved into a hook-free wrapper so a route that stops resolving
  unmounts the detail view rather than changing a mounted component's hook
  count.

  SPEC.md is also maintained canonically at trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec;
  the matching change lands there in parallel.



### Fixed

- **rooms/owner**: A host cannot see the MLS group, so stop implying it can ([#361](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/361))

Both tasks required a host to check that a party is a member of the
  room's group. A host holds no roster and no group state, so neither check
  was implementable as written. Found while starting the implementation,
  which is what implementation is for.

  claim now carries a presentation. The host has exactly one membership
  signal available - the VMC the room itself issued - and the claim payload
  did not ask for it, so condition 3 was unimplementable and the claimant's
  own standing went unverified. It is now required, and it is the same
  presentation every other room task carries.

  The spec is also exact about what that proxy is worth: a party removed
  from the MLS group while still holding an unexpired VMC would pass. That
  gap closes by revoking the credential, which is the room's job, not the
  host's. Better said than implied.

  transfer moves the obligation to the party who can discharge it. The
  incoming owner is not the one making the request, presents nothing, and
  may be someone the host has never seen - so 'MUST refuse if not a member'
  asked a host to judge a third party from no evidence. The requirement is
  now on the transferring owner, who can see the group; a host that can
  independently establish non-membership MAY still refuse, and one that
  cannot MUST NOT invent a check or treat its own ignorance as evidence.

  That last point is the same boundary the rest of the family draws,
  arriving from an unfamiliar direction: a host verifies what is presented
  to it, and a claim about a third party is not that.

title: feat(pnm-cli): add memory command group
body:
Adds a `pnm memory` command group wrapping the VTA's per-context agent-memory Trust Tasks (`spec/vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1`).

Subcommands:
- `plant <key> <value>` — upsert an entry
- `recall [key]` — list entries, or one by key
- `forget <key>` — delete one entry
- `wipe` — delete all entries in a context (confirmation unless `--force`)

All are context-scoped via `--context` (default `default`) and support `--json`.
author: marat-affinidi

title: feat(pnm-cli): add memory command group (#1222)
body:
feat(pnm-cli): add memory command group (#1222)

* feat(pnm-cli): add memory command group

Add `pnm memory` for CRUD over the VTA's per-context agent memory
(`spec/vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1`): plant, recall, forget, wipe.
Context-scoped via `--context` (default `default`); `--json` supported.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Marat Shakirov <marat.s@affinidi.com>

* fix(pnm-cli): require --context on memory, and correct its gate docs

Three things on top of the memory command group, all found reviewing it
against main after #1234 landed underneath it.

--context no longer defaults to "default". Nothing in `vta setup` creates
a context with that id — ids are operator-chosen slugs — and a
super-admin's `require_context` is `ActScope::Unrestricted.covers(_)`,
true for any string, with no existence check in the memory handlers. So
the no-flag path wrote into a context that need not exist, and `recall`
answered "Context 'default' has no memories", which reads as a
legitimate empty answer rather than "you forgot to scope this". A
mistyped `--context` did the same. Required, like `pnm keys create
--context`, with clap refusing as the guard and a test pinning it.

The gate description was stale. #1234 put `MemoryRead` / `MemoryWrite`
in front of the context check, so `wipe` needs both capabilities (it
lists before it deletes) and a `reader` is refused every write. The help
text, the shared module docs and `docs/02-vta/personal-ai-agents.md`
(which still said "the gate is context access, not a capability") now
say so, and the doc gained the `pnm memory` walkthrough it was missing.

Flag and name consistency with the rest of the CLI: `--force` means
"hard-delete rather than soft-delete" on the vault commands, so the
skip-the-prompt flag is `--yes` here as it is on `pnm keys create`, with
`--force` kept as an alias. The novel `-c` / `-f` shorts are gone — no
other pnm subcommand has command-level shorts. `LlmMemory` /
`llm_memory.rs` become `Memory` / `memory.rs`, matching the command, the
shared module and the workspace's "agent memory" vocabulary; each
subcommand also takes a hidden alias under the Trust Task's own verb
(put / list / delete / clear).

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(persona): a holder's own identity, composed once and disclosed under control
body:
Adds the `persona` family — 24 tasks under `category: identity` — for the identity information a holder keeps about themselves, and the contact records peers disclose to them.

This is a fourth holder store, beside the credential vault, agent memory and application state. It is distinct because **disclosure control is its point**: a maintainer that cannot read a record cannot decide which of its members may leave, cannot audit which ones did, and cannot answer *"what have I shared with whom."* `vta/app-state` promises never to interpret its records, so it cannot host this; and a namespace there is collision avoidance rather than a trust boundary, so a compromised application sharing a context could remove a holder's identity data.

## The shape

A holder keeps a pool of **attributes** — atomic facts, each self-asserted, credential-backed or minted per verifier. A **profile** is a named *projection* over that pool that references facts rather than copying them, so a phone number changed once is changed everywhere. A **binding** assigns a profile to a persona DID in a context. **Disclosure** projects a bound profile to one verifier, after a preview. A **contact** is the same claim set arriving from the other direction.

## Decisions the schemas make normative

**Two scopes, and the split is a control rather than filing.** The pool and profiles are *agent-scoped*, above every context, so the correlation check can see the risk it most needs to report: the same value presented by two personas in two different contexts, which a per-context index cannot see by construction. Bindings, contacts and disclosure records are context-scoped.

Eleven tasks are therefore **holder-authorized and unscoped**, and each says so normatively. The check is on the *scope* axis, not the role axis — a guard written as "is this caller an administrator" passes for an administrator scoped to a single context, who could then read every other context's identity data.

**`binding/set` is the critical gate.** An application able to call it could bind any profile to a persona it controls and read the result back through a disclosure it requests of itself. Every other read leaks; this one is directly exploitable.

**`preview` and `present` cannot be collapsed.** `present` consumes a single-use `previewId`, so there is no code path to a disclosure that did not first produce the summary a human can be shown — structural, not a flag someone can forget.

**Proof rung is reported and never silently downgraded.** *"You will prove you are over the threshold without disclosing your date of birth, and this proof cannot be linked to any other site you have used it at"* is a materially different offer from *"this verifier receives your entire licence."* A request that cannot be met at the rung asked for is refused, because a silent privacy downgrade discloses material the holder believed was hidden.

**Renderer lossiness is declared, not discovered.** Most general-purpose contact formats have nowhere to put provenance. A disclosure containing a predicate through a renderer that cannot carry one fails at negotiation rather than dropping the claim — a verifier receiving fewer claims than were approved cannot tell that from a holder who approved fewer.

**Correlation severity is a function of value *and* rung.** The inversion is easy to get backwards: a credential presented **whole** correlates *more* than a self-asserted value, because the issuer signature is identical at every verifier, while a derived proof correlates *less* because it differs every presentation. Scoring on provenance alone would push holders toward the riskier option.

**Write tasks return counts; `correlation/analyze` returns identifiers.** A count is enough to warn, and identifiers on a write would disclose the holder's other compositions to whatever tool made it. `analyze` is holder-authorized and its purpose is to let the holder *act*, which nobody can do on a number — including via `reissueCredentialToThisDid`, without which a holder told "this links your personas" has no action but to abandon the attribute.

**Contacts are revisioned, never overwritten.** An address book that silently replaces a payment address is a phishing surface; one that reports what changed and when is a defence. A contact belongs to a *relationship* — the same peer met through two personas is two contacts, because collapsing them would correlate the holder's own personas inside their own address book.

**The local surface is isolated by address space, not by a filter.** Authoring *below* the boundary is safe; the rule exists to stop reading *across* it. Local profiles occupy their own address space and admit only inline entries, so a reference is unrepresentable rather than rejected. `local/binding/set` is context-callable precisely because both objects it names live below the boundary — and must refuse a `profileId` naming a pool profile, which is the one escalation that would otherwise reappear in the task that looks harmless.

## Checks

- `npm run build` — 401 specs validated, no warnings from this family
- `TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY=1 npm run build` — clean; all 24 carry the four mandated sub-headings and none is on the allowlist
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — 396 Rust modules; the `persona` feature registered itself
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 464 TS modules
- `npm run check-bindings` — 401 specifications against 401 TypeScript and 396 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` — 786 passing
- DCO sign-off on all 7 commits

No version bumped and no CHANGELOG written — release-plz owns those.

## Notes for review

`category: identity` already existed and its own description names *"persona tasks"*, so no taxonomy change and no `data.js` update is needed.

The design these come from is in `design-docs/persona-profiles-design.md`, with the first consumer — a vetting and joining flow — in `design-docs/persona-to-membership-design.md`.

Two things I would particularly value a second opinion on: whether `persona` belongs at the top level (alongside `vault/`) or under `vta/` (alongside `app-state`), and whether the agent-scoped/context-scoped split is better expressed as two families than as one with a per-task authorization note.

title: feat(persona): a holder's own identity, composed once and disclosed under control (#360)
body:
feat(persona): a holder's own identity, composed once and disclosed under control (#360)

* feat(persona): attribute pool — shared schema and attribute/put

First slice of the persona family: the holder's own identity attributes,
agent-scoped above the context boundary.

The shared schema carries the family's load-bearing definitions — the three
provenance kinds, the four profile-entry forms, the proof-rung ordering, and
the two-scope rule that keeps a context-scoped caller from reading the pool.

attribute/put establishes the pattern: holder-authorized and unscoped,
value validated against its declared type, credential-backed provenance
resolved at write time so an attribute cannot read back stale forever, and an
advisory correlation count returned on the write so a builder can warn while
the holder is still composing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(persona): complete the attribute family — list and delete

list withholds values by default, because the common case (rendering a picker)
needs type and label, not plaintext; making includeValues opt-in puts the
sensitive path behind an explicit ask rather than behind forgetting. Stale
credential-backed attributes are returned rather than hidden, so a holder
learns a claim has stopped being presentable instead of seeing a pool that
looks smaller than it is.

delete refuses a referenced attribute by default and names the referring
profiles. Profiles reference rather than copy, so removing one fact would
change what several profiles disclose; cascade does that deliberately and
returns which changed. A repeat delete converges — existed: false, and
pointedly no new version, so watchers never see a change that did not happen.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(persona): profile/put — composition over the pool

A profile references attributes rather than copying them, so a fact edited
once is edited everywhere it appears. Four entry forms cover the cases
reference alone handles badly: pin a version for a profile that must keep
presenting what a counterparty verified, override a value for one profile,
or inline a value that never enters the pool and so can never leak into
another profile.

Omission is exclusion — a profile is a whitelist, because a blacklist over a
growing pool leaks by default the first time an attribute is added.

An override replaces value and label only. Letting it replace provenance
would let a self-asserted value present as attested, which is the one thing
provenance exists to prevent.

An unresolved reference refuses the whole write: a partially-applied
composition would disclose less than the holder composed and say nothing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(persona): profile get/list/delete and the binding pair

profile/get resolves on request only — resolution decrypts values and
re-derives credential-backed ones, so the default returns the composition,
which is enough to edit it. profile/list has no resolve option at all:
offering it would decrypt the whole pool to answer a question about names.

profile/delete refuses while a persona is bound, because a persona that
silently stopped presenting anything is a failure the holder discovers from
the other side. The pool is untouched — a profile references rather than
owns, which is the asymmetry with attribute/delete.

binding/set is the family's critical gate. It is the push that carries a
composition across the context boundary, and what lands is a materialised
claim set with no back-reference into the pool — so a compromised context
sees what was pushed and nothing leads anywhere else. Correlation is scored
here as well as at composition, because composing is hypothetical and
binding is when a value actually crosses.

binding/get is context-callable and deliberately thin: whether a profile is
bound, its label, and a claim count. Never contents. With the disclosure
path it exhausts what a context-scoped caller can obtain — an application in
a context is a verifier, not an insider.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(persona): the contact family

A contact is what a peer disclosed, filed by revision and never overwritten.
An address book that silently replaces a payment address is a phishing
surface; one that reports what changed and when is a defence — which is what
changedClaims and hasUnreviewedChange are for. A revision history nobody is
shown is an archive, not a defence.

A contact belongs to a relationship, not to the holder at large: the same
peer met through two personas is two contacts. Collapsing them would
correlate the holder's own personas inside their own address book, which is
the one place nobody would think to look for that linkage.

The claim set a peer discloses is structurally the claim set a holder
composes — one schema seen from two sides — so one validator serves both.

Two honesty rules. A reaped revision reports revisionReaped and not
notFound, because a caller comparing against history must tell 'never
existed' from 'no longer kept'. And delete reports how many revisions
survived because a disclosure record references them: an incomplete erasure
the holder believes is complete is worse than one they know about.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(persona): disclosure, correlation and renderer negotiation

preview and present are two calls that cannot be collapsed: present consumes
a single-use previewId, so there is no code path to a disclosure that did not
first produce the summary a human can be shown, and a maintainer cannot
accidentally provide one.

The preview reports three things a flat field list would not. The proof rung
per claim, because 'you will prove you are over the threshold without
disclosing your date of birth' is a materially different offer from 'this
verifier receives your entire licence'. What the renderer drops, declared
rather than discovered. And what is anomalous for the stated purpose —
fourteen fields at fourteen equal weights is the pattern that trains people
to click through.

present refuses whole rather than issuing short when a claim has gone stale:
a verifier receiving fewer claims than were approved cannot tell that from a
holder who approved fewer. The disclosure record is written before the
artifact is returned, so a crash cannot release data that was never recorded.

history pays a debt the design incurred. Putting the pool above the context
boundary bought cross-context correlation checking; the cost is that a holder
can no longer tell from one context where a fact has gone. Filtering by
attributeType settles it.

analyze returns identifiers where the write tasks return counts, because its
purpose is to let the holder act and nobody can act on a number. It names
reissueCredentialToThisDid, without which a holder told 'this links your
personas' has no action but to abandon the attribute.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(persona): persona/list, the context-local surface, and regenerated bindings

persona/list carries the same thin summary as binding/get and for the same
reason: an application needs to know which identity is in use, not what it
contains. isLocal distinguishes what the application authored from what the
holder pushed down, because treating the two identically is how a throwaway
comes to be trusted like a curated identity.

The local surface exists because authoring BELOW the boundary is safe, and
forbidding it would over-apply a rule that exists to stop reading ACROSS it.
The isolation is structural rather than a check: local profiles occupy their
own address space, so a context-scoped enumeration scans somewhere a pool
profile cannot be, and the schema admits only inline entries — a reference is
not a rejected input but an unrepresentable one.

local/binding/set is context-callable where its pool counterpart is not,
because both objects it names live below the boundary. Its one load-bearing
obligation is the refusal: a profileId naming a POOL profile must be refused,
because resolving it would let a context-scoped caller bind the holder's
composition and read it back through a disclosure it requests of itself.

Local profiles are correlation-indexed like any other. The naive
implementation that skips them loses the guard exactly where a human most
needs it — a throwaway identity is precisely where somebody reuses a real
value.

Both binding sets regenerated; conformance checks 401 specs against 401 TS
and 396 Rust modules, all agreeing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(persona): rename persona/persona/list to persona/binding/list

The nested slug generated `pub mod persona;` inside module `persona`, which
clippy rejects as module_inception — caught by CI because I ran cargo check
locally rather than clippy with -D warnings.

The slug was the defect rather than the lint. What the task returns is one
row per binding — persona DID, whether bound, the profile's label, a claim
count — so it is binding/get in the plural and belongs beside it. That also
removes a doubled path segment that read badly in every URI it appeared in.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: fix(rooms/owner): a host cannot see the MLS group, so stop implying it can
body:
Both tasks in #359 required a host to check that a party is a member of the room's group. **A host holds no roster and no group state**, so neither check was implementable as written.

Found while starting the implementation — which is what implementation is for.

## `claim` gains a `presentation`

The host has exactly one membership signal available: the **VMC the room itself issued**. The claim payload didn't ask for it, so condition 3 was unimplementable *and* the claimant's own standing went unverified. It's now required, and it's the same presentation every other room task carries.

The spec is also exact about what that proxy is worth: a party removed from the MLS group while still holding an unexpired VMC would pass this check. That gap closes by revoking the credential — the room's job, not the host's. Better said than implied.

## `transfer` moves the obligation to whoever can discharge it

The incoming owner isn't the party making the request, presents nothing, and may be someone the host has never seen. "MUST refuse if not a member" asked a host to judge a third party from no evidence.

The requirement now sits with the **transferring owner**, who *can* see the group. A host that can independently establish non-membership **MAY** still refuse; one that cannot **MUST NOT** invent a check it has no basis for, and **MUST NOT** treat its own ignorance as evidence.

That last clause matters: without it, the safe-looking reading is "refuse when unsure", which would make every transfer fail on a host that is behaving correctly.

## Why this is the same rule as everywhere else

A host verifies what is presented to it, and a claim about a third party is not that. It's the boundary the whole room family draws — it just arrived from an unfamiliar direction here, because the natural way to write the condition put it on the wrong party.

## Verified

`npm run validate` (379 specs), `npm run check-bindings` (379 TS and 374 Rust modules agree), `cargo test`. Bindings regenerated on both sides.

title: feat(rooms/owner): transfer and claim, so a room outlives one person
body:
§10 of the data-rooms design was the last part with no specification.

Ownership there is **load-bearing for liveness, not just administration**: a room's owner is its sole committer, so a room with no reachable owner cannot advance an epoch, cannot be renewed, and lapses to read-only on the `rooms/epoch/mint` schedule. Without succession, one person becoming unreachable ends a shared space.

## Two tasks, not one with a flag

They end the same way and differ in everything else:

| | `transfer` | `claim` |
|---|---|---|
| initiated by | the outgoing owner | the incoming one |
| authorized by | the owner's own `admin` chain | a nomination the owner issued earlier |
| requires the room to be | anything | **dormant** |
| the outgoing owner is | present | not |

Collapsing them would mean either a transfer that waits for the room to lapse, or a claim that works while the owner is still renewing. Both are wrong.

## There is deliberately no `nominate` task

A nomination is a credential the room issues and the claimant presents — the same shape as an invitation, for the same reason. A host keeping a roster of successors would hold part of the room's authority structure, and the room could no longer move hosts without rebuilding it.

The consequence is worth stating: to a host, *"this room has no successor"* and *"the successor has not claimed yet"* are the same observation. That's fine — both resolve identically when retention runs out.

## A claim is an act, never an automatic promotion

Not ceremony. An automatic promotion is an ownership change **nobody performed**: no actor to audit, no moment to point at, and an owner who returns finds the room changed hands with no event to examine.

**Three conditions, all required**, each closing a different route to a takeover:

1. **A nomination the room itself issued**, naming this claimant. The owner decided in advance; the host checks a decision rather than making one.
2. **The room is dormant** — not merely lapsed. An epoch expiring is often somebody on holiday; a room still unrenewed after the grace window is a room whose owner has stopped.
3. **The claimant is already a member.** A successor who can't commit inherits a room they can't renew — the one thing ownership exists to do.

**Renewing cancels a pending claim**, and that's the property worth noticing: *the defence against a hostile claim is the same act as ordinary use*. An owner who was merely away fixes it by doing what they'd have done anyway — nothing revoked, no dispute raised.

## Three things the Security sections say plainly

**A transfer does not remove the outgoing owner.** They keep whatever their credentials confer, usually still `admin`. Handing over and leaving are two further acts, and a surface implying otherwise would leave someone with standing they believed they'd given up.

**Every credential stays valid**, because the room's identifier doesn't change. That's the whole reason a room has an identifier of its own rather than borrowing its owner's — one that belonged to a person would have to be rebuilt every time a person moved on.

**The host is not an arbiter.** It records what an authorized party told it. Ownership of an identifier is settled by whoever controls that identifier — the DID's own controller and its witnesses — not by a service that stores ciphertext.

## Verified

`npm run validate` (379 specs, every conformance sweep clean), `npm run check-bindings` (379 TS and 374 Rust modules agree), `cargo test`, `tsc --noEmit`, 79 TS tests. Bindings regenerated on both sides.

title: feat(rooms): a VTA joins a room, keeps up, and opens what it holds
body:
Implements `rooms/keys/{key-package,welcome,commit,open}` — the delivery flow specified in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#355 and the decryption oracle from #349, on the custody layer from #1248.

**This is the piece that makes a data room readable by an agent that never holds a key.**

## Four tasks, four different gates — and only one is a capability

| | authorized by |
|---|---|
| `key-package` | an invitation — minting retains a private key, so a VTA that minted for anyone is one anyone can fill |
| `welcome` | that same invitation, **consumed** |
| `commit` | the group itself — MLS authenticates the committer as a member of the group we already hold |
| `open` | `Capability::RoomOpen` |

The asymmetry is the point. The delivery three are *inbound* — a room's owner reaching this VTA — and an ACL of ours has no opinion about who a room's owner is. `commit` especially: a list we kept would be this service deciding who may commit to a room it isn't part of. Only `open` is our own principal's agent asking us to decrypt.

## The invitation is what makes a Welcome acceptable

A Welcome carries a **group's secrets**, so anyone able to reach a VTA could otherwise push group state into it. §4.1 already said joining is consent and the VIC is the artefact; this is where that stops being ceremonial.

Five checks, none optional — it parses as an invitation, its proof verifies, the issuer is the room, the subject is us, and it's live and unspent. Dropping any one leaves a way in. `VerifiedInvitation` is constructible only by the verifier, so a caller can't reach consumption with something nobody checked.

**Consumed only after the join succeeds.** Burning it on a Welcome that then failed to process would strand the member: invitation spent, not in the room.

**Joining twice is refused, not merged.** Two group states for one room is a condition nothing downstream can resolve — `open` has no way to choose, and choosing wrong returns "did not open" for a record the member can plainly see.

## A missed commit says so

`open` reports **which epoch the VTA holds** when a record is sealed under a later one. A member who missed a commit is stuck at their last epoch, and the raw symptom is "this record does not open" — which reads like corruption. Naming the epoch turns it into "a commit has not been delivered", which an operator can act on.

## Two keyspaces, both `Cascade`

`room_groups` holds group secrets and belongs at the same protection level as the key store. `room_invitations` **outlives the groups it admitted**: while the member exists, a consumed invitation must survive leaving a room, or the same invitation would work twice.

## Four censuses, and the retry one earned its keep

- **MCP guard** — `open` and `welcome` are `Sensitive` (plaintext out, key material in); `key-package` and `commit` are ordinary mutations.
- **Retry safety** — four *different* answers, which is a good sign the classification is real: `open` is `ReadOnly`; `commit` is `RetrySafe` because the spec made replay a no-op precisely so delivery could retry; `key-package` and `welcome` are `Keyed` — one leaves a second private half behind, the other can't tell a lost reply from a completed join.
- Conformance witnesses and the canonical-namespace list.

## A note on timing

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.17.8 landed mid-build carrying #351, #354 and #355 — so all four request types are **generated** rather than hand-written, and the debt census that would otherwise have blocked three of them is satisfied at the source rather than by an allowlist entry.

## Verified

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features` clean; `cargo test --workspace` with no failures, including all `vta-service` trust-task censuses.

title: docs: base every example on the registered acl/change-role task
body:
## Why

The framework illustrates itself with `kyc-handoff/1.0` — in the Abstract and in five worked examples. That slug has never been registered.

It is not an inert placeholder. `https://trusttasks.org/spec/kyc-handoff/1.0` is a live URL: the registry site serves its SPA for any `/spec/` path, and its spec page fell back to the first entry in the registry when a slug did not resolve. Following the link in the Abstract therefore rendered a complete, confident page for **ACL — Change Role** under a `kyc-handoff` URL. (The registry repo's companion PR makes that route render a not-found page instead.)

Two further costs:

- **The examples had no check.** The registry build validates every fenced JSON block against the framework envelope schema for the target framework version of the spec its `type` names. A payload naming a slug with no published schema is structurally unverifiable — so the framework's own worked examples were the least-checked JSON in the ecosystem.
- **One example was non-conforming.** The extended-code example answered an ACL request with a `kyc-handoff:`-namespaced code, which *Extension by Individual Trust Task Specifications* forbids in the same breath as it defines namespacing ("the namespace **MUST NOT** be the slug of a related or referenced specification").

## What changed

Examples 1–6 and Appendix A now use `acl/change-role/0.1`, a registered specification:

- Payload members are the ones its schema defines (`subject`, `fromRole`, `toRole`); Appendix A reproduces its actual front matter, its published `payload.schema.json`, and the two error codes it declares with their real `details` shapes.
- The examples share one cast (`org.example` → `maintainer.example`, subject `bob.example`) and one coherent thread: Example 1's document expires and draws the `expired` error of Example 5; Example 4's proof-less request draws `proofRequired`, which is now *correct* rather than incidental, because the specification declares `proof` REQUIRED.
- The extended-code example uses `acl/change-role:roleNotRecognized` — namespaced under the emitting slug, as rule 1 requires.
- Where the registered spec cannot support an illustration, the prose says so: Example 2 notes that `acl/change-role` publishes no JSON-LD context and that the entry shows *where* one would appear; Example 3 notes its `proof` is omitted for brevity.
- The slug-grammar bullet and the discovery examples name registered slugs (`trust-task-discovery`, `consent/request`).

Prose that mentions KYC as a *kind of work* ("a KYC handoff, a consent grant, a payment commitment") is untouched — only identifiers that look resolvable changed.

## Verification

- `npm run render` succeeds; the rendered `docs/index.html` contains no `kyc-handoff`.
- Every example payload in `spec/` validated against the published `acl/change-role/0.1` schema (`$ref`s resolved off disk) — 8 examples, 0 failures.

## Companion

trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#356 carries the identical change to that repo's copy of `SPEC.md`, plus the registry-site fix and the library examples that used the same invented slug.

## Why

`https://trusttasks.org/spec/kyc-handoff/1.0` appears in the Abstract and in five worked examples of `SPEC.md`, in both READMEs, in the loopback example and across the framework unit tests. It has never been a registered slug.

The same fallback fired for a known slug at an unknown version (`/spec/acl/grant/9.9`).

Two further costs of an invented slug:

- **Nothing could check the examples.** `checkExampleDocuments()` validates every fenced JSON block against the framework envelope schema, but a payload naming a slug with no published schema is structurally unverifiable.
- **One example was non-conforming.** The `trust-task-error` extended-code example answered an ACL request with a `kyc-handoff:`-namespaced code — which §8.5 forbids in the same breath as it defines namespacing ("the namespace **MUST NOT** be the slug of a related or referenced specification").

## What changed

**Examples → `acl/change-role/0.1`.** SPEC.md Examples 1–6 and Appendix A now use the registered task, sharing one cast (`org.example` → `maintainer.example`, subject `bob.example`) and one coherent thread: Example 1's document expires and draws the `expired` error of Example 5; Example 4's proof-less request draws `proofRequired`, which is now *correct* because the spec declares `proof` REQUIRED. Generated Rust bindings regenerated accordingly (`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen`, `npm run build-ts-bindings`); no schema changed, so no version folder was added.

**The library** — quickstart, `examples/loopback.rs`, and every unit test that used the slug as an arbitrary string. The loopback example now demonstrates the spec's own optimistic-concurrency failure with a §8.5 extended code rather than a bare `taskFailed`. Parser tests that specifically needed a *single-segment* slug use `trust-task-discovery` / `trust-task-control`, which are also real.

**`SpecPage` is strict.** No `|| TT_TASKS[0]`. An unregistered slug, or a known slug at an unknown version, renders a not-found page that offers the versions that do exist — the behaviour `BindingSpecPage` and `CeremonyPage` already had, with comments naming this exact failure. The lookup moved into a hook-free wrapper so a route that stops resolving (back/forward onto a stale URL) unmounts the detail view rather than changing a mounted component's hook count, which would have traded a silent wrong render for a white screen.

English prose that merely mentions KYC as a kind of work is untouched; only identifiers that look resolvable changed.

## Verification

docs: base every example on the registered acl/change-role task (#356)

SPEC.md, both READMEs, the loopback example and the framework unit tests
all illustrated themselves with `kyc-handoff/1.0`, a slug that has never
been registered. Three consequences, in increasing order of cost:

- `https://trusttasks.org/spec/kyc-handoff/1.0` is a live URL in the
  Abstract and in five worked examples. It resolves — the registry site
  serves the SPA for any /spec/ path — and rendered `acl/change-role`,
  the alphabetically first entry, because SpecPage fell back to
  `TT_TASKS[0]` for an unresolvable slug. A reader following the URL in
  §1 got a complete, confident page for a different task.
- No example could be checked against anything. The build validates every
  fenced JSON block against the framework envelope schema; a payload
  naming a slug with no schema was structurally unverifiable.
- The `trust-task-error` extended-code example was non-conforming: it
  answered an ACL request with a `kyc-handoff:`-namespaced code, which
  §8.5 forbids in the same breath as it defines namespacing.

Everything now names `acl/change-role/0.1`, whose payloads validate
against its published schema, whose error codes are the two it declares,
and whose REQUIRED `proof` the examples honour. Appendix A is reproduced
from that registry entry rather than invented. The framework parser tests
that used the slug as an arbitrary string now use real ones —
`trust-task-discovery` and `trust-task-control` where a single-segment
slug is the point.

SpecPage is strict as a result: an unregistered slug, or a known slug at
an unknown version, renders a not-found page offering the versions that
do exist, the way BindingSpecPage and CeremonyPage already did. The
lookup moved into a hook-free wrapper so a route that stops resolving
unmounts the detail view rather than changing a mounted component's hook
count.

title: feat(rp-login): log in as Trust Tasks, over whichever transport the RP advertises
body:
## The client half of affinidi-webvh-service#171

`loginDidcomm` sent a bespoke DIDComm message and the RP authenticated on the **authcrypt sender**, reading nothing from the body. Three consequences, none visible from the client:

- it existed on **one transport** — a wallet connected over TSP could not use it;
- the RP applied a **different rule** than it applies over HTTPS, where the canonical challenge-response holds;
- and `challenge`, which `auth/authenticate/0.1` declares REQUIRED, was **a field nobody read**.

That last one matters most. A challenge that is never checked isn't a weaker guarantee than one that is — it's no guarantee, and the wire looked identical either way.

Login is now `auth/challenge/0.1` → `auth/authenticate/0.1` over a `TrustTaskSender`. It runs on TSP, DIDComm or REST by what the RP publishes, and the RP applies one rule on all three.

## Why one rule works across three transports

The channel signs every outbound document (`signOutboundTask`, SPEC §7.2 item 7a), and the RP establishes the caller from that signature — binding it to the asserted `issuer`, or filling the issuer from the authenticated transport when the document asserts none.

Possession of a challenge proves nothing alone. Possession **plus a signature over a document carrying it** proves control of the VID. The guarantee rides with the document, not the pipe — which is precisely why it doesn't need three implementations.

## `buildVtaSession` builds the RP session unchanged

It resolves whatever services the peer publishes and orders them TSP > DIDComm > REST. Nothing in it was ever VTA-specific but the name. A caller-supplied `mediatorDid` still seeds the DIDComm channel, because a bare `did:peer` RP has no document to resolve and the page naming one is answering for it.

## Two details worth review attention

- **The granted scope is reported, not the requested one.** The task says the issued bundle's `scope` MAY be a subset; echoing the request back would tell the caller it holds capabilities it doesn't. A test pins this.
- **A signing identity that isn't the holder is refused before anything is sent.** The proof is the authentication, so a signature by another key authenticates nobody — and the RP's answer for that is an opaque `permissionDenied` that says nothing about the cause being local. This is the one place that knows.

A refused *challenge* and a refused *authenticate* stay distinct: the first means the RP won't talk to this DID at all (no ACL entry, rate limited), the second that the challenge was rejected (expired, replayed, wrong subject). Those want different things from a caller, so they surface differently rather than collapsing into "login failed".

## Tests

`rp-login.trust-task.mjs` (5): the challenge's exact values are what get spent on the authenticate; the session reports the RP's granted scope rather than the request; a refresh token is omitted rather than invented; a non-holder signer is refused with nothing reaching the RP; a refused challenge surfaces as itself and does **not** go on to authenticate.

622 workspace tests green, lint and build clean, `dist/background.js` still a single bundle.

## Deployment ordering

**Requires an RP at affinidi-webvh-service#171** — merged, and it needs deploying before this is relied on. `loginViaDidcomm` is left in place and the RP's bespoke route still exists, so that remains the fallback until it's retired.

## Now driveable

This is the first thing in this run that can be exercised end to end while it's written: `npm run login-harness --workspace @openvtc/pnm-demo-rp` against a local `did-hosting-control`, challenge → authenticate over DIDComm, then flip `preferTsp` and watch the same flow take the TSP channel. That's the check I'd want before merging.

title: test(vault): drive the release paths against a VTA that can pack
body:
**Coverage 102 → 105 of 109 (96%).** First of the stacked harness PRs.

`vault/{release,proxy-login,sign-trust-task}` seal their answer into a DIDComm envelope addressed to the caller, so the VTA needs an ATM with real secrets to pack with. The in-process fixture has none — `release` stops at `ATM not configured`, and an offline ATM gets as far as packing and no further (I tried, in #1151, and took it back out).

`MockVta::start_with_transports` was already there and **unused**: a real embedded mediator, a `did:peer:2` VTA advertising DIDComm and TSP, and the secrets behind it. That is the whole unlock.

The test does **not** open the sealed answer, and does not need to. Packing it is the half that was untested, and the response document's own type is what the conformance gate reads.

## Each refusal along the way was the operation being right

- **`proxy-login` really does log in.** It refused a password entry with no `loginConfig` (`notProxyable`, pointing at `vault/release` instead), then refused the third party's 405. So there is a wiremock stand-in for the third party now — denying it somewhere to log in would have tested the failure path and called it coverage.
- **`sign-trust-task` refuses a password entry outright** (`notSignable`): there is no principal to sign as. Only the DID-bearing secret kinds carry one, so it gets its own entry with a `DidSelfIssued` secret, whose principal is the VTA's own DID — the only identity this fixture holds a key for.
- And the envelope's `issuer` must equal that principal (`envelopeIssuerMismatch`). The VTA signs *as* the principal, so a document claiming a different issuer would carry a signature contradicting it.

## Four left

`passkey-vms/{enroll-submit,revoke}` share a blocker — revoke refuses a fragment the document does not carry, and enrolling needs an authenticator attestation over `enroll-challenge`'s nonce. `credential-exchange/pending/approve` needs a held credential matching the deferred query. `webvh/dids/register-with-server` needs a serverless DID with a valid log.

Next PRs in the stack, one harness at a time.

## Verification

- `vta-service --all-features`: **0 failed**, zero response-conformance violations
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets`: exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: exit 0
- `TRUST-TASK RESPONSE COVERAGE 105/109 (96%)`

title: feat(credentials)!: move vta/credentials/issue to 0.2
body:
The last family behind its latest published spec. Verified against `website/registry.json` (the authoritative list, rather than the schema files on disk — a family can be registered without shipping a schema): **every other implemented family is already on the newest published version.**

```
== BEHIND LATEST (registry.json, 297 families) ==
  vta/credentials/issue: code 0.1 -> latest 0.2   (published: 0.1,0.2)
```

### What actually changed

0.1 and 0.2 have **identical payloads**. The response differs only in how it's written — 0.2 composes from `credentials/_shared/0.2`'s `IssuedCredentialBase` instead of restating the members inline, which is what stops the two drifting. The composition brings one new member, `issuedAt`.

That member costs nothing to fill: `IssuedCredentialRecord` has carried `issued_at` since the family existed, and 0.1 simply had nowhere to put it — the value was being computed, stored, and then dropped on the way out. It stays `Option` on our side because the shared definition declares it optional (a response without it is schema-valid and must still deserialize), but the VTA always sends it.

### What the sweep caught

The conformance sweep's drifted-witness check asserts the generated type rejects an unknown member. 0.2's response type does not:

| | 0.1 | 0.2 |
|---|---|---|
| schema closes with | `additionalProperties: false` | `unevaluatedProperties: false` |
| generated struct | `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` | *(nothing)* |

Closing a *composed* object requires `unevaluatedProperties` — `additionalProperties` is evaluated per-subschema and would reject the `allOf`-supplied members — and `trust-tasks-codegen` maps only `additionalProperties: false` onto `deny_unknown_fields`.

**The wire is unaffected.** The schema itself is strict, so `validate_payload` still rejects the unknown member. What's lost is the *type-level* guard, which makes the drifted-witness check pass vacuously. Rather than let it give false assurance, it's recorded in a new `PERMISSIVE_GENERATED_TYPE` list with its reason and skipped. Deleting the entry re-arms the check.

Only two published schemas use this pattern today (`vta/credentials/issue/0.2` and `credentials/_shared/0.2`), but it's the composition style the registry is moving toward, so the codegen fix matters. Following up on `trust-tasks-rs` separately.

`cargo test -p vta-service --all-features` green, clippy 0.

title: fix(vtc): surface the daemon's message when wallet sign-in fails
body:
The admin console's VTA-proxied SIOP login threw on the status code alone — `/auth/challenge failed (403)` — and discarded the response body, which is where the daemon says what actually went wrong. `Login.tsx` renders that message verbatim in the sign-in error card, so the operator got a number and nothing else.

403 is the ambiguous one. `handle_challenge`'s second gate is `check_acl`, and `resolve_auth_role` (`vtc-service/src/acl/storage.rs:72`) answers it three different ways:

| cause | message |
|---|---|
| no ACL row for the DID | `forbidden: DID not in ACL: <did>` |
| row present, past its expiry | `forbidden: ACL entry expired: <did>` |
| row present, role is not `Admin` | `forbidden: DID is not permitted to authenticate on this VTC` |

The distinction exists only in the body, so diagnosing a failed sign-in meant reading the daemon log — or the source. Worth noting the DID that needs the row is the chosen vault entry's **`principalDid`**, not the VTA's own DID; `loginWithWalletProxy` posts that as the challenge subject.

## Change

The message extraction `request()` already did privately is now `daemonErrorMessage()`, exported from `lib/api.ts` and used by both. The wallet path cannot route through `request()` itself: it deliberately uses raw `fetch` so it sends no `X-CSRF-Token` and does not fire `vtc-session-expired` mid-ceremony. Sharing the helper keeps one implementation of the `{ error | message }` shape rather than a second copy that can drift from `AppError`.

The messages stay as terse as they were on the unauthenticated path — this forwards what the daemon already chose to say (P0.16 keeps it free of role names and serde internals), it does not widen it.

An operator now reads:

```
/auth/challenge failed (403): forbidden: DID not in ACL: did:key:z...
```

## Scope

Both throw sites in `loginWithWalletProxy` (`/auth/challenge` and `/auth/`). `Install.tsx` has three more bare-status toasts on the install ceremony — same shape, different flow, left alone here.

## Verification

- `npm run lint` (`wire:check` + `tsc -b --noEmit`) — clean
- `npm run build` — clean

title: feat(transports): report the transport actually in use, and why one is not
body:
## The incident this came from

A user reported two warnings and a CORS error in `chrome://extensions`:

```
[pnm tsp] skipping TSP channel: Failed to fetch
[pnm didcomm] skipping DIDComm channel: Failed to fetch
Access to fetch at 'https://mediator.…/mediator/v1/authenticate/challenge'
from origin 'chrome-extension://…' has been blocked by CORS policy
```

They had correctly allowlisted the extension on their **VTA** — which is why REST still worked. The refusal was from the **mediator**, a different service they did not operate. Diagnosing it required leaving the wallet entirely and running `curl` against someone else's server, and `curl` is exactly the tool that *cannot* reproduce it: a terminal sends no `Origin` header, so the endpoint answers perfectly and the operator concludes nothing is wrong.

Meanwhile the wallet had silently fallen back to REST, its inbox was dark, and the status line was confidently displaying **TSP**.

## Three linked defects

### 1. Advertisement is not availability

`buildVtaSession` skips a channel whose mediator it cannot reach and falls through to the next — but `activeTransport` derived its answer from the stored connection alone, so the UI named transports that had never carried a byte. The `transports.ts` header already said a status display that disagrees with the router "is worse than none"; it was that.

`activeTransport` now takes a `TransportHealth` recorded by `buildVtaSession` at the two places that actually decide, and skips a `down` transport exactly as the session does.

Three states, and the third is load-bearing:

| state | meaning |
|---|---|
| `up` | positive evidence — for TSP/DIDComm a completed mediator handshake and an open socket |
| `down` | skipped, with a diagnosed reason |
| `unknown` | **REST**: a `RestChannel` is built from a URL without contacting anything, so construction proves nothing |

Marking a constructed REST channel `up` would reintroduce the same overconfidence one layer down. `unknown` is not a failure and never removes REST from selection.

With nothing observed yet the answer is **unchanged** — only the label moves, from "Transport in use" to "Transport expected".

### 2. A CORS refusal is unreadable, so it is inferred

Chrome hands JS a bare `TypeError: Failed to fetch` for a policy refusal, a dead host and a DNS failure alike. The actual reason goes to the devtools console and nowhere an extension can read — it cannot be recovered from the exception, so `transport-diagnosis.ts` infers it from one bit instead:

> a request that fails at the network layer, against a host that answers an opaque (`mode: "no-cors"`) request a moment later, was refused by browser **policy**, not by the network.

Errors are discriminated **structurally** — `TypeError`, `DOMException.name === "TimeoutError"` — never on message text (R3.7). Codes: `origin-not-allowed`, `unreachable`, `timeout`, `rejected`, `unknown`.

The remediation names the mediator's own config key and **deliberately never suggests a host permission** (there is a test asserting it doesn't). A grant would exempt the REST handshake but not the WebSocket upgrade, which the mediator checks server-side against the same policy — a half-fix that sends people down the wrong path is worse than no suggestion.

### 3. The inbox has its own row

"Connected" and "can be reached" are different states, and only the second decides whether an approval request ever arrives (R7.2). A wallet that has fallen back to REST looks entirely healthy on the operating row while nothing can be pushed to it. The state was already tracked in `mediatorState`; it just had no UI.

## The self-test

`runDiagnostics` walks the chain and names the broken link, from the wallet's own origin — the only place the answer is true. Read-only throughout: nothing authenticates, mutates or spends a credential, because a diagnostic that changes state is one people are afraid to run.

`checkCorsReachable` uses a plain `GET` against the *same* endpoint that fails: no custom headers means no preflight, so the browser checks `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the actual response and a refusal surfaces exactly as it does on the real path. **Any status is a pass** — a `405` from a POST-only auth route proves the origin was allowed, which is the only question. Swapping it for a health endpoint would test a different policy than the one that breaks.

Output is plain text, not Markdown, because it gets pasted into chat clients and issue trackers that each render differently — and it carries the extension origin verbatim, since that is the one string the recipient must copy exactly:

```
[FAIL] TSP+DIDComm mediator accepts this wallet's origin
       The mediator at https://mediator.example is up and answering, but
       refused this request. …
       code: mediator/origin-not-allowed
       fix: Whoever operates this mediator needs to add the origin to
       `[security] cors_allow_origin` in its `mediator.toml` and restart it. …
```

## Also

Corrects the claim in `host-permissions.ts` that the mediator is "not subject to CORS". Its WebSocket is not; the auth handshake that must precede it is two ordinary `fetch` calls, and that is what fails. That comment is why the mediator sat outside the one system built for this problem.

`CLAUDE.md` gains both invariants, with what breaks them.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] `npm run lint` clean (`tsc -b`, not `--noEmit`)
- [x] `npm run build` clean
- [x] `npm test` — 646 tests, 0 failures (31 new)
- [x] MV3 invariants: `dist/background.js` single bundle, no dynamic `import()`, no `chrome.cookies`, no static `content_scripts`, no `cookies` permission
- [x] Module boundaries + entry points unchanged (core untouched)
- [x] R1.2 — every new fetch bounded via `withFetchTimeout` at the injection point
- [x] R3.7 — new codes are stable constants; no matching on message text
- [x] New runtime message is **not** in `PAGE_FACING_RUNTIME_TYPES` — which of a user's transports work is wallet diagnostics, not something an RP page should enumerate

title: fix(secure-store): store the profile secret as one line, not pretty JSON
body:
## What was wrong

Saving a profile on Linux corrupted the user's whole login keyring — every
secret in the collection, not just the OpenVTC one. From the daemon log:

```
keyring was in an invalid or unrecognized format: .../Default_keyring.keyring
```

`SecuredConfig::save` wrote the envelope with `serde_json::to_string_pretty`,
so the secret handed to the Secret Service contained real newlines.
gnome-keyring writes an item's secret into its `.keyring` file verbatim but
reads it back through GKeyFile *unescaping*, so those newlines came back as
extra lines of the file and made the whole file unparseable.

The cascade from there is worse than a lost entry: with no readable default
collection, the next application's unlock prompt is really a *create a new
keyring* prompt. Answer it and you get a fresh `Default_Keyring.keyring`, the
`default` pointer repointed at it, and the real keyring orphaned.

macOS and Windows treat a secret as opaque bytes, so a formatting choice that
had no reader survived this long. Only the Secret Service backend parses it.

## The fix

One encoder, `encode_blob`, is now the only thing that produces the bytes the
credential store sees: compact single-line JSON. It also refuses to emit a
secret containing a line break, a control character, a backslash, or any
non-ASCII byte — the envelope's payloads are all BASE64URL, so anything else
is a bug on our side, and the save fails loudly instead of corrupting a
keyring quietly.

Existing entries are unaffected on read: serde ignores the old whitespace, so
a profile written by an earlier build loads and is rewritten single-line on
its next save.

## Recovery for anyone already hit

The data is orphaned, not destroyed. `docs/secured-configuration-management.md`
gains the steps: stop the daemon, copy `~/.local/share/keyrings/`, rejoin or
delete the item whose secret spills across lines, point `default` back at the
original keyring.

## Tests

- `encoded_blob_is_a_single_line` — all three envelope variants, over payloads
  chosen to be awkward (`0xff`, `0x00`, `0x0a`): no line break, printable
  ASCII only, no backslash, and still parses as the envelope the loader
  expects.
- `encode_blob_refuses_a_non_round_trippable_secret` — a payload that isn't
  base64 fails the save with `SecureStoreFault::Corrupt`.

Local gates green: `cargo fmt --check`, `clippy --workspace --all-targets`,
`test --workspace`, `test --workspace -- --ignored` (the MockVta/mediator
e2es), and `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`.

title: ci(publish): skip crates already on crates.io so a run is resumable
body:
Publishing three crates is not atomic. An earlier one uploads, a later one
fails, and the tag has half-published — which is exactly what v0.4.7 did:
`cargo publish` rejected `verify-trust` because it takes `trql-client` by
`git` with no version requirement, after `vgi-core` 0.4.7 had already gone
up. crates.io now holds vgi-core 0.4.7 against verify-trust and did-git-sign
0.4.6.

Before this change there was no way back. Re-running the tag dies on "crate
version is already uploaded" for the crate that did land, so finishing the
release meant bumping every crate to a version none of them needed, purely to
get past a name that was already correct.

Each crate is now checked against the sparse index for its workspace version
first and skipped if it is there, so a re-run finishes whatever the failed run
started. The check reads index.crates.io directly rather than parsing cargo's
error text, which is not a stable interface. A 404 — a name that has never
been published — is a clean "not published" and falls through to publishing,
so a brand-new crate is unaffected.

Verified against the live index: vgi-core 0.4.7 reports as already published
while verify-trust and did-git-sign 0.4.7 do not, which is precisely the
resume this is for.
